Zur Charakteristik deshinduistischen Pantheons

A. J. Syrkin(Moskau)

Zusammenfassung

Der Verfasser behauptet,dass die Untersuchungen im Bereiche einzelner Zeichensysteme (insbesonderemythologischer und ritueller Art) in den letzten Jahren wahlgemäss durchdie Gegenüberstellung einiger differentieller Kennzeichen, die in diesenSystemen die semantischen Felder bilden und in den Funktionen gewisser Elementareinheitenzutage treten, charakterisiert werden. Von den Tendenzen einer ambivalentenBeschreibung von Gottheiten in den Kulttexten rühren auch dieBeobachtungen und Vermerke des Verfassers bezüglich der Hauptgottheitendes hinduistischen (vor allem vedischen) Pantheons her. Gemäss derBehauptung des Verfassers sei der Frage nach der Ambivalenz der Funktionen derGottheiten in der Unmenge der den Hinduismus und Vedaismus betreffendenLiteratur bis jetzt noch keine erschöpfende Behandlung zuteil geworden.

\n

text: The legend of Kṛṣṇaand Rādhā is perhaps unsurpassed in term of the extent of itsinfluence upon different spheres of Indian culture: belles lettres, theatre,painting, etc.1 Its most famousembodiment is the «Gitagovinda» of Jayadeva (G.) — a peculiar combinationof the lyric and the dramatic genres, which determined to a large degree thecharacter of subsequent trends in later Indian (primarily Bengali) devotionalliterature and provoked scores of imitations and commentaries.The theme of the poem isthe love between Kṛṣṇa (avatāra of Viṣṇu)and the cowherdess Rādhā. Jayadeva himself calls his work a sequenceof sweet and tender words of love (1.3madhurakomalakāntapadāvalīm)2.And, indeed, the sphere of amorous relations is represented here in itsfullest. Independently of their possible interpretation, the scenes of G. areimbued with sensuality, constituting an evident parallel to analogous classicalIndian texts (including special didactic treatises)3. It rings quite naturally when the last verses of G.pronounce the poem a source for judging the essence of the passion of love(12.26: śṛñgāravivekatattva: cf. 12.28: śṛñgārasāraṃ).In fact, every verse beginning with III (after the first two introductoryincantations) is dedicated here to describing the different stages of love: thelanguor of Rādhā (1.27; 2.10; 20), the games played by Kṛṣṇawith Cowherdesses (1.28 sq., 38 sq., 2.2 sq.), his repentance(3.1 sq.), the new sorrows of the amorous Rādhā (4.2 sq.,11 sq.), the languor of Kṛṣṇa (5.2 sq.),Rādhā’s readiness for a rendezvous (6.2 sq.), her nightlylamentations (7.2 sq.), the scenes of Kṛṣṇa’sunfaithfulness jealously imagined by her (7.31 sq.), her wrath against Kṛṣṇa(8.1 sq.), his craving forgiveness (10.1 sq.), his love rapture andRādhā’s efforts to overcome bashfulness (11.24 sq.; 32 sq.;12.2 sq.), and, finally, the joys of their union (12.10 sq.) Theenumeration of Rādhā’s emotional states, which gradually intensify upto the point of fainting (4.19; 11.10; cf. 4.7) is reminiscent of the tenfoldscale traditional in classical Sanskrit literature — cf.Vetālapañcaviṃśatikā, rec. Śivadāsa, 16;Vātsyayāna’s Kāmasūtra (K) 40.5 etc. Another typicaldevice is the systematic use of Rādhā’s characteristics in shortprosaic formulas concluding some parts of G. According to these formulas(which differ in different variants) the part in question is dedicated to thedescription of abhisārikā (a woman going to a rendezvous), vāsakasajjā(a woman ready to accept her lover), etc. — here G. likewise reflectsfamiliar classification of a heroine’s slates found in Sanskrit treatises ondramatic art: e. g. Bharata’s Nāṭyaśāstra XXII,199–206; Dhanañjaya’s Daśarūpa II, 24–27 etc.4. A traditional notion of «love play»(līlā, krīḍa)5,as well as its accessories (music, songs, dances) is very importanthere, — cf. for example, reminiscences of pañcama (I.40; literally«the fifth» — i.e. one of the rāgas associated with passionate love),rāsa (1.44; 2.2 — a certain cowherd’s dance traditionally believed tohave been invented by Kṛṣṇa), playing a pipe (vaṃśa —1.44; 2.2; 19; etc.; veṇu — 5.9), and so on. According to canonizedpoetic devices, heroes’ emotions are constantly accompanied by the cuckooing ofkokilas (Indian cuckoo — 1.28; 37, etc.), the humming of bees (1.29; 31;37; 5.4; 11.9), the waft of a spring breeze (1.28; 3.2; 5.2; 7.39; 41; 9.2),the fragrance of flowers (1.30; 33; 36; 3.2) etc. We find here some importantdetails of etiquette that also correspond to Indian erotological tradition;such as, for instance, the role of Rādhā’s girl friend(sahacarī, sakhī), who serves as an intermediary (dūti —7.30; cf. K. 5.47, etc.). She goes from one lover to another, conveys messagesof love, tells Kṛṣṇa about Rādhā’s state of mind(4.1 sq.; 6.1 sq.), encourages Rādhā (5.1 sq.;9.1 sq.; 11.1 sq.; 13 sq.), listens to their confessions, etc.Other widespread motifs in G. are the lovers’ quarrel (cf. K. 226 and in other traditions: Ovid, Arsamatoria. I.36; III, 1 sq.; idem, Amores, I.7.9; Lucianus, Asinus 9—10,etc.), comparing love to battle (7.13; 11.7; 12.10; 12), embellishment of thecouch (4.4; 5.10; 16), etc. Numerous analogies are connected with such detailsas coquettish glances (2.9; 3.12; 13; 15, etc. — cf. K. 27), embraces(1.45; 47; 49; 2.5; 6; 13; 3.8; 5.8 sq., etc.—K. 8), kisses (1.42;45; 2.4; 13; 16; 4.23; 5.18, etc. — K. 9), exclamations (cf.kūjita — 2.15; 7.17; sītkara — 4.9; 6.10; 12.15 — K. 15—16),scratches (2.15; 5.18; 8 4; 10.3 etc. — K. 10), bites (8.6; 10.3; 11;12.11; 13 — K. 11), etc.7.Different stages of the amorous union are depicted, beginning withRādhā’s timid approach to Kṛṣṇa’s bower and endingwith the latter’s attempts to restore his beloved’s toilet (cf. K.20.14) — see XI, XXIII, XXIV and the analogous description of Kṛṣṇa’sinfidelity in XIV, XV — including various «technical» details (e. g. puruṣāyita:5.12; 7.19 — cf. K. 17–18)8.At the same time a certain naturalism9is combined here with an undoubtedly psychological approach. Such is, forexample, the link between the lovers’ mood and the ambient odours, sounds andsights10. It is interestingthat Rādhā identifies herself with the object of her love (6.5:madhuripuraham). Another characteristic motif is subjugation in love: cf. theevidently masochistic words of Kṛṣṇāin XIX (10.3 sq.; 6.11; cf. 12.11)11.Theplace of G. in Indian culture leads us from the sphere of its immediatethematic to another aspect of investigation. Independently of the feelingof «secularity» (cf. below) that the poem evokes (this feeling is evidentenough to European and Indian scholars as well)12, the functioning of G. is inseparable from Vaiṣṇavabhakti. In the framework of this cult both the poem as a whole and its separatedetails (including highly naturalistic ones) were traditionally interpreted,not only by later generations, but evidently already by contemporaries13. Moreover, this is not only because oftraits of the author’s vishnuism (cf. the invocations to Kṛṣṇaconcluding each part of G.; the character of songs I and II beingvirtually hymns dedicated to Viṣṇu; motifs such as the annihilationof sins by Kṛṣṇa in 2.8; 7.20; 29; 12.24, etc.) — suchdigressions are typical for different genres of classical Indian literature.This approach derives from the symbolic perception of the poem as a whole. Thefirst reference directly suggesting such an interpretation is found at thebeginning of the third part (3.1) where we read that Kṛṣṇaleft the beautiful women of Vraja and placed in his bosomRādhā — a chain fettering the delusion of saṃsāra (saṃsāravāsanābaddhaśṛṅkhalām) — i.e., the world’sdelusions leading to a cycle of rebirth in this world. The mundane attachmentssymbolized by cowherdesses have here as their antithesis Rādhā —the supreme principle leading to freedom from worldly vanity. Ch. Lassenalready defined the Kṛṣṇa — Rādhā relationshipas the state of divine mind assuming a human appearance and absorbed in thecontemplation of the highest beauty (cf. 3.15: mānasaṃ tasyāṃlagna)14.On the other hand, Kṛṣṇahimself no less often appears in G. as the object of Rādhā’sadoration — (cf. for example, verses where she is absorbed in thecontemplation of her lover: 4.2 sq. bhāvanayā tvayilīnā; cf. also 4.19; 21; 6.10; 11 etc.)15. This motif presenting a counterpart to G. 3.1, givesgrounds for another interpretation that seems to be more widespread: theattitude of Rādhā to Kṛṣṇa symbolizes the cravingof the soul (a feminine principle) to unite with the Highest deity. Othercowherdesses may also symbolize the soul (not negative powers as in theprevious case) and the scene of the action-groves of Vṛndāvana —may symbolize the «field of consciousness»16.This symbolism, giving a certain equivocality to the content of G., wasobserved already by W. Jones17.At the same time various authors are inclined to stress that such symbolismbelongs only to the traditional interpretation of the poem18, while some see in G. a purelysecular lyric19.Considering the differentinterpretations of G., the scholar is certainly justified in emphasizingwhichever one he favours according to the aspect of his research. Theallegorical «sacral» interpretation is indisputable when the poem is studied inthe context of Vaiṣṇava tradition; its importance as a specimen ofa «secular» lyric is evident as well when we compare G. with other Sanskritlyrical texts or think of the immediate reaction of the readers staying outsidethe Kṛṣṇa cult. It must, however, be emphasized that in theframework of the cultural environment of G., the opposition of these twoaspects seems to be incorrect — it as if destroys «from without» thecharacter of its functioning that is specific to Indian culture. The poem wasevidently perceived by its audience as an indivisible fusion of sacred text andlove lyric, by no means demarcated as modern readers and researchers(especially non-Indian) are inclined to do. It is to be noted that theopposition of the «sacral» and the «secular» is not the same in modern Europeanand mediaeval Indian cultures20and the use of such a dichotomy can scarcely be of help here. We knowspecifically that within Hindu dogmatics love with its most sensuous aspectswas naturally combined with other aspects of life21 including the directly «sacral» (cf. the essentiallydifferent approach presented in the old European tradition — ancient Greekor later Christian)22.One can mention thewell-known system of the four life’s goals (caturartha, caturbhadra),suggesting the interaction of kāma (sensuous love) with artha, dharma andmokṣa including specifically the performance of ritual duties and therelinquishing of worldly attachments23.Sanskrit poetry presents an example of a deliberate union of love andresignation motifs (cf. for instance, a similar effect achieved by a refinedwordplay in Ramacandra’s Rasikarañjana)24. On the other hand, one must not forget the role of theerotic element in different religious trends of ancient and mediaeval India(see below)25. At the same timethe fact of G.’s ambiguous meaning (as we see, the equivoque is maintained alsowithin the framework of the «sacral» interpretation) seems to be natural forevery specimen of belles lettres (regardless of a possible connection with thereligious sphere of behaviour); it corresponds particularly to some importantprinciples of classical Indian poetics; cf. for example, the idea of twolevels: a level of the explicit or expressed (vācya) meaning and a levelof the implicit or «being manifested» (vyaṅgya) meaning (seeĀnandavardhana’s Dhvanyāloka III. 33, etc.). The devotionalinterpretation of the Rādhā — Kṛṣṇārelations can possibly be correlated here to the implicit meaning that is to beguessed.Thisinterpretation has numerous analogies in classical Indian literature — andnot only in Vaiṣṇava bhakti tradition. To begin with more ancientand oblique examples reflecting certain erotic traits of Hinduism at its veryearliest stages and touching rather the content and direct meaning of the poem,we may refer to Vedic hymns26 —cf. images of rain as a seminal fluid fertilizing the earth (ṚgvedaI.100.3; 128.3; III.55.17, V.83.4; Atharvaveda IV.15.11; VIII.7.21, etc.), ofHeaven and Earth as of Father and Mother (Rv. I.164.8; VI.70.2, etc.), ofcultivating the soil (Rv. V.56.3; Śatapathabrāhmaṇa XI.5.11,etc.). Certain functions of gods are also very typical — cf.characteristics of Agni (dampatī — Rv. V.3.2; jāra — Rv. X.11.6 etc.), Tvaṣṭar, Prajāpati, Viṣṇu (cf. Rv.X.184.1; Av V. 25.5 etc.; his functions develop in later cult including theconcept of avatāras, one of which is the hero of G.). Turning to Vedicritual27, one can mentionsacrificial fire, being produced by the friction of two sticks — an upperand a lower — with, respectively, male and female symbolism (cf. Rv.III.29.1; a later image from Bṛhadāraṇyaka up. IV.4.22, etc.),its relation to the altar (Vedi) with whom it represents, correspondingly, manand woman in union (Śatapathabrāhmaṇa I.2.5.15–16). Anothersimilar allegory was connected with the parts of the hand press for extractingsoma and the act of pressing itself (soma pavamāna — cf. Rv. I.28.2,etc.). In early Upaniṣads we find allegories that are more abstract andat the same time closer to G. — comparing the highest state ofillumination to the joy of love: «As a man when in the embrace of his belovedwife knows nothing without or within, so the person when in the embrace of theintelligent Self (Prajñenātmanā) knows nothing without orwithin» (Bṛhadāraṇyaka up. IV.3.21)28. The concept of Ātman and Brahmanas blissful joy (ānanda) is generally typical for Upaniṣads (cf. Kauṣītaki3.8; Taittirīya 3.6; Bṛhadāraṇyaka IV.3.8 sq.;Chāndogya IV.10.5; 7.28; VIII.4.2, etc.)29.Оn the other hand, we find here not only the sexualization of cult but also thesacralization of sex. Such is the deification of desire (kāma)already in Vedic texts (Rv. X.129.4; Av. III.21; 25; IX.2; XIX.52;Taittirīya brāhmaṇa II. 4.1, 10; 8.9.4; Taittirīyaāraṇyaka I.23.1, etc.) and in Upaniṣads (BṛhadāraṇyakaII.4.5, etc.)30. There areallegories here comparing the genitals to parts of the sacrificial altar (seeabove) and prescribing certain rites for obtaining desirable progeny (BṛhadāraṇyakaVI.2.13; 4.2 sq.; Chāndogya V.8 etc.). Another scope of examplesrelates to liṅgam and yoni worship in some Śivaite cults, intantrism (corresponding evidence can be traced back to Proto-Indian culture)31. It must be noted that sometimes(e. g. in such trends as śakti) it is difficult to delimit theseprocesses — sacralization and sexualization — since we can trace bothin the same passage — cf. example, a passage from BṛhadāraṇyakaII. 4.5; IV.5.6, where love for a husband, wife, sons, etc. finds itsonly justification in love for Ātman (ātmanas tu kāmāyasarvam priyam bhavati), an idea reflected in later trends of bhakti.We shall briefly referonly to some parallels akin to G., that can be explained within the context ofthe same tradition and partly by direct influence. The sensuous aspect of Kṛṣṇaworship is found in Vaiṣṇava texts preceding G. Suchtestimonies occur already in Bhagavatgītā (9.29), one can perceivethe further development of bhakti forms — from rather speculative to morepassionate — in Bhāgavata purāṇa (cf. X.29–33), whereparticularly passion (rati) appears as an intermediary between faith(śraddhā) and devotion (bhakti) (cf. III.25.25)32.There are many moreparallels in later Indian literature, some of them directly influenced byG. Several poems — by Kalyāna, Bhānudatta, Prabhākara,Vaṃśamaṇi, and others — written after the samestereotype, describe other divine lovers (Rāma-Sītā,Śiva-Parvatī)33. Anot so direct influence can be traced in the poetic tradition of Vaiṣṇavabhakti, using the same allegory we see in G.: the soul, striving to unite withGod, is the bride, while the divine love cleansing and sanctifying the soul isthe bridegroom. This symbolism (with modifications of more or less sensuouscharacter in different trends) is typical for mediaeval bhakti, above all inBengali literature34, but alsoin Hindi, Tamil35 and so on. Adescription of love for Kṛṣṇa is found in the hymns ofChandidas (XIV–XV cc.), called «a new Jayadeva» in the poetry ofVidyāpati (XV c.), whose songs in Maithili are closer to folklore andfull of details of everyday life, in certain verses by Caitanya (1486–1533), afamous preacher esteemed as an embodiment of Kṛṣṇa andRādhā (cf. below). The same can be said of Hindi devotionalpoetry — of Kabīr (XIV–XV), whose Bijak is imbued with the sameallegory; of Sūrdās (XV–XVI), author of Sūrsāgar, based onBook X of Bhāgavata purāṇa; of the poetessMīrābāī (circa 1498–1546), who also wrote a commentary toG.36. It is interesting thatthe evaluation of this lyric is also different — for example, the songs ofVidyāpati, like those of Jayadeva, are perceived by some scholars not onlyin the traditionally devotional sense but also as «secular» lyrics37. Different kinds of bhakti aredistinguished here; the emotional is only one of them and it also varies: itmay be like the love for a husband (love of Rādhā), for a child38, for a master, etc. According to thesekinds we can denote, for instance, the second and the third as typical forPeriyāḷvar, the first as typical for Āṇḍāl andMīrābāi, the first and second as typical for Sūrdāsand so on. The devotees (not only women) often identified themselves withRādhā — such was the case with Vidyāpati, with Caitanya,with the sect Vallabhācarya founded in the XV century, whose members,regardless of their sex, saw in Kṛṣṇa their husband39. A similar bhakti attitude is foundalso in Śivaism — cf. for example, Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa’sStavacintāmani, Utpaladeva’s Śivasūtrāvall etc.40.Noteworthy parallels oftypological character can be traced outside India. Relatively close analogiesare presented by Sufism with its concept of God as a lover and man’s soul as abeloved woman (Aḥmad Ghazālī, Jalāl al-DīnRūmī and others) — cf. the respective terminology: «friend»,«lover», «intoxicating» — «amorous», «drinking wine», etc.41. Ideas of Sufism in some respects wereclose to Neoplatonism (and possibly influenced by it) and were reflected laterin mediaeval Jewish philosophy and European mysticism. At the same time, theypresent interesting evidence of Muslim-Hindu interaction42. «The reader of Sufi poetry, if he hasno special acquaintance with it, will not even suspect that he is reading areligious text — the erotic descriptions are sometimes so natural andbright that commentators’ explanations begin to seem false and forced»43. These words of E. Bertel’s alsoremind us of a similar approach to G. (by Ch. Lassen,A. Macdonell, and others).Analogousideas can be found in Judaic tradition beginning with the Scriptures(Deuteronomy 6.5; 11.1, Isaiah 56.6, etc.) and later — cf. Philo; sometrends connected with Judaism44in mediaeval philosophy and poetry45,in Cabbala and especially Hasidism. But first of all, we must mention in thisconnection the «Song of Songs» — the most popular specimen of canonizedlyric poetry outside India. Analogies between G. and ancient Hebrew text werefirst drawn by W. Jones and became typical for the perception of G. by menof European culture46, as well,perhaps, as for the perception of the «Song of Songs» by Indians47. Some traits common to both texts wereoften noted, not only in their content (woes of love, pastoral theme) orpeculiarities of genre and composition (combination of lyric and dramaticelements — cf. attempts of corresponding reconstruction48) but also in the symbolicinterpretation common to the fate of both49.Such allegories, beginning with ancient Judaic tradition, in the Talmud andlater commentaries, identify generally the bridegroom, the beloved with God andthe bride with the people of Israel; their love union is the divineunion between God and the Chosen people (the tradition presents also numerousallegoric details through the text). The interpretation of the «Song of Songs»has likewise a long Christian tradition — the union between Solomon andShulamit symbolizes here the union between God and the devotee’s soul and alsobetween Christ and the Church. This tradition begins with Origenes and iscontinued by Augustinus, Gregorius Nyssenus and other Fathers50. It can be traced throughout thedifferent trends of Eastern and Western Christianity in the works of SymeonTheologos, Bernard of Clairvaux, Luther (cf. «Von der Freiheit einesChristenmenschen»), Herder, etc.51.We find it particularly in the old Russian tradition, where it is accompaniedby violent censure of those interpreting the «Song of Songs» in a «secular»way — cf. for example, the preface to an old South - Russian translationin a Ms. dated XV–XVI centuries or a corresponding treatise of archbishopTheophan Prokopovich written in 1730 where such a reproach is even inserted inthe title of the work52.Independent of thisinterpretation we find in Western tradition similar allegories of Christ as acelestial bridegroom and the Virgin as a celestial bride, of the Church as afeminine being engaged to Christ, (cf. Ephes, 5.25 sq.), of a nun as abride of Christ, of spiritual marriage etc. expressed by Bernard of Clairvaux,Richard of St. Victor, John Ruysbroek, St. Therese, Jacob Boehme,Emanuel Swedenborg, and others53.On the other hand, there is a definite sacralization of love and of woman imagein European culture that is reminiscent to a certain extent of G. 3.1; 15 (seeabove). In the framework of strictly religious behaviour the samesanctification of matrimony is observed here (cf. for instance, the ritualwords pronounced by the bridegroom: «with my body I thee worship»). The«secular» sphere of behaviour is presented, for example, by the well-knownbeatification of the Lady in mediaeval courtly lyrics of troubadours — cf.ideas of mundane and of celestial love and their synthesis (Andreas Capellanus,Raimon de Cornet, and others). These notions flourished first in Provencalpoetry54 (among other examplescf. Dante’s image of the Lady) and had evident ties with the sacral traditionmentioned above. One can suggest here the possible influence of Christianmystics (St. Bonaventura, Bernard of Clairvaux)55. The cult of the Lady is often unitedin this lyric with the cult of the Virgin, sometimes giving place to it(cf. songs of Raimon de Cornet, known also as a monk, author of a Latin hymn tothe Virgin, of Peire Cardenal, Albertet de Sestaro, and others). Anotherlink-with Muslim tradition is represented likewise not only by lyric poetry(cf. Andalusian poetry, above all of Ibn Ḥazm) but by philosophy aswell — cf. ideas of Avicenna, bearing traces of neoplatonic influence(particularly the sacralization of love as furthering the soul toward ascensionand unity with God)56.Such a mundanesacralization survived in different forms until the New Era. We can mention,for example, the French gallant style — cf. such typical metaphoricalexpressions as «le seuil du temple», «le sacrifice», «l’autel d’amour» etc.(e. g. in the Memoirs of Casanova), also bearing an analogy to somereferences discussed above (G., 3.1; 15 — the first interpretation ofJayadeva’s poem)57.It goes without sayingthat each of these phenomena is distinguished by specific causal and functionalpeculiarities in the framework of its cultural context (thus e. g.referring to some of the last cases one might suggest a kind of reactionperhaps unconscious — an attempt to compensate in some respects for theprogressive secularization of sexual relations in the life of society)58. Such peculiarities are certainly to beconsidered in every concrete detailed comparison to make it methodologicallyjustified and to show to what extent the given comparison is correct. We canassume here that the analogies briefly mentioned above, however remote they mayseem to be from the interpretations of Jayadeva’s poem, are at the same timeconnected to them by certain semantic and functional ties. The degree of suchaffinity and moreover — of the acceptability of the comparison itselfevidently varies in each separate case — from the closest parallels inlyric texts of Vaiṣṇava bhakti to rather oblique and remoteones — in specimen of the European court and gallant style or in manifoldsymbolism of the feminine principle. Further detalization of this kind is thesubject of special studies.

The legend of Kṛṣṇaand Rādhā is perhaps unsurpassed in term of the extent of itsinfluence upon different spheres of Indian culture: belles lettres, theatre,painting, etc.1 Its most famousembodiment is the «Gitagovinda» of Jayadeva (G.) — a peculiar combinationof the lyric and the dramatic genres, which determined to a large degree thecharacter of subsequent trends in later Indian (primarily Bengali) devotionalliterature and provoked scores of imitations and commentaries.

The theme of the poem isthe love between Kṛṣṇa (avatāra of Viṣṇu)and the cowherdess Rādhā. Jayadeva himself calls his work a sequenceof sweet and tender words of love (1.3madhurakomalakāntapadāvalīm)2.And, indeed, the sphere of amorous relations is represented here in itsfullest. Independently of their possible interpretation, the scenes of G. areimbued with sensuality, constituting an evident parallel to analogous classicalIndian texts (including special didactic treatises)3. It rings quite naturally when the last verses of G.pronounce the poem a source for judging the essence of the passion of love(12.26: śṛñgāravivekatattva: cf. 12.28: śṛñgārasāraṃ).In fact, every verse beginning with III (after the first two introductoryincantations) is dedicated here to describing the different stages of love: thelanguor of Rādhā (1.27; 2.10; 20), the games played by Kṛṣṇawith Cowherdesses (1.28 sq., 38 sq., 2.2 sq.), his repentance(3.1 sq.), the new sorrows of the amorous Rādhā (4.2 sq.,11 sq.), the languor of Kṛṣṇa (5.2 sq.),Rādhā’s readiness for a rendezvous (6.2 sq.), her nightlylamentations (7.2 sq.), the scenes of Kṛṣṇa’sunfaithfulness jealously imagined by her (7.31 sq.), her wrath against Kṛṣṇa(8.1 sq.), his craving forgiveness (10.1 sq.), his love rapture andRādhā’s efforts to overcome bashfulness (11.24 sq.; 32 sq.;12.2 sq.), and, finally, the joys of their union (12.10 sq.) Theenumeration of Rādhā’s emotional states, which gradually intensify upto the point of fainting (4.19; 11.10; cf. 4.7) is reminiscent of the tenfoldscale traditional in classical Sanskrit literature — cf.Vetālapañcaviṃśatikā, rec. Śivadāsa, 16;Vātsyayāna’s Kāmasūtra (K) 40.5 etc. Another typicaldevice is the systematic use of Rādhā’s characteristics in shortprosaic formulas concluding some parts of G. According to these formulas(which differ in different variants) the part in question is dedicated to thedescription of abhisārikā (a woman going to a rendezvous), vāsakasajjā(a woman ready to accept her lover), etc. — here G. likewise reflectsfamiliar classification of a heroine’s slates found in Sanskrit treatises ondramatic art: e. g. Bharata’s Nāṭyaśāstra XXII,199–206; Dhanañjaya’s Daśarūpa II, 24–27 etc.4. A traditional notion of «love play»(līlā, krīḍa)5,as well as its accessories (music, songs, dances) is very importanthere, — cf. for example, reminiscences of pañcama (I.40; literally«the fifth» — i.e. one of the rāgas associated with passionate love),rāsa (1.44; 2.2 — a certain cowherd’s dance traditionally believed tohave been invented by Kṛṣṇa), playing a pipe (vaṃśa —1.44; 2.2; 19; etc.; veṇu — 5.9), and so on. According to canonizedpoetic devices, heroes’ emotions are constantly accompanied by the cuckooing ofkokilas (Indian cuckoo — 1.28; 37, etc.), the humming of bees (1.29; 31;37; 5.4; 11.9), the waft of a spring breeze (1.28; 3.2; 5.2; 7.39; 41; 9.2),the fragrance of flowers (1.30; 33; 36; 3.2) etc. We find here some importantdetails of etiquette that also correspond to Indian erotological tradition;such as, for instance, the role of Rādhā’s girl friend(sahacarī, sakhī), who serves as an intermediary (dūti —7.30; cf. K. 5.47, etc.). She goes from one lover to another, conveys messagesof love, tells Kṛṣṇa about Rādhā’s state of mind(4.1 sq.; 6.1 sq.), encourages Rādhā (5.1 sq.;9.1 sq.; 11.1 sq.; 13 sq.), listens to their confessions, etc.Other widespread motifs in G. are the lovers’ quarrel (cf. K. 226 and in other traditions: Ovid, Arsamatoria. I.36; III, 1 sq.; idem, Amores, I.7.9; Lucianus, Asinus 9—10,etc.), comparing love to battle (7.13; 11.7; 12.10; 12), embellishment of thecouch (4.4; 5.10; 16), etc. Numerous analogies are connected with such detailsas coquettish glances (2.9; 3.12; 13; 15, etc. — cf. K. 27), embraces(1.45; 47; 49; 2.5; 6; 13; 3.8; 5.8 sq., etc.—K. 8), kisses (1.42;45; 2.4; 13; 16; 4.23; 5.18, etc. — K. 9), exclamations (cf.kūjita — 2.15; 7.17; sītkara — 4.9; 6.10; 12.15 — K. 15—16),scratches (2.15; 5.18; 8 4; 10.3 etc. — K. 10), bites (8.6; 10.3; 11;12.11; 13 — K. 11), etc.7.Different stages of the amorous union are depicted, beginning withRādhā’s timid approach to Kṛṣṇa’s bower and endingwith the latter’s attempts to restore his beloved’s toilet (cf. K.20.14) — see XI, XXIII, XXIV and the analogous description of Kṛṣṇa’sinfidelity in XIV, XV — including various «technical» details (e. g. puruṣāyita:5.12; 7.19 — cf. K. 17–18)8.At the same time a certain naturalism9is combined here with an undoubtedly psychological approach. Such is, forexample, the link between the lovers’ mood and the ambient odours, sounds andsights10. It is interestingthat Rādhā identifies herself with the object of her love (6.5:madhuripuraham). Another characteristic motif is subjugation in love: cf. theevidently masochistic words of Kṛṣṇāin XIX (10.3 sq.; 6.11; cf. 12.11)11.

Theplace of G. in Indian culture leads us from the sphere of its immediatethematic to another aspect of investigation. Independently of the feelingof «secularity» (cf. below) that the poem evokes (this feeling is evidentenough to European and Indian scholars as well)12, the functioning of G. is inseparable from Vaiṣṇavabhakti. In the framework of this cult both the poem as a whole and its separatedetails (including highly naturalistic ones) were traditionally interpreted,not only by later generations, but evidently already by contemporaries13. Moreover, this is not only because oftraits of the author’s vishnuism (cf. the invocations to Kṛṣṇaconcluding each part of G.; the character of songs I and II beingvirtually hymns dedicated to Viṣṇu; motifs such as the annihilationof sins by Kṛṣṇa in 2.8; 7.20; 29; 12.24, etc.) — suchdigressions are typical for different genres of classical Indian literature.This approach derives from the symbolic perception of the poem as a whole. Thefirst reference directly suggesting such an interpretation is found at thebeginning of the third part (3.1) where we read that Kṛṣṇaleft the beautiful women of Vraja and placed in his bosomRādhā — a chain fettering the delusion of saṃsāra (saṃsāravāsanābaddhaśṛṅkhalām) — i.e., the world’sdelusions leading to a cycle of rebirth in this world. The mundane attachmentssymbolized by cowherdesses have here as their antithesis Rādhā —the supreme principle leading to freedom from worldly vanity. Ch. Lassenalready defined the Kṛṣṇa — Rādhā relationshipas the state of divine mind assuming a human appearance and absorbed in thecontemplation of the highest beauty (cf. 3.15: mānasaṃ tasyāṃlagna)14.

On the other hand, Kṛṣṇahimself no less often appears in G. as the object of Rādhā’sadoration — (cf. for example, verses where she is absorbed in thecontemplation of her lover: 4.2 sq. bhāvanayā tvayilīnā; cf. also 4.19; 21; 6.10; 11 etc.)15. This motif presenting a counterpart to G. 3.1, givesgrounds for another interpretation that seems to be more widespread: theattitude of Rādhā to Kṛṣṇa symbolizes the cravingof the soul (a feminine principle) to unite with the Highest deity. Othercowherdesses may also symbolize the soul (not negative powers as in theprevious case) and the scene of the action-groves of Vṛndāvana —may symbolize the «field of consciousness»16.This symbolism, giving a certain equivocality to the content of G., wasobserved already by W. Jones17.At the same time various authors are inclined to stress that such symbolismbelongs only to the traditional interpretation of the poem18, while some see in G. a purelysecular lyric19.

Considering the differentinterpretations of G., the scholar is certainly justified in emphasizingwhichever one he favours according to the aspect of his research. Theallegorical «sacral» interpretation is indisputable when the poem is studied inthe context of Vaiṣṇava tradition; its importance as a specimen ofa «secular» lyric is evident as well when we compare G. with other Sanskritlyrical texts or think of the immediate reaction of the readers staying outsidethe Kṛṣṇa cult. It must, however, be emphasized that in theframework of the cultural environment of G., the opposition of these twoaspects seems to be incorrect — it as if destroys «from without» thecharacter of its functioning that is specific to Indian culture. The poem wasevidently perceived by its audience as an indivisible fusion of sacred text andlove lyric, by no means demarcated as modern readers and researchers(especially non-Indian) are inclined to do. It is to be noted that theopposition of the «sacral» and the «secular» is not the same in modern Europeanand mediaeval Indian cultures20and the use of such a dichotomy can scarcely be of help here. We knowspecifically that within Hindu dogmatics love with its most sensuous aspectswas naturally combined with other aspects of life21 including the directly «sacral» (cf. the essentiallydifferent approach presented in the old European tradition — ancient Greekor later Christian)22.

One can mention thewell-known system of the four life’s goals (caturartha, caturbhadra),suggesting the interaction of kāma (sensuous love) with artha, dharma andmokṣa including specifically the performance of ritual duties and therelinquishing of worldly attachments23.Sanskrit poetry presents an example of a deliberate union of love andresignation motifs (cf. for instance, a similar effect achieved by a refinedwordplay in Ramacandra’s Rasikarañjana)24. On the other hand, one must not forget the role of theerotic element in different religious trends of ancient and mediaeval India(see below)25. At the same timethe fact of G.’s ambiguous meaning (as we see, the equivoque is maintained alsowithin the framework of the «sacral» interpretation) seems to be natural forevery specimen of belles lettres (regardless of a possible connection with thereligious sphere of behaviour); it corresponds particularly to some importantprinciples of classical Indian poetics; cf. for example, the idea of twolevels: a level of the explicit or expressed (vācya) meaning and a levelof the implicit or «being manifested» (vyaṅgya) meaning (seeĀnandavardhana’s Dhvanyāloka III. 33, etc.). The devotionalinterpretation of the Rādhā — Kṛṣṇārelations can possibly be correlated here to the implicit meaning that is to beguessed.

Thisinterpretation has numerous analogies in classical Indian literature — andnot only in Vaiṣṇava bhakti tradition. To begin with more ancientand oblique examples reflecting certain erotic traits of Hinduism at its veryearliest stages and touching rather the content and direct meaning of the poem,we may refer to Vedic hymns26 —cf. images of rain as a seminal fluid fertilizing the earth (ṚgvedaI.100.3; 128.3; III.55.17, V.83.4; Atharvaveda IV.15.11; VIII.7.21, etc.), ofHeaven and Earth as of Father and Mother (Rv. I.164.8; VI.70.2, etc.), ofcultivating the soil (Rv. V.56.3; Śatapathabrāhmaṇa XI.5.11,etc.). Certain functions of gods are also very typical — cf.characteristics of Agni (dampatī — Rv. V.3.2; jāra — Rv. X.11.6 etc.), Tvaṣṭar, Prajāpati, Viṣṇu (cf. Rv.X.184.1; Av V. 25.5 etc.; his functions develop in later cult including theconcept of avatāras, one of which is the hero of G.). Turning to Vedicritual27, one can mentionsacrificial fire, being produced by the friction of two sticks — an upperand a lower — with, respectively, male and female symbolism (cf. Rv.III.29.1; a later image from Bṛhadāraṇyaka up. IV.4.22, etc.),its relation to the altar (Vedi) with whom it represents, correspondingly, manand woman in union (Śatapathabrāhmaṇa I.2.5.15–16). Anothersimilar allegory was connected with the parts of the hand press for extractingsoma and the act of pressing itself (soma pavamāna — cf. Rv. I.28.2,etc.). In early Upaniṣads we find allegories that are more abstract andat the same time closer to G. — comparing the highest state ofillumination to the joy of love: «As a man when in the embrace of his belovedwife knows nothing without or within, so the person when in the embrace of theintelligent Self (Prajñenātmanā) knows nothing without orwithin» (Bṛhadāraṇyaka up. IV.3.21)28. The concept of Ātman and Brahmanas blissful joy (ānanda) is generally typical for Upaniṣads (cf. Kauṣītaki3.8; Taittirīya 3.6; Bṛhadāraṇyaka IV.3.8 sq.;Chāndogya IV.10.5; 7.28; VIII.4.2, etc.)29.Оn the other hand, we find here not only the sexualization of cult but also thesacralization of sex. Such is the deification of desire (kāma)already in Vedic texts (Rv. X.129.4; Av. III.21; 25; IX.2; XIX.52;Taittirīya brāhmaṇa II. 4.1, 10; 8.9.4; Taittirīyaāraṇyaka I.23.1, etc.) and in Upaniṣads (BṛhadāraṇyakaII.4.5, etc.)30. There areallegories here comparing the genitals to parts of the sacrificial altar (seeabove) and prescribing certain rites for obtaining desirable progeny (BṛhadāraṇyakaVI.2.13; 4.2 sq.; Chāndogya V.8 etc.). Another scope of examplesrelates to liṅgam and yoni worship in some Śivaite cults, intantrism (corresponding evidence can be traced back to Proto-Indian culture)31. It must be noted that sometimes(e. g. in such trends as śakti) it is difficult to delimit theseprocesses — sacralization and sexualization — since we can trace bothin the same passage — cf. example, a passage from BṛhadāraṇyakaII. 4.5; IV.5.6, where love for a husband, wife, sons, etc. finds itsonly justification in love for Ātman (ātmanas tu kāmāyasarvam priyam bhavati), an idea reflected in later trends of bhakti.

We shall briefly referonly to some parallels akin to G., that can be explained within the context ofthe same tradition and partly by direct influence. The sensuous aspect of Kṛṣṇaworship is found in Vaiṣṇava texts preceding G. Suchtestimonies occur already in Bhagavatgītā (9.29), one can perceivethe further development of bhakti forms — from rather speculative to morepassionate — in Bhāgavata purāṇa (cf. X.29–33), whereparticularly passion (rati) appears as an intermediary between faith(śraddhā) and devotion (bhakti) (cf. III.25.25)32.

There are many moreparallels in later Indian literature, some of them directly influenced byG. Several poems — by Kalyāna, Bhānudatta, Prabhākara,Vaṃśamaṇi, and others — written after the samestereotype, describe other divine lovers (Rāma-Sītā,Śiva-Parvatī)33. Adescription of love for Kṛṣṇa is found in the hymns ofChandidas (XIV–XV cc.), called «a new Jayadeva» in the poetry ofVidyāpati (XV c.), whose songs in Maithili are closer to folklore andfull of details of everyday life, in certain verses by Caitanya (1486–1533), afamous preacher esteemed as an embodiment of Kṛṣṇa andRādhā (cf. below). It is interesting thatthe evaluation of this lyric is also different — for example, the songs ofVidyāpati, like those of Jayadeva, are perceived by some scholars not onlyin the traditionally devotional sense but also as «secular» lyrics37. Different kinds of bhakti aredistinguished here; the emotional is only one of them and it also varies: itmay be like the love for a husband (love of Rādhā), for a child38, for a master, etc. According to thesekinds we can denote, for instance, the second and the third as typical forPeriyāḷvar, the first as typical for Āṇḍāl andMīrābāi, the first and second as typical for Sūrdāsand so on. A similar bhakti attitude is foundalso in Śivaism — cf. for example, Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa’sStavacintāmani, Utpaladeva’s Śivasūtrāvall etc.40.

Noteworthy parallels oftypological character can be traced outside India. Relatively close analogiesare presented by Sufism with its concept of God as a lover and man’s soul as abeloved woman (Aḥmad Ghazālī, Jalāl al-DīnRūmī and others) — cf. the respective terminology: «friend»,«lover», «intoxicating» — «amorous», «drinking wine», etc.41. Analogousideas can be found in Judaic tradition beginning with the Scriptures(Deuteronomy 6.5; 11.1, Isaiah 56.6, etc.) and later — cf. Philo; sometrends connected with Judaism44in mediaeval philosophy and poetry45,in Cabbala and especially Hasidism. But first of all, we must mention in thisconnection the «Song of Songs» — the most popular specimen of canonizedlyric poetry outside India. Analogies between G. and ancient Hebrew text werefirst drawn by W. Jones and became typical for the perception of G. by menof European culture46, as well,perhaps, as for the perception of the «Song of Songs» by Indians47. Some traits common to both texts wereoften noted, not only in their content (woes of love, pastoral theme) orpeculiarities of genre and composition (combination of lyric and dramaticelements — cf. attempts of corresponding reconstruction48) but also in the symbolicinterpretation common to the fate of both49.Such allegories, beginning with ancient Judaic tradition, in the Talmud andlater commentaries, identify generally the bridegroom, the beloved with God andthe bride with the people of Israel; their love union is the divineunion between God and the Chosen people (the tradition presents also numerousallegoric details through the text). The interpretation of the «Song of Songs»has likewise a long Christian tradition — the union between Solomon andShulamit symbolizes here the union between God and the devotee’s soul and alsobetween Christ and the Church. This tradition begins with Origenes and iscontinued by Augustinus, Gregorius Nyssenus and other Fathers50. It can be traced throughout thedifferent trends of Eastern and Western Christianity in the works of SymeonTheologos, Bernard of Clairvaux, Luther (cf. «Von der Freiheit einesChristenmenschen»), Herder, etc.51.We find it particularly in the old Russian tradition, where it is accompaniedby violent censure of those interpreting the «Song of Songs» in a «secular»way — cf. for example, the preface to an old South - Russian translationin a Ms. dated XV–XVI centuries or a corresponding treatise of archbishopTheophan Prokopovich written in 1730 where such a reproach is even inserted inthe title of the work52.

Independent of thisinterpretation we find in Western tradition similar allegories of Christ as acelestial bridegroom and the Virgin as a celestial bride, of the Church as afeminine being engaged to Christ, (cf. Ephes, 5.25 sq.), of a nun as abride of Christ, of spiritual marriage etc. expressed by Bernard of Clairvaux,Richard of St. Victor, John Ruysbroek, St. Therese, Jacob Boehme,Emanuel Swedenborg, and others53.On the other hand, there is a definite sacralization of love and of woman imagein European culture that is reminiscent to a certain extent of G. 3.1; 15 (seeabove). In the framework of strictly religious behaviour the samesanctification of matrimony is observed here (cf. for instance, the ritualwords pronounced by the bridegroom: «with my body I thee worship»). The«secular» sphere of behaviour is presented, for example, by the well-knownbeatification of the Lady in mediaeval courtly lyrics of troubadours — cf.ideas of mundane and of celestial love and their synthesis (Andreas Capellanus,Raimon de Cornet, and others). These notions flourished first in Provencalpoetry54 (among other examplescf. Dante’s image of the Lady) and had evident ties with the sacral traditionmentioned above. One can suggest here the possible influence of Christianmystics (St. Bonaventura, Bernard of Clairvaux)55. The cult of the Lady is often unitedin this lyric with the cult of the Virgin, sometimes giving place to it(cf. songs of Raimon de Cornet, known also as a monk, author of a Latin hymn tothe Virgin, of Peire Cardenal, Albertet de Sestaro, and others). Anotherlink-with Muslim tradition is represented likewise not only by lyric poetry(cf. Andalusian poetry, above all of Ibn Ḥazm) but by philosophy aswell — cf. ideas of Avicenna, bearing traces of neoplatonic influence(particularly the sacralization of love as furthering the soul toward ascensionand unity with God)56.

Such a mundanesacralization survived in different forms until the New Era. We can mention,for example, the French gallant style — cf. such typical metaphoricalexpressions as «le seuil du temple», «le sacrifice», «l’autel d’amour» etc.(e. g. in the Memoirs of Casanova), also bearing an analogy to somereferences discussed above (G., 3.1; 15 — the first interpretation ofJayadeva’s poem)57.

It goes without sayingthat each of these phenomena is distinguished by specific causal and functionalpeculiarities in the framework of its cultural context (thus e. g.referring to some of the last cases one might suggest a kind of reactionperhaps unconscious — an attempt to compensate in some respects for theprogressive secularization of sexual relations in the life of society)58. Such peculiarities are certainly to beconsidered in every concrete detailed comparison to make it methodologicallyjustified and to show to what extent the given comparison is correct. We canassume here that the analogies briefly mentioned above, however remote they mayseem to be from the interpretations of Jayadeva’s poem, are at the same timeconnected to them by certain semantic and functional ties. The degree of suchaffinity and moreover — of the acceptability of the comparison itselfevidently varies in each separate case — from the closest parallels inlyric texts of Vaiṣṇava bhakti to rather oblique and remoteones — in specimen of the European court and gallant style or in manifoldsymbolism of the feminine principle. Further detalization of this kind is thesubject of special studies.

London, 1963, p. 30 (aboutthe «male approach of Jayadeva and almost feminine of Vidyāpati»); N.M. Sazanova.Ob osnovnyx žanrax literatury bxakti — «Literary Indii», Moskva 1973,str. 60 sq., etc. As we see, the bhakti displays thus certain traitsof travestism.40 Cf. La bhakti. LeStavacintāmaṇi de Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa, texte,trad. et comm. par L. Silburn. Paris, 1964, p. 22 sq.,35 sq., and others. Among recent publications see in this connection: M. Dhavamony,Love of God according to Śaiva siddhānta, A Study in mysticism andtheology of Śaivism. Oxford, 1971, p. 70 sq., 352 sq.41 SeeM. Horten, Lexicon wichtigster Termini der Islamischen Mystik.Heidelberg, 1928; H. Ritter, Philologica. Arabische und PersischeSchriften über die profane und die mystische Liebe — «Der Islam».XXXI, 1933, S 93 sq.; Aḥmad Ghazzālī’s Aphorismenüber die Liebe, hrsg. v. H. Ritter, Istanbul, 1942,S. I sq.; L. Massignon, Essai sur les origines du lexiquetechnique de la mystique Musulmane, Paris, 1954, p. 248 sq., andothers; A. Schimmel. The symbolical language of MaulānāJalāl al-Dīn Rūmī, — «Studies in Islam», vol. I,no. 1, 1964, p. 37 sq.; E.É. Bertel’s,Izbrannye trudy. Sufizm i sufijskaja literatura, Moskva, 1965,s. 88 sq.; 457, and others; I.P. Petruševskij, Islamv Irane v VII–XV vekax. Leningrad, 1966, s. 331 sq.; 340–341; H. Udam,O probleme znašenija v sufijskix tekstax, — «Uč. zapiskiTartuskogo gos. universiteta», vyp. 198, 1967, str. 317 sq.; H. Corbin,Creative imagination in the Sufism of Ibn ‘Arabī’, Princeton, 1969,p. 146 sq. We find numerous reflections of the kind in Muslimliteratures influenced by Sufism (cf. e.g., in the Kurdish poem of the XIVcentury: Faki Tejran. Šejx San’an, Moskva, 1965, verses10 sq., 37, 57 and others).42 See in this connection: M. Horten,Indische Strömungen in der islamischen Mystik. Bd. I–II, Heidelberg.1927-28; Massignon, Essais, p. 81 sq.: Y. Husain.Glimpses of mediaeval Indian culture. London, 1959, p. 33 sq.; R. Chopra,Sufi poets of Bengal — «The Islamic Review», vol. 48, no. 2, I960,p. 11 sq.; Ch. White, Sufism in mediaeval Hindiliterature — «History of Religions», vol. 5, no. I, 1965,p. 114 sq. etc.43 E.È. Bertel’s.Očerk istorii persidskoj literatury, Leningrad, 1928, str. 52–53.44 Cf. for instance, gnostic ideasof sacred matrimony between God and Sophia (see C.G. Jung, Answerto Job. London, 1955, p. 142).45 Cf. motifs of love for God inthe writings of Maimonides, Jehuda Halevy (possibly connected with Sufitradition), etc. Another noteworthy parallel is the «amor dei intellectualis»of Spinoza. It is interesting to note here that R. Rolland (Le voyageinterieur, Paris, 1942, p. 46) called the latter: «notre Krishnad’Europe».46 Cf. F. Edgerton. TheHindu Song of Songs — «The Song of Songs. A Symposium», Philadelphia,1924, p. 43 sq. See in this connection: Jones, On the Mystical,p. 222; Weber, Akademische, S. 227; L. de laVallee - Poussin, Dynasties et histoire de l’Inde depuis Kanishka,jusqu’aux invasions musulmanes. Paris, 1935, p. 104 (ce «Cantique des cantiques»),Gītagovinda... üb v. F. Rückerts new hrsg. v.H. Kreyenborg, Leipzig, s. a., S. 55 («Jayadeva ein indischerSalomo»); F. Dornseiff, Antike und alter Orient, Leipzig, 1958,S. 197 sq.; Filliozat, Continence, p. 60 etc. Cf. the title ofE. Arnold’s translation: The Indian Song of Songs (Gita-govinda) (cf.e. g., Bombay, 1949, p. 157 sq.).47 See: The Song of Songs. A Hebrewpastoral drama... with notes and plates by Satyam Jayati, London, 1867,p. VI, 63 — a translation of G. («a poem of like nature to the Song»)is added here.48 Compare, for instance,E. Renan’s attempt in respect to the «Song of Songs» (Le Cantique desCantiques. Paris, 1929); ibid., p. 88: «Le Cantique des Cantiques doitdonc être envisage comme tenant le milieux entre le drameregulier et l’eclogue ou la pastorale dialoguee»; seeibid., p. 116 sq., parallels to G.49 Here we consider only thesimilar traits in their functioning and do not touch on the question oforiginal intentions (in this respect the case of the «Song of Songs» isevidently different from that of G).50 Cf. respectively: Patrologiaecursus completus. Series graeca, t. 13, Parisiis, 1862, col. 37 sq.;t. 17, Parisiis, 1857, col. 253 sq.; t. 44, Parisiis, 1863,col. 755 sq.; idem, Series latina, t. 34, Parisiis 1841,col. 925 sq., etc.51 See, for example, J.A. Montgomer,The Song of Songs in early and mediaeval Christian use — «The Song ofSongs. A Symposium», 18 sq.; Renan, Le Cantique,p. 124 sq., etc.52 Seein: Pesn’ pesnej Solomona, perevod s drevne-evrejskogo i primečanijaA. Èfrosa, izd, 2, Sanktpeterburg, 1910, str. 91 sq.,101 sq.53 Cf.for instance, De diligendo Deo of Bernard in: Patrologiae cursus completus,Series latina, t. 182, Parisiis, 1854, col. 973 sq.; Thecomplete works of Saint Theresa of Jesus. London–New York, vol. II, 1946,p. 333 sq. (ibid., p. 357 sq. on the «Song of Songs») etc.The genre of sectarian songs close to folklore also presents interestingexamples — cf. Pesni russkix sektantov - mistikov, Sanktpeterburg.1912, s. 500 sq. Concerning some affinities between Hindu andChristian devotional traditions see: K. Hutten. Die Bhakti Religionin Indien und das Christliche Glaube im Neuen Testament. Stuttgart, 1930; ThePrincipal Upaniṣads, p. 263, 635–636 and others; De, Sanskrit,p. 135; K. Klostermayer, Hṛdayavidyā: a sketch of aHindu-Christian theology of love — «Journal of Ecumenical Studies»,vol. IX, no. 4, 1972, p. 750 sq. Ideas of cosmic love, of mysticmatrimony uniting all in one, also have their reflection in music (not onlypertaining to worship) — cf. L. Sabaneev, Skrjabin.Moskva–Petrograd, 1923, str. 45.54 See: M. Lot - Borodine,De l’amour profane a l’amour sacre (etudes de psychologiesentimentale au Moyen Âge), Paris, 1961; V.F. Šišmarjov,K istorii ljubovnyx teorij romanskogo srednevekov’ja — «Izbrannye stat’i.Francuzskaja literatura», Moskva–Leningrad, 1965, str. 191 sq.;226 sq.; M. Meilakh, The structure of the courtly universe ofthe Troubadours — «Semiotica», vol. XIV, no. 1, 1975,p. 71 sq.55 Cf. E. Gilson, Latheologie mystique de Saint Bernard. Paris, 1934, p. 193 sq.; Lot -Borodine, De l’amour, p. 77 sq.; A. de Rougemont,L’amour et l’Occident. Paris, 1962, p. 312 sq., etc.56 Cf. A.J. Denomy, Theheresy of courtly love. New York. 1947, p. 29 sq.; G.E. v. Grünebaum,Avicenna’s Risâla fî ʾl-ʿišq and courtly love —«Journal of Near Eastern Studies», Vol. XI, no. 4, 1952,p. 233 sq. Another noteworthy parallel is found in the cult of QueenTamar in Georgian court poetry of XII century that was likewise subject toneoplatonic influence (Rustaveli, Tchachruchadze) — cf. Š. Nucubidze,Tvorčestvo Rustaveli, Tbilisi, 1958, str. 206 sq., 378 sq.57 Concerning this interpretation(cf. above, note 14) one can refer also to the manifold allegorical use ofthe archaic but still preserved image of the femine principle — fordescribing original matter (Sanskrit: prakṛti; cf. the meaningfulcoincidence in Latin «materia»), Earth, tree, native land, town, capital (cf.well-known evidence from the Scriptures), liberty, etc. cf. example, C.G. Jung,Symbols of transformation — «Collective works», vol. V, London, 1956,p. 207 sq.; idem, The Archetypes and the CollectiveUnconscious — ibid, vol. IX, pt. 1, 1959, p. 81 sq.;Heimann, Studien, S. 278 a.o.; Sh. Indradeva, Correspondencebetween woman and nature in Indian thought — «Philosophy East and West»,vol. 16, no. 3–4, 1966, p. 161 sq.58 Cf. Bleeker, Sexuality,p. 222 sq.

ПРИМЕЧАНИЯ

 

1 Concerningthe history of the motif cf. W. Ruben, Krishna. Konkordanz und Kommentar der Motive seinesHeldenlebens. Istanbul, 1944; A.K. Majumdar, A note on thedevelopment of the Rādhā cult — «Annals of the BhandarkarInstitute», vol. 36. 1955, p. 231–257; S.L. Katre, Kṛṣṇa,gopas, gopīs and Rādhā — «P.K. Gode commemoration volume»,Poona, 1960, pt. III, p. 83–92; Kṛṣṇa. Myths, ritesand attitudes, ed. by M. Singer, Honolulu, 1966; Ch. Vaudeville,Aspects du mythe de Kṛṣṇa - Gopāla dans l’Indeancienne — «Mélanges d’indianisme à la mèmoirede L. Renou». Paris. 1968, p. 737–761; B. Majumdar. Kṛṣṇain history and legend. Calcutta, 1969; B.S. Miller,Rādhā: consort of Kṛṣṇa’s vernal passion —JAOS, vol. 95, 1975, p. 655–671; A. Ch. Chakravarti, The storyof Kṛṣṇa in Indian literature. Calcutta, 1976, etc. I amgrateful to Dr. Shulman, who kindly facilitated my acquaintance with somerecent publications.

2 TheGītagovinda of Jayadeva with the commentaries Rasikapriyā of KingKumbha and Rasamañjari of Mahāmahopādhyāya ShankaraMishra ed. with various readings by M.R. Telang and W.L. Panslkar.Bombay, 1904. Cf. also: Gītagovinda mahākāvyam of Jayadeva withthree commentaries, ed. by A. Sharma, K. Deshpande, andW.S. Sharma. Hyderabad, 1969. The Arabic numerals denote correspondinglythe parts (sarga) and the strophes (according to the Bombay ed.) and the Romannumerals the songs (pādavāli), distributed respectively: 1 (I–IV), 2(V–VI), 3 (VII), 4 (VIII–IX), 5 (X–XI), 6 (XII), 7 (XIII–XVI), 8 (XVII), 9(XVIII), 10 (XIX), 11 (XX–XXII), 12 (XXIII–XXIV). Concerning the compositionand style of G., combining, in the framework of separate parts, songs andverses, apparently not destined to be sung, see from among the recentpublications: Love song of the Dark Lord. Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda, ed. andtr. by B.S. Miller, New York, 1977, p. 7 sq.; S. Sandhal-Forgue,Le Gītagovinda. Tradition et innovation dans le Kāvya. Stockholm,1977; cf. A.Ja. Syrkin, O Kompozicii Gitagovindy — «Literaturanarodov vostoka». Moskva, 1970, str. 175–188.

3 Among the traditionalcommentaries to G., we can mention Vanamālibhaṭṭa’sSañjīvani, which pays special attention to such parallels (see G.,Hyderabad, ed., Introduction). See also: S.K. De, Ancient Indianerotics and erotic literature. Calcutta. 1955, p. 55–56; V.S. Naravane,Jayadeva. — «The times of India. Annual». Bombay, 1961, p. 25; V. Varadachari,A history of the Saṁskṛtaliterature. Allahabad, 1960, p. 95; S. Sen, History of Bengaliliterature. New Delhi, 1971, p. 15 sq.; D. Kinsley, Without Kṛṣṇathere is no song — «History of religions», vol. 12, N. 2, 1972,p. 149 sq., etc. Concerning separate erotological parallels cf. R. Schmidt,Beiträge zur indischen Erotik. Leipzig, 1902, p. 352 f.,430 f., 541 f., 552 f, 752 f.

4 Cf. Miller, Rādhā,p. 671.

5 On the more general aspects ofthis see J. Huisinga, Homo ludens. A study of the play element inculture. London, 1949, p. 43 sq. With respect to Indian culture(particularly in connection with religious cosmogonical symbolism) see, forinstance, J. F. Butler, Creation, art andlīlā — «Philosophy East and West», vol. X, nov. 1–2.1960, p. 3–12; Sh. Dasgupta, Obscure religious cults as a background toBengali literature. Calcutta 1962, p. 123 sq. (eternallīlā - eternal Truth).

6 Cf. Schmidt. Beiträge,S. 553 sq.

7 Ibid., 430 sq.

8 Compare with explanations ofKumbha’s Rasikapriyā and Śankaramiśra’s Rasamañjarī(G., Bombay ed., p. 82) or Vanamālibhaṭṭa’sSañjīvanī and Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍita’sPadadyotanikā (G., Hyderabad ed., p. 191). The second passage isexplained in Rasamañjarī (Bombay, ed., p. 102–103) with referenceto the treatise Ratirahasya as haṃsalīlāka (cf.Sañjīvanī in the Hyderabad ed., p. 234). See Schmidt,Beiträge, S. 541 sq., 578 sq.

9 R. Smith (Contrastsbetween Sanskrit and Western literature — «Asian Review», N. S.vol. I, no. 3, 1964, p. 158–159) notes that the ancient Indian cultof woman, unlike the European, is physical and sensuous rather than romantic.

10 Cf. for example, about the roleof musical impression: Th. Reik, The Search Within, New York, 1956,385 sq.

11 Cf. also about puruṣāyitamentioned above (5.12 — K. 17–18.3). Concerning Indian parallels, one may referto tantric symbolism connected with Śakti cult (see below). See, forexample, J. Le Roy Davidson, Mannerism and neurosis in the eroticart of India — «Oriental Art», vol. 6, no. 3, 1960, p. 84. We donot dwell here on analogous examples from other traditions (see e. g., astriking parallel in the preface to the third edition of Heine’s «Buch derLieder»). Cf. also typical traits of the corresponding vocabulary (Lat.«domina», Fr. maîtresse», etc.).

12 See: Gita Govinda.Jayadevae poetae indici drama lyricum... rec... C. Lassen, Bonnae 1836,p. XIII: A. Weber, Akademische Vorlesungen über indischeLiteraturgeschichte. Berlin, 1876, S. 227; S.N. Dasgupta, AHistory of Sanskrit literature, Classical period, vol. I. Calcutta, 1962,p. 157, 665 sq.; Miller, Love Song, p. 17 etc. Cf. also:Varadachari, History, p. 95: Although its value as a devotional lyriccannot be minimized, its value as an erotic lyric is greater.

13 Cf., for instance. A.B. Keith,A history of Sanskrit literature. Oxfoid, 1961, p. 194; P. Thomas.Kāma Kalpa or the Hindu ritual of love. Bombay 1959, p. 128 sq.;W. Eidlitz, Die indische Gottesliebe. Olten, Freiburg im Breisgau,1955, S. 139 sq.; Ch. Vaudeville. Evolution of lovesymbolism in Bhagavatism — JAOS, vol. 32. no. 1, 1962,p. 31 sq.; Sh. Dasgupta, Obscure, p. 125–126; S.K. De,Bengal’s contribution to Sanskrit literature. Calcutta, 1960, p. 126 sq.; A. Daniélou,Les quatre sens de la vie et la structure sociale de l’Inde traditionnelle. Paris. 1963,p. 182 sq.; R. Sarkar. Gītagovinda: towards a totalunderstanding — «Publikaties van het Instituut voor Indische talen enculturen, no. 2, Rijksuniversiteit te Gronigen, 1974; L. Siegel.Sacred and profane dimensions of love in Indian traditions as exemplified inthe Gītagovinda of Jayadeva, Oxford, 1975, p. 209 sq.(Ph.D. thesis; idem: Delhi 1978).

14 G., Bonn, ed. XVIII–XIX (mensdivina in homine manifestata... deus. humana specie indutus... Defixus estanimus in contemplanda summa eius pulcritudine), 89; cf. also commentaries inG., Hyderabad ed., p. 130–131; The Song of Songs, A Hebrew pastoraldrama... with notes and plates by Satyam Jayati, London, 1867, p. 63 etc.There is another more «secular» interpretation of G. 1.3: «Rādhā cheha la cintura, gli ornamenti e le Vesti mondane» (Valentini, De Rigo, Un anticocodice inedito del Gītagovinda — «Rivista degli studi orientali»,v. XVIII, f. 1, 1939, p. 68–69). The motif of sanctity achievedthrough woman is presented here — cf. the cult of Śakti in Indiantradition (relations of Viṣṇu to Laksmī, of Śivato Parvatī, etc.), of the Great Mother, similar trends in Shamanism (motifof the «heavenly wife»), Islam (the legend of Muḥammad and Ā’isha),and others. See: W. Nolle. Die Sehnsucht nach Harmonie. DerShaktismus und die archaische Welt — «Jahrbuch der Museums fürVölkerkunde zu Leipzig» Bd. XV, 1956, Berlin, 1957, S. 55 sq.;H. Fane. The female element in Indian culture — «Asianfolklore studies», vol. 34, no. 1, 1975, p. 75 sq.; A. Wayman,Female energy and symbolism in the Buddhist tantras — «History ofReligions», vol. 2, no. 1, 1962, p. 73 sq.; S. Kramrish,The Indian Great Goodess — ibid., vol. 14, no. 4, 1975,p. 235 sq., 261 sq., etc., See also: Gestalt und Kultur der«Grossen Mutter». Eranos Jahrbuch, 1938, vol. VI, Zurich, 1939: C.J. Bleeker,The Sacred Bridge. Leiden, 1963, p. 83 sq.; L.Ja. ŠternbergIzbranničestvo v religii «Etnografija», no. 1, 1927, p. 1–56; E.A. Krejnovič.Nivxgu, Moskva 1973, s. 441 sq.: I.N. Vinnikov. Legenda oprizvanii Muxammeda v svete etnografii — «S.F. Ol’denburgu k50-letiju naučno obščestvennoj dejatei’nosti», Leningrad, 1934,str. 142 sq., etc. The most famous expression of the idea in recentEuropean literature is perhaps to be found in the last lines of Goethe’s Faust(«Das Ewig- Weibliche Zieht uns hinan»).

15 Cf. G., Bonn ed., p.XIX sq.

16 See, for example, S.L. Gulick.The East and the West. A study of psychic and cultural characteristics. Tokyo,1963, p. 264–265. F. Edgerton (The Hindu Song of Songs — «Songof Songs. A Symposium», Philadelphia, 1924, p. 46) suggests that thisinterpretation «fits very ill the plot of the poem since it is Kṛṣṇawho does the seeking and Rādhā who is the sought,» and prefers theprevious variant. We would not, however, as he does, call that variantpredominant. It is also clear that in the plot of G. there is no one-sidedcraving — both hero and heroine are striving for each other, either inturn or simultaneously.

17 W. Jones.On the mystical poetry of the Persians and Hindus — The Works of SirW. Jones, vol. IV, London, 1807, p. 234. Cf. also, for example,Le Gīta-govinda et le Ritou-sanhara, tr. par H. Fauche, Paris 1850,p. VI; K. Hutten. Die Bhakti-Religion in Indien und diechristliche Glaube im Neuen Testament. Stuttgart, 1930, S. 57; M. Winternitz.A history of Indian literature, vol. III, f. 1. Calcutta 1959,p. 137; H. Glasenap, Die Literaturen Indiens von ihren Anfangbis zur Gegenwart, Stuttgart, 1961, S. 322; M.S. Randhawa.Kangra paintings of the Gīta Govinda. New Delhi, 1963, p. 55; K. Chaitanya.A new history of Sanskrit literature. Bombay, 1977, p. 411; Miller, LoveSong, P. IX etc.

18 Cf. G., Bonn ed., p. XIII,XVII sq.; L. Schroeder, Indiens Literatur und Cultur in historischerEntwicklung. Leipzig, 1887, S. 581; Keith, History, p. 194, etc.

19 Cf. above p. 15. See also:Weber, Akademische, S. 227. A. Macdonell (A History of SanskritLiterature, London, 1917, p. 346) is surprised that G. could be given aninterpretation of this kind; and M. Mansinha (Indian literature, ed.Dr. Nagendra, Agra, 1959, p. 476) sees the fault of the poem as lyingin its superfluous sensuality. It is interesting to note that alreadyF. Schelling who read G. (the first German translations by F. Mayerand F. Dahlberg were published at the very beginning of the XIX century),denied the symbolic character of the poem and suggested that even if the amorousadventures of Kṛṣṇa sometimes had such a character, they havealready lost it in G. (F. Schelling’s Werke, 3 Hauptband, Munchen,1922 — Philosophie der Kunst, S. 443).

20 Cf. L. Renou et: J. Filliozat,L’Inde classique, t. I, Paris, 1947, p. 443; I. Fiser,Indian erotics of the oldest period, Prague, 1966, p. 43. Concerning therelations of the corresponding elements in modern culture (particularly thenon-obvious presence of the «sacred» element within the «secular») see M. Eliade.The sacred in the secular world — «Cultural hermeneutics», Dordrecht,1973, vol. I, no. 1, p. 101–113.

21 Cf. Smith, Contrasts,p. 158–159.

22 Such is, for instance, theancient opposition of «earthly» and «divine» love continued in the ideas ofneoplatonics, Boetius (De consolatione philosophiae II.8), Thomas Aquinas (cf.his «amor sensitivus — amor intellectivus»), etc. (see below, p. 26),Cf. E.G. Rabinovič. Afrodita Uranija i AfroditaPandemos — «Antičnost i Vizantija», Moskva, 1975,s. 306 sq.; A.Ja. Syrkin. Notes on the KāmaSūtra — «Semiotica» 11, no. 1, 1974, p. 40.

23 Daniélou, Les quatre,p. 169 sq.; A.Ja. Syrkin. K sistematizacii nekotoryxponjatij v sanskrite — «Semiotika i vostocnye jazyki», Moskva, 1967,str. 147 sq.

24 Cf. R. Schmidt.Liebe und Ehe in alten und modernen Indien. Berlin, 1904, S. 31 sq.;Winternitz, History, p. 165.

25 Considering here some parallelsin respect to G. ’s interpretation — first of all from Indiantradition — we shall not dwell upon the more general problem of the roleof sexuality in religion and in the interaction of the correspondingprinciples. From later works cf. in this connection: C. Bleeker.Sexuality and Religion — «The Rainbow. A collection of studies in thescience of religions». Leiden, 1975, p. 208 sq.

26 Cf. Fišer, Indian,p. 42 sq., 92.

27 Ibid, p. 48, 109 sq.

28 The Subject of knowledgeperceiving the highest principle is evidently meant here. Cf. F. Heiler,Die Mystik in den Upanishaden. München, 1925, S. 16; Vaudeville,Evolution, p. 32. See: The Principal Upaniṣads ed. byS. Radhakrishnan. London, 1953, p. 262–263 (with parallels from othertraditions — cf. below).

29 Cf. B. Heimann,Studien zur Eigenart indischen Denkens. Tübingen, 1930, S. 180 sq.;Eadem, Die Tiefschlafspekulation der alten Upanishaden. München, 1922,S. 16.

30 See A. Macdonell, Vedicmythology. Strassburg, 1897, p. 13 sq., 120; A. Daniélou Le polythéisme hindou, Paris,1960, p. 268 sq., 343 sq.; Fišer, Indian, p. 89 sq.;J. Macy, The dialectics of desire — «Nurmen». Vol. XXII,fasc. 2, 1975, p. 145 sq. etc.

31 See Fišer, Indian,p. 33 sq.; 85 sq.; cf. in this connection: W. Foy,Über das Indische Yoni-Symbol — «Aufsatre zur Kultur und Sprachgeschichtevornehmlich des Orients E. Kuhn gewidmet». — München, 1916,S. 423 sq., P. Dekeyser, Propos sur le symbolismephallique dans l’hindouisme — Synthèses», 1961, no. 181,p. 307 sq.; W.D. O’Flaherty. Asceticism and eroticism in the mythology orŚiva, London, 1973, p. 255 sq.; J. Filliozat.Continence et sexualité dans le bouddhisme et les disciplines deYoga — «Laghu Prabandhāh», Leiden, 1974, p. 66 etc. It isinteresting to mention here the Chinese tradition (that possibly interactedwith Indian tantrism) where the relationship of the masculine and feminineprinciples (Yang–Yin) was regarded as a regulating factor for cosmic harmony(cf. text: Толкования «Гитаговинды» и параллели из другихтрадиций [к № 7]
html: Толкования «Гитаговинды» и параллели из другихтрадиций [к № 7]

text: (резюме) Поэма Джаядевы«Гитаговинда» (2 пол. XII в.) — знаменитый образец средневековойиндийской лирики многообразно отразилась в различных жанрах художественноготворчества (поэзия, театр, музыка) и одновременно функционировала как важныйтекст кришнаитского бхакти. В этой связи любовные отношения Кришны (одного извоплощений бога Вишну) и пастушки Радхи стали объектом традиционноготолкования, основанного на ряде непосредственных свидетельств поэмы (ср.«Гитаговинда», 4.19; 21; 6.10; 11 и др.), — как стремление души (Радха) квысшему божественному началу (Кришна). Одновременно стих 3.1 поэмы далоснования для почитания Радхи, чье влечение к Кришне как бы обуздывает исвязывает земные привязанности, сансару.Толкования эти рассмотрены,в частности, в связи с традицией сакрализациилюбовных отношений уже в ведийской литературе — ср. уподобление высшейпросветленности любовным объятиям (напр., в Бр IV.3.21). Интересныетипологические параллели мы находим и в других традициях — ср. символикусуфизма (Бог — «друг», «возлюбленный», суфий — «влюбленный»,«опьяненный» и т.п.). Наиболее интересно здесь сопоставление с библейской«Песнью песней» в иудейской и христианской традициях (здесь, в частности,Суламифь — душа, ищущая Бога; слияние ее с Соломоном — союз Бога сдушой, Христа с церковью). Подобная символика прослеживается в европейскойкультуре Средневековья и Нового времени уже в рамках светского творчества (ср.Джаядева. Гитаговинда. Пер. с санскрита, вступительная статья, комментарий иприложения А.Я. Сыркина), М. 1995, с. 53 сл.).  \n

text: The scientific interestfor the analysis of dream interpretations needs not be justified. Independentlyfrom the practical evaluation of its plausibility by modern man, we can assumethat every single interpretation of the kind is by no means arbitrary. It hasits own motivation — not only on psychological or physiological levels butin the whole complex of corresponding cultural values — in mythology andritual, in social relations, in views on nature and ethics. This motivationevidently has its own principles, its semantic and structural rules that repeatthemselves in different traditions. A number of ancient and mediaeval treatisesdealing especially with dream interpretation provide an indispensable materialfor the study of such regularities, for the analysis of similarities anddigressions testified in different systems of symbols. At the same time, wefind here unique data on corresponding cultural traditions in its originalityand in affinity with other traditions, including our own.We shall refer here tosome traits of Ancient Indian interpretation of dreams — namely, on thematerial of Svapnacintāmaṇi («Magic jewel of dreams») written byJagaddeva (JS) — one of the most exhaustive and well known Indian specimenof this genre1. It was compiledrelatively late (XII–XIII cc.) on the basis of earlier texts as Jagaddevahimself remarks (JS 2.160).Indiantradition of dream interpretation is represented in numerous texts — theearliest Vedic hymns, in epic poetry, above all — the purāṇas(Agni, Bhaviṣya, Matsya a.o.) where certain chapters constitute in factindependent treatises on dreams, in narrative prose literature, in texts onnatural sciences etc. To mention some of these testimonies2 we can begin with the hymns of Ṛgveda.The notion of «evil dream» (duḥsvapna) played a prominent role in theVedic world outlook — cf. corresponding motifs in Rv 5.82.4; 8.47.14–183; 10.36.4;10.37.4 etc. One can be reminded of characteristic invocations to the Sun(Sūrya, Savitar — cf. also JS 1.22), to the goddess of Dawn (Uṣas).The charms of «killing evil dreams» (duḥsvapnaghna — cf.Rv 10.164)4 are found inAtharvaveda as well (cf. Av 6.45; 16.6; 7; 19.56; 57 etc.) — inparticular the reign of Yama, god of Death, is called here the source of suchdreams. An important testimony is preserved in the poetical supplement toAv-Atharvapariśiṣṭa in72 chapters dealing with different rites and prophecies. It was compiledevidently in late Vedic period (ca. middle of the 1st millennium B. C.)and thus precedes the major part of ancient Indian texts on the subject5. Its last five chapters (Athp 61–72) areespecially dedicated to dreams. In particular, Athp 68 deals with connectionsbetween dreams and man’s temperament and distinguishes between dreams that donot require interpretation (caused by physiological factors or by certainevents experienced before) and those sent by gods and having prophetic value.Further concrete explanations are given; they are divided (like JS) into twoparts — auspicious and non-auspicious. A part of them is dedicatedespecially to kings and their actions. Certain means against evil dreams arelikewise recommended (cf. JS 1.21 sq.)There are evidences ondreams in other parts of the Vedic canon — in brāhmaṇas,āraṇyakas, upaniṣads. Such is e.g. the text of Aitareyaāraṇyaka 3.2.4.17–18, mentioning some unfavorable dreams, known toJagaddeva also (connected with black colour, with moving southward, withassault of boars or monkeys etc.) and advising how to prevent undesirableconsequences (fasting, observing milk ration, reading ofRv. 10.127 etc.)6. Wefind here also certain views on the nature of dreams. Texts of early Upaniṣads —Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Chāndogya, Kauṣītaki, Aitareya,Maitrī, Praśna, Māṇḍūkya —are perhaps most instructive7. So Bu IV.3; Mnu 3 sq.; Mtu VIIset forth a theory of the four states: 1) waking (jāgaritasthāna); 2) dream (svapna sthāna), when the conscience is stillinfluenced by exterior objects, man continues to experience different affects(e. g. fear) and experiences dreams; 3) deep sleep (suṣuptasthāna) when the person is freed from notions and affects connected withthe external world, ceases to feel his own individuality and does notexperience dreams; 4) a transcendental state of emerging in highestreality (turīya, verbally: «the fourth»). According to their dogmatics,the Upaniṣads pay special attention to the last two states (cf.Bu II.1.16 sq.; Cu IV.3.3; VI.8.1–2; VIII.6.3; VIII.10–12; KsuIV.19–20; Pu IV.1 sq.; etc.). The state of deep sleep is sometimes equatedhere with death (Bu IV.4.1 sq.; Cu VIII.6.3 sq.; Ksu III.3). Bu IV.3.14advises not to wake the sleeping person suddenly for it can result in disease«that is difficult to cure» (cf. analogous notion in ŚX.5.2.12)8.At the same time, we find here some concrete interpretations (cf.Cu V.2.7–8; auspicious meaning of dreaming of a woman after performingcertain rites).Similar notions aredeveloped further in epic poetry. We read about dreams in Mahābhārataand Rāmāyana (cf. II.69; V.27). The most valuable material ispreserved, however, in relatively later poems — purāṇas datedapproximately from IV–V cc. A.D. Some of them contain special chaptersdedicated to dreams. Such is the 229 chapter of Agni purāṇa,beginning with auspicious dreams, followed by non-auspicious (cf. alsoAp. 231 dedicated to different omens). Omens and dream interpretations arefound respectively in 241–242 chapters of Matsya purāṇa; from otherpuranic texts we can mention Bhaviṣya (194), Brahmavaivarta (Kṛṣṇajanmakhaṇḍa.63, 70, 77, 82), Mārkaṇḍeya (40, 43 etc.), Vāyu(19 — near to Mārkaṇḍeya 43), Garuḍa (UttarakhaṇḍaXI), etc. These chapters are usually designated as «chapters on dreams»(svapnādhyāya); often they functioned independently fromcorresponding poems. On the other hand, some evidently independent treatiseswere ascribed to certain greater texts — perhaps to make them moreauthoritative. Such is e.g. Svapnādhyāya from the collection of theDepartment of Manuscripts in the Institute of Oriental Studies in Leningrad(Ms. Ind. II.19) — it resembles Bvp but according to Colophon is ascribedto Skanda purāna; the sequence of dreams reminds here of Ap., JS etc.9. Among other specimen of thisgenre — a relatively late treatise Svapnādhyāya ofĀcāramayūkha, Adbhutasāgara of Vallālasena etc.10. There are two Mss published byR. Harshe11. One of them,according to the editor, is of Jaina origin and was compiled not later than inXIV–XV cc. Its first and last lines are lost; in preserved ślokas (4–94) predictions are alternated(one favourable — one unfavourable). The second Ms. — also withoutbeginning and end — is still later (ca. XVII c). The text is partlynear to the previous one and is also built on the principle of alternationthough not so strict.Ancient views on dreams,including concrete interpretations and more general notions, are reflected insome scientific treatises, particularly on medicine12. Their authors are partly referred to in JS 2.160(Bhadrabāhu, Suśruta,Vācaspati, Caraka, cf. also Athp 68.1.1–2; Kroṣṭuki, Śaunaka); some of these names are perhapslegendary. In particular, SuśrutaSaṃhitā was compiled in first century A.D.; it includes (in chapter29) a number of such interpretations; the author of Caraka Saṃhitāwas said to be the court physician of Kanishka. In another treatise — Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha of Vāgbhaṭa(VII C.) in the sixth chapter (svapnādhyāya) of the part concerningbody (śarīra) we find firstpositive and then negative interpretations.There are also numerousevidences in texts of different genres where the motif of dream is significantfor their composition or didactics. Such is e.g. the playSvapnavasavadattā ascribed to Bhāsa (ca.IV c. A.D.). The same can besaid of fables13 — cf. theframe story of the fifth book of Pañcatantra (see JS I.5, below, note27), some subjects of Kathāsaritsāgara, Vikramacarita (23) etc. wherebesides concrete interpretations certain theories are exposed, e.g. thedependency of the term of dream’s realization on the time of dreaming (seebelow). In Kīrtikaumudī 84 of Someśvaradeva(XIIIc.) we read about the custom of telling the dream to the father (cf. JSI.19)14. The Sūtraliterature (cf. Thus, for example, the upaniṣadicviews on the deep sleep are reflected in śaktism(Tripūrarahasya)16, inKashmir śivaism — cf. Śiva- sūtraof Vasugupta (IX c.), in Kṣemendra’s commentary on it (ca.X–XII cc.), etc.17. Ideasabout light dreams (svapna) and deep sleep (suṣupti) were developed alsoin sāṃkhya18; they are evidently reflected in theYoga’s notion of pratyāhāra (cf. about sleep — nidrā inYoga-sūtra I.6.10; 38)19.Authors of vaiśeṣika systemwere interested in physiological and psychological grounds of dream — seee.g. Kaṇāda’s Vaiśeṣika-sūtraIX. 2.7. Analogous problems were discussed also in the Buddhist tradition.So Milindapañha (IV.8.33 sq.) distinguishes six different kinds ofdreams: those caused by one of the three elements in organism — «wind»,bile or phlegm (vāta, pitta, śleṣma),dreams sent by God, caused by one’s own actions and at last — «prophetic»dreams — the only ones serving as omens.
