B. C.) mentioned above — cf. e.g.on dreams of Devānandā, Mahāvīra’s mother (Kalpa-sūtra 1)21.Svapnacintāmaṇiis preserved under the name of Jagaddeva of whom very little is known. In theend of every part of JS the name of his father — Durlabharāja —is mentioned. The latter was the son of Narasiṃhaand wrote a treatise on prophecies. This treatise (Sāmudratilaka) wascompiled in 1160 A. D. under the Guzerat ruler Kumārapāla andwas finished by Jagaddeva himself22.The author of Svapnacintāmaṇi thus lived evidently in the secondhalf of XII — the beginning of XIII century, at any rate much later thansome authors used and mentioned by him (Caraka, Suśrutaetc.) or Vāgbhata — a famous authority in medicine23.JS is preserved in severalmanuscripts used in J. v. Negelein’s critical edition24. It consists of two parts of 15, 150and 161 strophes respectively in āryā metre (based on determinedquantity of feet with certain variations of the number of syllables in each;its two hemistiches consist of 7 or 8 feet each with caesura after the thirdfoot; the length of a single foot is usually 4 units). Some verses presentdigressions from this scheme caused perhaps by copyist’s mistakes25.The versified form of adidactic or scientific treatise is rather common in Indian literary tradition.This form, however, does not exhaust the artistic qualities of JS. Jagaddevaoften uses alliterations, assonances, word-repetitions which occur not so oftenin this genre. These devices encompass a prominent part of the text leadingsometimes to peculiar choice of synonyms26.From another device a chiasmus can be mentioned here.The first part of JS isdedicated to auspicious (śubhāni)dreams, the second to non-auspicious (aśubhāni) —cf. the composition of Ācāramayūkha’s Svapnādhyāya,Agni purāṇa 279 and some other texts (not Indian only — cf.below). The digressions from this principle are few (cf. 2.46, 49a,49b, 145a in JN) and can be explained by corruptions ofthe original text.In the first part aftertraditional invocation to Sarasvatī, goddess of eloquence, sciences andarts (1.1) some general notions on dreams are exposed (1.2 sq.); theirrole with reference to physical and moral qualities of man (1.3),classification of dreams according to their prophetic significance(1.4–5) — six kinds that do not bring results (niṣphalam —i.e.caused by things heard, experienced, seen, corresponding to one’s own nature,caused by worry and by disturbances in health) and three that are prophetic(brought about by God, by one’s own merits and by sins). Further (1.6) someother dreams that bear no consequences are mentioned — those experiencedduring daytime, often repeating themselves, quickly replacing one another etc.(1.6–8), partly they illustrate the cases already summed up in 1.4. Certaininterdependency is established between the character of things appearing indreams and man’s temperament connected with predominance of one of the threeelements — «wind», bile or phlegm (l.9–14 cf. above onMilindapañha). Another interdependency — between the exact time ofthe dream occurrence and the term of its realization: the later in the night wego through the dream — the sooner it results in reality (1.15–17).Jagaddeva advises how to preserve the effectiveness of auspicious dreams and toprevent non-auspicious; when such contrary omens replace one another the lastone is decisive (1.18–24). Further the concrete interpretation of favourabledreams follows (1.25–147). Last verses of the first part (1.148–150) containmore general notes — particularly on reverse meaning of gain and loss ofcertain objects or of the same omen seen in dreams and in everyday life(lokavyavahāra), on predominant symbolics of black and white colours. Thesecond part is more homogeneous. After corresponding announcement (2.1)Jagaddeva begins directly with the non-auspicious interpretations (2.2–155).More general remarks are almost absent here (cf. only 2.73, on dying within ayear after having constantly experienced very unfavourable dreams beforewaking) and appear only in concluding verses (2.156–159). It is also said herethat the results refer only to the person dreamt about (2.157) and that traditionaleveryday omens preserve their meaning in dreams as well (2.158 — a possiblecontradiction with 1.149; see below). The ablution is advised as a purifyingmeans after certain deeds including daydreams (2.159). Indeed,Jagaddeva’s interpretation encompasses a large scope of Indian life. Besidesinformation on dreams themselves and on their connection with physiological andpsychological factors (cf. JS 1.2 sq., 2.156 sq.), we find here someother notions reflecting the level of Indian natural science — about thehuman body, its functions (1.8 sq., 34, 37, 55, 99; 2.44, 45, 61, 154,159) and affects (1.8, 12, 65, 70; 2.43, 74, 153). As we see JS has manifoldly reflected different aspects of Indianculture.Apart from theintroductory (1.1–2; 2.1) and concluding (2.160–161) stereotype verses, thetext of JS can be divided into three parts generally following each other. Thefirst can be conditionally called «diagnostic» (1.4, 9–14). The phenomena ofdream, its sources and contents are explained here according to physical andpsychic state of person. The second part is «pragmatic» (1.5–8, 15–24; 2.159).It deals first of all with evaluation of the dream in respect to its efficiency(disregarding its positive or negative meaning). The prophetic andnon-prophetic dreams are specified here (1.5–8; cf. above)27. Further, the term of the dream’srealization is settled according to the time of dreaming. The dream of thefirst night watch (yāma; 6–9 p. m.) is realized within one year;of the second (9–12 p.m.) — within six months, of the third(0–3 a. m.) — within three months, of the fourth(3–6 a. m.) — within one month, of the last two ghaṭikasof the night28 — withinten days. The dream visioned during the sunrise is realized on the same day(1.15–17). «Pragmatic» precepts include also means to preserve the result ofauspicious omens and to prevent the non-auspicious ones (1.18–24; the principleof comparative efficacy of the dream visioned later is used here). One of theconcluding verses (2.159), containing similar advice for necessary purificationcan also be regarded as a part of these precepts. The third part can be called«semantic». It includes the actual interpretations constituting the main bodyof JS. Some inherent principles of this part will be discussed below.A large part is dedicatedhere to interpretations themselves, i.e. correlating definite dreams withdefinite results. There are, however, several verses containing more generaloperational rules concerning different dreams (cf. above on 1.148–149;2.156–158).The dreams interpreted byJagaddeva can be divided into those represented by simple signs and those bycomposite signs. Simple signs are reduced to single actions, qualities ofsubjects (or objects) emerging in dreams or to single objects which by themselvesare consigned by a positive or a negative meaning. The composite signs suggestdefinite situations where a number of elements (actions, qualities etc.) canusually be traced without difficulty — these elements are as a rule,identified by their function of simple signs with unequivocal sense whichdetermines the meaning of the whole situation. The boundary between these twokinds of signs is sometimes rather conditional (cf. e.g., such situations asmilking the cow with one’s own mouth or playing the reed (1.92) etc. (cf.below).There are morecharacteristic positive simple signs (used either separately or combined withthe composite signs). Actions and situations: ascending, mounting (a tree, ahill, a palace etc. — 1.25, 33, 43, 63, 79, 84–88, 94, 95, 109,132 etc.),victory over enemies (1.40, 41), release from bonds (1.60), drinking (ofintoxicating liquor, of water from a tank etc — 1.35, 60, 90, 113 etc.),irrigation (1.112), playing the reed, vīṇa, tūrya (1.92, 108,127); hearing a song, sounds of animals (1.135), weeping, lamenting (1.70),catching animals, birds, fishing (1.114, 117); there are also some supernaturalactions often including certain additional signs — swallowing sun or moon,transformation of hand into banner, growing of bush out of one’s navel29 etc. (1.31, 108 etc.). This peculiar complementarity of dream and vigilance is reflectedin a number of cases. One cansuppose that this principle does not refer to situations which functioned asomens (nimittāni) in everyday life for the latter according to traditionalviews (cf. 2.158) preserved their significance in dreams as well43. As we know, the dream interpretationswere included in a broader sphere of different omens and this connection isreflected in the composition of certain texts (cf. corresponding chapters ofAp, Mp etc.). Jagaddeva himself sometimes goes beyond the frames ofdreams — so, for example, in 2.54 the penetration of bees into the houseis said to be unfavourable «in dreams and by daytime as well» (svapne divasethavā); in 2.127 certain tastes (astringent, salty etc.) that «bythemselves are unpleasant to men» are also interpreted negatively in dreamsand so on.At the same time one moreprinciple carried out rather consistently can be established here — theopposite interpretation of opposed objects, qualities or situations. Thus, e.g. the man whose legs are pulled by lion, elephant,crocodile, or by another man must be freed soon, if by that time he isimprisoned or to be imprisoned if he is free (2.46). Among such ambivalent signs we can name a wedding(1.47–2.27, 74, 148)46, losingcertain parts of the body (1.27 sq. — 2.6 sq.), death (1.46,131–2.154), binding (1.61–2.10), competition (1.40–42, 52, 61–2.141)47, playing the lute (vīṇā1.73, 127–2.61), rain (1.77–2.95)48,fire (1.74, 75, 77, 80, 111 etc. — 2.88, 134)49, snake (1.26, 81, 109, 115–2.10, 11, 16, 78), bee(1.64–2.23, 54), rice (vrīhl 1.30, 38, 96, 126–2.28, 31, 107, 125, 126),lotus (1.65, 67, 93–2.29), certain plants (lavalī 1.142–2.116; marica,black pepper 1.141–2.124), grain (1.125, 126–2.88, 97, 125, 126), wreath (1.90,133; 2.150–2.49, 62, 69), plant growing from one’s own body (1.108 — 2.34–36;cf. above, note 29), sickle (1.147–2.132)50.Themost usual result of the positive dream — its «signified» — isforthcoming welfare in this or that form (vṛddhi, śubham, śivam,grace of goddess Lakṣmī etc. — 1.37, 39–41, 44, 50, 57, 89,138,139, etc. — altogether about half of the interpretations of the firstpart. Then follows receiving gold, money etc., the expression «wealth andgrain» — dhana-dyānya is also frequent (1.42, 47, 58, 82, 87etc.) — about one-fourth of all positive prophecies. Another frequentpromise— kingship, power (1.25, 27, 29, 31–33 etc — about one-fifth).Among relatively rare predictions — progeny (1.27, 32, 54, 61, 84), happymarriage (1.64, 73, 78, 104), recovering from illness (1.46, 83), duty ofcounsellor (1.91) mental achievements (buddhi-siddhi — 1.93) etc. In thesecond part the most common «signified» is likewise general mentioning of theunfavourable situation — misfortune, suffering (aśubham, kaṣṭam, duḥkhametc. — 2.8,15–19, 21, 23, 26, 39 etc.) — over one-third of allnegative predictions. With approximately the same frequency the death isforetold — its circumstances are sometimes described here; on the next day(2.40, 41), in the course of five days (2.12, 24), in the course of a year(2.73), from certain diseases — leprosy (kuṣṭha — 2.29),consumption (kṣaya — 2.31 cf. 89), dysentery(atīsāra — 2.32) etc. In comparison with the first part, theloss of wealth, particularly of dhana-dhānya (cf. 2.2, 3, 7, 22, 37 etc.)is rarely (about one-tenth) mentioned. Among other misfortunes we find herediseases (2.44, 64, 144 etc.), troubles from the king (2.3, 101, 151), death ofwife (2.5, 14) and children (2.6), fire (2.33), exile (2.44), imprisonment (2.46) etc.Thecomparison of Jagaddeva’s work with other ancient Indian sources shows howcertain ideas concerning the nature of dreams were preserved in Indiantradition for thousands of years — from archaic Vedic hymns down tomediaeval treatises and it elucidates some specific traits of classical Indianculture. On the other hand, it presents a large material for further parallelspermitting to establish certain typological affinities and divergencies ofdifferent traditions. We come thus to perceive some more general principles ofdream interpretation, and therefore to understand better certain relevanttraits of natural and humanitarian phenomena. Rich material for suchinvestigation is supplied already by other ancient traditions51, beginning perhaps with the oldestinterpretations of Egyptian papyrus — Chester Beatty III (ca. 2000–1790B.C.), like JS dealing first with auspicious and then with non-auspcious dreams52. Apart from these testimonies(Babylonian, Assyrian, Hebrew, Greek, Roman, Muslim, Mediaeval European etc.),we can find perhaps still further examples in frames of oral folkloretradition, that can be traced back to most ancient times and doubtlessly servedas a source for the tradition of literary (and «scientific») interpretationdiscussed above53.Thenumerous analogies drawn from these sources evidently go beyond the scope ofpresumable coincidence and are not accidental. One can suppose that definitepatterns of mentality and psychology are reflected here; as a result, a certainaffinity of notions and symbols can be traced along the history of humanculture54. Among suchparallels, first of all some more general principles of dream-theory must bespecified. Referring to designations proposed above, we can begin with«diagnostic» universalities: views on dependence of dream upon temperament,upon the mental and physical state of man can be mentioned55. Another kind of universalities is«pragmatic» — distinctions between dreams influenced by a certain event,i.e. non-prophetic, and those demanding interpretation with possible hierarchyset among them56, belief in thedecisive role of the last dream in the night (the later the dream is seen, thesooner it will bring results)57and so on. The next, perhaps the largest sphere of analogies is presented by anumber of «semantic» universalities. Among them we can likewise discern somemore general rules. Such is e.g. the principle of opposite interpretation ofopposed situations, qualities, etc.58.Another principle is the complementarity of the same sign’s meaning in dreamand in reality. Such tendency displays itself e.g. in positive interpretationsof crying, grief, burial and negative — of laughter, joy, marriage etc.testified in different and evidently independent sources — ancient Egyptian,Indian, Arabian, Byzantine, Russian, Estonian, Karaite and so on59. At last there are certainuniversalities in respect of concrete signs — actions, objects,situations. Such are, respectively, positive and negative meanings of black andwhite60, rise and fall61,favourable interpretation of blood62, of mirror63,associations between excrements and gold64, unfavourableinterpretations of clergy, of teeth falling out65, of snake66,monkey, tiger67, etc.The analysis of thoseparallels is the subject of special investigations. Corresponding worksinevitably go beyond the scope of dream itself and involve important problemsof mythology, folklore, technique of artistic creations etc. These ties havealready been discussed in some works68,One of such connections concerns the role of dreams in myth creation, on onehand, and the reflection of myth in the material of dream on the other69, Likewise mutual for both spheres aresymbols of tree, snake, fire; such motifs as meeting the dead, nakedness etc.We have seen that JS and other texts often mention certain gods, spirits,mythological objects etc. — such as, for example, celestial treefulfilling desires and presenting its positive meaning in dream70,interpretations concerning certain animals — elephant, cow, gooseetc. — playing a prominent role in Indian mythology71,references to more general ideas and symbols72. Among motifswidespread in other traditions one can be reminded of a tree growing out ofone’s body (cf. above, n. 29), the symbolism of horse, deer, bear,insects, snakes etc73. The samerefers to the sphere of ritual — its connection with dreams also deservesspecial attention. We have already mentioned some details of Hindu ritual asreflected in JS — cf. also on sacrificial butter (1.134 — JN, 140),grass (darbha — 2.36), and other accessories of sacrifice (2.88 etc., cf.JN 352–353)74, on details ofburial ceremonies (2.40, 48 — JN 236), on certain ritual prohibitions andimpurity (1.60, 113; 2.24, 25, 159 etc. — cf. JN 118 sq.). There arelikewise numerous testimonies of dream sacralization in other traditions (cf.ancient Greek rituals in the sanctuary of Asclepios, rituals ofGermans, etc.).Other problems areconnected rather with folklore and literary studies. The interaction of dream andoral folk tradition seems to be quite natural since the latter usually includessuch interpretations as its component (cf. publications mentioned above inn. 37, 59 etc.). We find here numerous thematic reflections (e.g. the roleof hero’s prophetic dream in fairy tales) and common traits of symbolics75. The same can be said of thecorresponding motifs of literary artistic traditions (cf. for example, popularlikening of life to dream — in Calderon’s «La Vida es sueño» a.o.)beginning with the most archaic texts — epos of Gilgamesh, Bible (cf.dreams of Joseph — Genesis 37, 5 sq.; 40, 5 sq.), Homeros etc.76.The dream often plays a decisive role not only in the plot but in thecomposition of the text — one can be reminded of M. Lermontov’s«Dream» — «a dream in cube» according to V. S. Soloviev’s aptexpression77; books of L. Carrol on Alice78 etc. Inthis respect the role of dream in creating an artistic text deserves specialattention (cf. creative activity of Goethe, Hoffmann, Heine, Hebbel, Maupassant,Flaubert, Baudelaire etc.)79. Similar problems arise in studyingfigurative art (works of Goya, of surrealists like Max Ernst, Delvaux etc.)80.These structural and semantic ties suggest further search for inherent traitsof a dream considered as a message in its own specific «language»; it isprobable that the study of this «language» can help for a better understandingof some linguistic phenomena81.And one more aspect of thesubject’s value can be reminded — the pragmatic one. Independently fromits verisimilitude, every such interpretation (like other kinds of predictions)by itself lessens in our opinion the uncertainty of forthcoming events82, and thus plays an importantpsychotherapeutic and regulating (in certain respect functionally near to scientific)role. It is to remember that our inherent (one may say biological) tendency toreduce the degree of such uncertainty cannot be satisfied by rationalistic waysonly — the history of civilization obviously demonstrates it.  NOTES 1 Der Traumschlüssel desJagaddeva. The scientific interestfor the analysis of dream interpretations needs not be justified. Independentlyfrom the practical evaluation of its plausibility by modern man, we can assumethat every single interpretation of the kind is by no means arbitrary. It hasits own motivation — not only on psychological or physiological levels butin the whole complex of corresponding cultural values — in mythology andritual, in social relations, in views on nature and ethics. This motivationevidently has its own principles, its semantic and structural rules that repeatthemselves in different traditions. A number of ancient and mediaeval treatisesdealing especially with dream interpretation provide an indispensable materialfor the study of such regularities, for the analysis of similarities anddigressions testified in different systems of symbols. At the same time, wefind here unique data on corresponding cultural traditions in its originalityand in affinity with other traditions, including our own.

We shall refer here tosome traits of Ancient Indian interpretation of dreams — namely, on thematerial of Svapnacintāmaṇi («Magic jewel of dreams») written byJagaddeva (JS) — one of the most exhaustive and well known Indian specimenof this genre1. It was compiledrelatively late (XII–XIII cc.) on the basis of earlier texts as Jagaddevahimself remarks (JS 2.160).

Indiantradition of dream interpretation is represented in numerous texts — theearliest Vedic hymns, in epic poetry, above all — the purāṇas(Agni, Bhaviṣya, Matsya a.o.) where certain chapters constitute in factindependent treatises on dreams, in narrative prose literature, in texts onnatural sciences etc. To mention some of these testimonies2 we can begin with the hymns of Ṛgveda.The notion of «evil dream» (duḥsvapna) played a prominent role in theVedic world outlook — cf. corresponding motifs in Rv 5.82.4; 8.47.14–183; 10.36.4;10.37.4 etc. One can be reminded of characteristic invocations to the Sun(Sūrya, Savitar — cf. also JS 1.22), to the goddess of Dawn (Uṣas).The charms of «killing evil dreams» (duḥsvapnaghna — cf.Rv 10.164)4 are found inAtharvaveda as well (cf. Av 6.45; 16.6; 7; 19.56; 57 etc.) — inparticular the reign of Yama, god of Death, is called here the source of suchdreams. An important testimony is preserved in the poetical supplement toAv-Atharvapariśiṣṭa in72 chapters dealing with different rites and prophecies. It was compiledevidently in late Vedic period (ca. middle of the 1st millennium B. C.)and thus precedes the major part of ancient Indian texts on the subject5. Its last five chapters (Athp 61–72) areespecially dedicated to dreams. In particular, Athp 68 deals with connectionsbetween dreams and man’s temperament and distinguishes between dreams that donot require interpretation (caused by physiological factors or by certainevents experienced before) and those sent by gods and having prophetic value.Further concrete explanations are given; they are divided (like JS) into twoparts — auspicious and non-auspicious. A part of them is dedicatedespecially to kings and their actions. Certain means against evil dreams arelikewise recommended (cf. JS 1.21 sq.)

There are evidences ondreams in other parts of the Vedic canon — in brāhmaṇas,āraṇyakas, upaniṣads. Such is e.g. the text of Aitareyaāraṇyaka 3.2.4.17–18, mentioning some unfavorable dreams, known toJagaddeva also (connected with black colour, with moving southward, withassault of boars or monkeys etc.) and advising how to prevent undesirableconsequences (fasting, observing milk ration, reading ofRv. 10.127 etc.)6. Wefind here also certain views on the nature of dreams. Texts of early Upaniṣads —Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Chāndogya, Kauṣītaki, Aitareya,Maitrī, Praśna, Māṇḍūkya —are perhaps most instructive7. So Bu IV.3; Mnu 3 sq.; Mtu VIIset forth a theory of the four states: 1) waking (jāgaritasthāna); 2) dream (svapna sthāna), when the conscience is stillinfluenced by exterior objects, man continues to experience different affects(e. g. fear) and experiences dreams; 3) deep sleep (suṣuptasthāna) when the person is freed from notions and affects connected withthe external world, ceases to feel his own individuality and does notexperience dreams; 4) a transcendental state of emerging in highestreality (turīya, verbally: «the fourth»). According to their dogmatics,the Upaniṣads pay special attention to the last two states (cf.Bu II.1.16 sq.; Cu IV.3.3; VI.8.1–2; VIII.6.3; VIII.10–12; KsuIV.19–20; Pu IV.1 sq.; etc.). The state of deep sleep is sometimes equatedhere with death (Bu IV.4.1 sq.; Cu VIII.6.3 sq.; Ksu III.3). Bu IV.3.14advises not to wake the sleeping person suddenly for it can result in disease«that is difficult to cure» (cf. analogous notion in ŚX.5.2.12)8.At the same time, we find here some concrete interpretations (cf.Cu V.2.7–8; auspicious meaning of dreaming of a woman after performingcertain rites).

Similar notions aredeveloped further in epic poetry. We read about dreams in Mahābhārataand Rāmāyana (cf. II.69; V.27). The most valuable material ispreserved, however, in relatively later poems — purāṇas datedapproximately from IV–V cc. A.D. Some of them contain special chaptersdedicated to dreams. Such is the 229 chapter of Agni purāṇa,beginning with auspicious dreams, followed by non-auspicious (cf. alsoAp. 231 dedicated to different omens). Omens and dream interpretations arefound respectively in 241–242 chapters of Matsya purāṇa; from otherpuranic texts we can mention Bhaviṣya (194), Brahmavaivarta (Kṛṣṇajanmakhaṇḍa.63, 70, 77, 82), Mārkaṇḍeya (40, 43 etc.), Vāyu(19 — near to Mārkaṇḍeya 43), Garuḍa (UttarakhaṇḍaXI), etc. These chapters are usually designated as «chapters on dreams»(svapnādhyāya); often they functioned independently fromcorresponding poems. On the other hand, some evidently independent treatiseswere ascribed to certain greater texts — perhaps to make them moreauthoritative. Such is e.g. Svapnādhyāya from the collection of theDepartment of Manuscripts in the Institute of Oriental Studies in Leningrad(Ms. Ind. II.19) — it resembles Bvp but according to Colophon is ascribedto Skanda purāna; the sequence of dreams reminds here of Ap., JS etc.9. Among other specimen of thisgenre — a relatively late treatise Svapnādhyāya ofĀcāramayūkha, Adbhutasāgara of Vallālasena etc.10. There are two Mss published byR. Harshe11. One of them,according to the editor, is of Jaina origin and was compiled not later than inXIV–XV cc. Its first and last lines are lost; in preserved ślokas (4–94) predictions are alternated(one favourable — one unfavourable). The second Ms. — also withoutbeginning and end — is still later (ca. XVII c). The text is partlynear to the previous one and is also built on the principle of alternationthough not so strict.

Ancient views on dreams,including concrete interpretations and more general notions, are reflected insome scientific treatises, particularly on medicine12. Their authors are partly referred to in JS 2.160(Bhadrabāhu, Suśruta,Vācaspati, Caraka, cf. also Athp 68.1.1–2; Kroṣṭuki, Śaunaka); some of these names are perhapslegendary. In particular, SuśrutaSaṃhitā was compiled in first century A.D.; it includes (in chapter29) a number of such interpretations; the author of Caraka Saṃhitāwas said to be the court physician of Kanishka. In another treatise — Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha of Vāgbhaṭa(VII C.) in the sixth chapter (svapnādhyāya) of the part concerningbody (śarīra) we find firstpositive and then negative interpretations.

There are also numerousevidences in texts of different genres where the motif of dream is significantfor their composition or didactics. Such is e.g. the playSvapnavasavadattā ascribed to Bhāsa (ca.IV c. A.D.). The same can besaid of fables13 — cf. theframe story of the fifth book of Pañcatantra (see JS I.5, below, note27), some subjects of Kathāsaritsāgara, Vikramacarita (23) etc. wherebesides concrete interpretations certain theories are exposed, e.g. thedependency of the term of dream’s realization on the time of dreaming (seebelow). In Kīrtikaumudī 84 of Someśvaradeva(XIIIc.) we read about the custom of telling the dream to the father (cf. JSI.19)14. The Sūtraliterature (cf. Āśvalāyana gṛhyasūtraIII.6.5 sq.; Gobhila gṛhyasūtra III 3.32 etc.) like Rvrecommends invocations to Sun in order to render an evil dream harmless.Traditional ideas on dreams were developed in later ethico-philosophical texts15 — of Vedānta (Śaṃkara,Rāmānuja) and other schools. Thus, for example, the upaniṣadicviews on the deep sleep are reflected in śaktism(Tripūrarahasya)16, inKashmir śivaism — cf. Śiva- sūtraof Vasugupta (IX c.), in Kṣemendra’s commentary on it (ca.X–XII cc.), etc.17. Ideasabout light dreams (svapna) and deep sleep (suṣupti) were developed alsoin sāṃkhya18; they are evidently reflected in theYoga’s notion of pratyāhāra (cf. about sleep — nidrā inYoga-sūtra I.6.10; 38)19.Authors of vaiśeṣika systemwere interested in physiological and psychological grounds of dream — seee.g. Kaṇāda’s Vaiśeṣika-sūtraIX. 2.7. Analogous problems were discussed also in the Buddhist tradition.So Milindapañha (IV.8.33 sq.) distinguishes six different kinds ofdreams: those caused by one of the three elements in organism — «wind»,bile or phlegm (vāta, pitta, śleṣma),dreams sent by God, caused by one’s own actions and at last — «prophetic»dreams — the only ones serving as omens. Dream-motif often recurs inBuddhist narrative literature — cf. Divyāvadāna XXVII,Jātaka 77, Lalitavistara VI, XIV, etc.20.Among Jaina evidences we can name Kalpa-sūtraof Bhadrabāhu (ca. IV. c. B. C.) mentioned above — cf. e.g.on dreams of Devānandā, Mahāvīra’s mother (Kalpa-sūtra 1)21.

Svapnacintāmaṇiis preserved under the name of Jagaddeva of whom very little is known. In theend of every part of JS the name of his father — Durlabharāja —is mentioned. The latter was the son of Narasiṃhaand wrote a treatise on prophecies. This treatise (Sāmudratilaka) wascompiled in 1160 A. D. under the Guzerat ruler Kumārapāla andwas finished by Jagaddeva himself22.The author of Svapnacintāmaṇi thus lived evidently in the secondhalf of XII — the beginning of XIII century, at any rate much later thansome authors used and mentioned by him (Caraka, Suśrutaetc.) or Vāgbhata — a famous authority in medicine23.

JS is preserved in severalmanuscripts used in J. v. Negelein’s critical edition24. It consists of two parts of 15, 150and 161 strophes respectively in āryā metre (based on determinedquantity of feet with certain variations of the number of syllables in each;its two hemistiches consist of 7 or 8 feet each with caesura after the thirdfoot; the length of a single foot is usually 4 units). Some verses presentdigressions from this scheme caused perhaps by copyist’s mistakes25.

The versified form of adidactic or scientific treatise is rather common in Indian literary tradition.This form, however, does not exhaust the artistic qualities of JS. Jagaddevaoften uses alliterations, assonances, word-repetitions which occur not so oftenin this genre. These devices encompass a prominent part of the text leadingsometimes to peculiar choice of synonyms26.From another device a chiasmus can be mentioned here.

The first part of JS isdedicated to auspicious (śubhāni)dreams, the second to non-auspicious (aśubhāni) —cf. the composition of Ācāramayūkha’s Svapnādhyāya,Agni purāṇa 279 and some other texts (not Indian only — cf.below). The digressions from this principle are few (cf. 2.46, 49a,49b, 145a in JN) and can be explained by corruptions ofthe original text.

In the first part aftertraditional invocation to Sarasvatī, goddess of eloquence, sciences andarts (1.1) some general notions on dreams are exposed (1.2 sq.); theirrole with reference to physical and moral qualities of man (1.3),classification of dreams according to their prophetic significance(1.4–5) — six kinds that do not bring results (niṣphalam —i.e.caused by things heard, experienced, seen, corresponding to one’s own nature,caused by worry and by disturbances in health) and three that are prophetic(brought about by God, by one’s own merits and by sins). Further (1.6) someother dreams that bear no consequences are mentioned — those experiencedduring daytime, often repeating themselves, quickly replacing one another etc.(1.6–8), partly they illustrate the cases already summed up in 1.4. Certaininterdependency is established between the character of things appearing indreams and man’s temperament connected with predominance of one of the threeelements — «wind», bile or phlegm (l.9–14 cf. above onMilindapañha). Another interdependency — between the exact time ofthe dream occurrence and the term of its realization: the later in the night wego through the dream — the sooner it results in reality (1.15–17).Jagaddeva advises how to preserve the effectiveness of auspicious dreams and toprevent non-auspicious; when such contrary omens replace one another the lastone is decisive (1.18–24). Further the concrete interpretation of favourabledreams follows (1.25–147). Last verses of the first part (1.148–150) containmore general notes — particularly on reverse meaning of gain and loss ofcertain objects or of the same omen seen in dreams and in everyday life(lokavyavahāra), on predominant symbolics of black and white colours. Thesecond part is more homogeneous. After corresponding announcement (2.1)Jagaddeva begins directly with the non-auspicious interpretations (2.2–155).More general remarks are almost absent here (cf. only 2.73, on dying within ayear after having constantly experienced very unfavourable dreams beforewaking) and appear only in concluding verses (2.156–159). It is also said herethat the results refer only to the person dreamt about (2.157) and that traditionaleveryday omens preserve their meaning in dreams as well (2.158 — a possiblecontradiction with 1.149; see below). The ablution is advised as a purifyingmeans after certain deeds including daydreams (2.159). The last verses(2.160–161), in conformity with tradition, name Jagaddeva’ s predecessors andspeak about the might of him who «knows the intentions of another’s heart andthe essence of another’s words» (an expert in dream interpretation is evidentlymeant here).

According to JS 2.156«There is no such an object in the world, animated or not animated, that couldnot appear in dreams» — otherwise cannot function as a sign. Indeed,Jagaddeva’s interpretation encompasses a large scope of Indian life. Besidesinformation on dreams themselves and on their connection with physiological andpsychological factors (cf. JS 1.2 sq., 2.156 sq.), we find here someother notions reflecting the level of Indian natural science — about thehuman body, its functions (1.8 sq., 34, 37, 55, 99; 2.44, 45, 61, 154,159) and affects (1.8, 12, 65, 70; 2.43, 74, 153). Different diseases are named(roga — 1.46, 83; 2.50, 57, 64 etc.), particularly of ears (2.11),eyes (2.13), leprosy (kuṣṭha — 2.29), dysentery(atīsāra — 2.32), diarrhea, vomiting (virecana, chardana —2.44, cf. 45), throat haemorrhage (2.69), insanity (unmāda —2.71), consumption (śoṣa —2.89) and certain remedies as well (sauvarcala, saindhava — 2.124). Thereare remarks on cosmography (cf. e.g. about heavenly bodies and differentphenomena — 1.11, 31, 89, 101, 131; 2.12, 13, 55, 94, 96, 137 etc.).Numerous interpretations deal with Indian fauna — lion, elephant, tiger,rhinoceros, bear, monkey, horse, cow, wild boar, goat, camel, donkey, ram,mule, deer, buffalo, hare, jackal, porcupine, cat, mouse, crocodile, snake,frog, worm etc. (cf. 1.25, 26, 30, 52, 53, 79, 81, 84, 94, 109, 115, 135;2.3, 11, 15–18, 22, 23, 37, 41, 67, 68, 78, 82, 85, 89, 99, 151). Among birdswe find here goose, crane, sparrow, crow, owl, wagtail, heron, falcon, eagleetc. (1.97, 98, 104; 2.19–21, 79, 83 etc.); among insects — gnat,bee, gadfly, ant etc. (cf. 1.64; 2.17, 23). A prominent part inJagaddeva’s interpretations belongs to plants. He mentions different kinds oflotus (nalinī, kamala, padma — 1.38, 65, 67, 93, 131; 2.29,130),rice, wheat, barley, beans, mustard (vrīni, godhūma, yava, māṣa,sarṣapa — 1.106, 126 etc.), cotton (kārpāsa —1.150); numerous trees, shrubs, flowers — in all over a hundred differentspecies (cf. 1.14, 43, 86, 138–144, 146; 2.34, 35, 38, 111–120, 122–126,129 etc.). The text often refers to manners and customs, to social relations.We read here about certain aspects of everyday family life (1.42, 47, 83; 2.6,91 etc.), about details of a household (1.43, 58, 72, 91, 121,125 etc.); different tools and instruments (1.120, 125, 147; 2.10,132 sq., 147); buildings (1.63, 115, 128; 2.26, 142 etc.);agriculture (1.112; 2.88, 97); clothing (1. 59,67 sq.; 2.62 sq.,etc.); food (1.10, 36, 38, 43, 90, 96, 105; 2.27, 28, 30, 32, 48 etc.);adornments and toiletries (1.10, 68, 92a; 2.3, 13, 33, 62 sq.,72, 103–105, 150, 152 etc.); about usual entertainments (1.73, 127, 135;2.43, 44, 69, 97 etc.).

Differentprofessions are mentioned — potter, tailor, dyer, weaver etc. (2.97,108—110); certain estates, such as brāhmaṇa (1.100; 2.62), kṣatriya(1.29), cāṇḍāla (2.31, 109.159a); «born byslave woman» (dāsījana — 1.33, cf. also 1.30, 31, 72;2.93 etc.). Jagaddeva makes references to the king and his insignia (1.25,29, 87, 88, 108, 121; 2.139 etc.) and to his counsellors (1.91). Numerousdata belong to religion; different gods are named, particularly Lakṣmī,goddess of luck (1.39, 57, 67, 108, 130, 133; cf. Śrī —1.68, 74), Sarasvatī (1.67, 130), the divine trinity: Hari, Hara, Viraṃci (i. e. Viṣṇu, Śiva and Brahman — 1.19a),Śiva (Sarvajña, «Knowingall» — 1.102,129; cf. Gaṇapati — 1.130), Sūrya, the Sun(1.19a), Yama, god of death, mentioned most often in respect tounfavourable dreams (2.25, 29, 63, 66, 67, 71, 84, 89, 92, 102, 105; cf. Kṛtānta —2.82), the personal protecting deity (svadevatā, iṣṭadeva —1.102; 2.56, 58), the ancestral deity (gotra-devatā — 1.130), amongother supernatural beings — king of the birds Garuḍa (1.132),different demons and ghosts (preta, piśāca,rākṣasa — 2.30, 42, 70, 71, 77, 90, 92), sea monster (2.22);among mythological objects — the mountain Meru (1.136), magic heavenlytree fulfilling desires (kalpataru — 1.136), etc. Jagaddeva often refersto rites and sacrifices (1.18 sq., 40, 55, 71, 91, 106, 129, 135; 2.38,40, 47, 48, 58, 88, 159 etc.); to ascetics and hermits (1.107; 2.50, 51,87, 93). As we see JS has manifoldly reflected different aspects of Indianculture.

Apart from theintroductory (1.1–2; 2.1) and concluding (2.160–161) stereotype verses, thetext of JS can be divided into three parts generally following each other. Thefirst can be conditionally called «diagnostic» (1.4, 9–14). The phenomena ofdream, its sources and contents are explained here according to physical andpsychic state of person. The second part is «pragmatic» (1.5–8, 15–24; 2.159).It deals first of all with evaluation of the dream in respect to its efficiency(disregarding its positive or negative meaning). The prophetic andnon-prophetic dreams are specified here (1.5–8; cf. above)27. Further, the term of the dream’srealization is settled according to the time of dreaming. The dream of thefirst night watch (yāma; 6–9 p. m.) is realized within one year;of the second (9–12 p.m.) — within six months, of the third(0–3 a. m.) — within three months, of the fourth(3–6 a. m.) — within one month, of the last two ghaṭikasof the night28 — withinten days. The dream visioned during the sunrise is realized on the same day(1.15–17). «Pragmatic» precepts include also means to preserve the result ofauspicious omens and to prevent the non-auspicious ones (1.18–24; the principleof comparative efficacy of the dream visioned later is used here). One of theconcluding verses (2.159), containing similar advice for necessary purificationcan also be regarded as a part of these precepts. The third part can be called«semantic». It includes the actual interpretations constituting the main bodyof JS. Some inherent principles of this part will be discussed below.

A large part is dedicatedhere to interpretations themselves, i.e. correlating definite dreams withdefinite results. There are, however, several verses containing more generaloperational rules concerning different dreams (cf. above on 1.148–149;2.156–158).

The dreams interpreted byJagaddeva can be divided into those represented by simple signs and those bycomposite signs. Simple signs are reduced to single actions, qualities ofsubjects (or objects) emerging in dreams or to single objects which by themselvesare consigned by a positive or a negative meaning. The composite signs suggestdefinite situations where a number of elements (actions, qualities etc.) canusually be traced without difficulty — these elements are as a rule,identified by their function of simple signs with unequivocal sense whichdetermines the meaning of the whole situation. The boundary between these twokinds of signs is sometimes rather conditional (cf. e.g., such situations asmilking the cow with one’s own mouth or playing the reed (1.92) etc. (cf.below).

There are morecharacteristic positive simple signs (used either separately or combined withthe composite signs). Actions and situations: ascending, mounting (a tree, ahill, a palace etc. — 1.25, 33, 43, 63, 79, 84–88, 94, 95, 109,132 etc.),victory over enemies (1.40, 41), release from bonds (1.60), drinking (ofintoxicating liquor, of water from a tank etc — 1.35, 60, 90, 113 etc.),irrigation (1.112), playing the reed, vīṇa, tūrya (1.92, 108,127); hearing a song, sounds of animals (1.135), weeping, lamenting (1.70),catching animals, birds, fishing (1.114, 117); there are also some supernaturalactions often including certain additional signs — swallowing sun or moon,transformation of hand into banner, growing of bush out of one’s navel29 etc. (1.31, 108 etc.). Qualities: whitecolour (1.30, 68, 70, 71, 84, 88, 109 etc., cf. 1.150 about a fewexceptions: cotton, salt, bones, ashes); northern or eastern direction30 (1.56 etc.); Objects: body excretions(blood, sperm, excrements — 1.34, 36, 55, 99 etc.); certain animals (lion,horse, elephant, ox, cow — 1.25, 30, 79, 94 etc.); birds (1.97, 98)31; plants (1.138 sq.); grain (wheat,barley etc. 1.85, 106, 125, 126); fruits and flowers on a tree (1.66, 76, 77,102 etc.); ponds, rivers, tanks (1.128, 131)32;corals, shells (1.114, 117); deities (Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī,svadevatā etc. — 1.103, 107, 129, 130 etc.); sight of teachers,brahmans, parents, friends etc. (1.83, 93, 100, 107 etc.)33; sacred symbols (nandyāvarta,svastika etc. (1.120); royal insignia (umbrella, palanquin, banner etc. —1.87, 88, 5, 121 etc.); army (1.116); jewels, adornments (1.69, 72, 95, 118,119 etc.); vessels of clay (1.19) etc.

Composite signs constitutemore complicated situations e.g. white snake biting the right hand (1.26),eating rice on the white elephant on the river bank (1.30), women in whiteclothes playing with a lotus flower (1.67) etc. (cf. also 1.33, 38, 43, 46, 47,52–56, 65, 67, 68, 73, 75, 79, 81, 82, 89, 93, 109, 113 etc.). As we havenoticed certain simple positive signs can be traced here (white colour, river,lotus, fearlessness, etc.). At the same time the combination of opposite signsis also possible with occasional preference of some of them — so, forexample, 1.56 riding northward or eastward on a buffalo is propitious (cf.however, on buffalo — 2.15, 85)34;cf. also certain exceptions concerning, respectively, white and blackcolours (1.150).

Among negative simplesigns we can mention: Actions, states: falling (from tree, rock, in somecavity etc. — 2.26, 60, 70, 80 etc.), defeat (2.53), loss of teeth, nails,hair etc. (2.7 sq.)35,loss of favourable signs (elephants, horses, jewels etc. — 2.2, 3,5), fallof palace, walls, banners etc. (2.139, 140), often feeling lust, hunger, thirst(2.158), rejoicing (2.74, 148), being ill (2.44, 45, 141), change of age(2.138), contention of pupils (2.148), hearing appeals, cries, abuse (2.149);certain supernatural events: lotus growing out of one’s heart (2.29,cf. 36; see above), demon pursuing the moon (2.55, cf. 2.12, 96)36. Qualities: black colour (2.37,63, 66, 72, etc.; cf. on darkness — 2.26, 67, 95); red37 (2.25, 35, 38, 49, 51, 52, 62, 69, 72,75, 103, 104; cf. also about reddish-brown, piṅga — 2.65, 66, 75,84; yellow, pīta — 2.65; cf. 2.105, 114; orange, kāṣāya —2.75, 76), southern direction (2.37, 42, 66, 67, 76 etc.). Objects:certain animals (camel, donkey, wild boar, deer, etc. — 2.15, 67, 68, 84,85, 89, 151 etc.), birds (2.19 sq.), insects (evidently all — 2.23),certain plants (2.111 sq.), earthquake (2.94, cf. 137), filth, rubbishetc. (2.67, 70, 75, 76, 81, 98–101 etc.), metals (evidently not precious,2.131), ghosts (preta, piśāca,etc. — 2.30, 42, 77, 90, etc.), sea monster (2.22, 137), monks ofdifferent sects (2.50, 51, 87, 93)38,certain professions (tailor, dyer, carpenter, fisherman, etc. —2.108 sq.).

These simple signs canlikewise be combined with composite. Cf. for example, being drawn southward bya naked black woman with loose hair and reddish-brown eyes (2.66), intercoursewith beautiful woman in dirty or orange clothes and dirty flowers (2.76) etc.(see also 2.30, 32, 37, 40–42, 46, 52, 60, 62–72, 76, 84, 85, 89, 90, 95, 146,155 etc.). As in previous mixed cases the prevalence of certain — thistime negative — signs is possible, for example, in mounting black horse,certain plants, etc. (cf. 2.37 sq., see also 1.150).

Besides concreteinterpretations there are some more general explanations already mentionedabove. So, e.g. 1.150 contains remarks about positive meaning of white andnegative — of the black, with certain exceptions; 2.73 deals with theresult of the same unfavourable dream constantly repeating itself etc.

There are also noteworthyviews concerning the reverse meaning of the same sign in dreams and in keepingawake (1.149). The principle of contraposition defining the relation betweenthe two parts of JS can thus be traced in the character of interpretationsthemselves. This peculiar complementarity of dream and vigilance is reflectedin a number of cases. So, e.g. 1.113 (see also 1.60) comments as favourableintercourse with a woman that should not be enjoyed (agamya) or eatingforbidden food (abhakṣya)39.According to 1.46 death by poison or drinking poison means health and delight.We find here positive interpretations of death, sorrow, tears (1.70, 116, 131)40, losing head, tongue, genital organ(1.27 sq.)41, damaging one’sown head (1.49), defeat from enemies or wife (1.42), bonds (1.61), of certainimpure actions causing disgust — eating other man’s flesh (1.32, 35),drinking blood or anointing oneself with blood (1.37, 47, 48), seeing orbesmearing with excrement (1.34, 37, 55, 99), urine (1.37, 55)42. On the other hand — joy,laughter, and feast are often interpreted negatively (2.43, 47, 69, 74, 94,148) which likewise has numerous parallels (cf. above, note 40). One cansuppose that this principle does not refer to situations which functioned asomens (nimittāni) in everyday life for the latter according to traditionalviews (cf. 2.158) preserved their significance in dreams as well43. As we know, the dream interpretationswere included in a broader sphere of different omens and this connection isreflected in the composition of certain texts (cf. corresponding chapters ofAp, Mp etc.). Jagaddeva himself sometimes goes beyond the frames ofdreams — so, for example, in 2.54 the penetration of bees into the houseis said to be unfavourable «in dreams and by daytime as well» (svapne divasethavā); in 2.127 certain tastes (astringent, salty etc.) that «bythemselves are unpleasant to men» are also interpreted negatively in dreamsand so on.

At the same time one moreprinciple carried out rather consistently can be established here — theopposite interpretation of opposed objects, qualities or situations. Such arepredictions associated with white and black (or red) colours (1.109, 150–2.25,37 etc.), North and South (1.56–2.37, 42 etc.), raw and boiled meat (1.32–2.27)44, with different attitudes (love-anger)towards parents (1.83–2.91), with acquisition (seeing) and losing (perishing,fall etc.) of the same objects (cf. 1.91–2.154 of cattle; 1.87, 88–2.150 ofadornments; 1.87, 88–2.139 of walls, umbrellas, banners, etc.; 1.147–2.132 ofsickle). This principle is clearly proclaimed in 1.148: «What is not auspiciousto acquire is auspicious to [see] ravished, what is not auspicious to lose, isauspicious to reach.»

Apart from certainirregularities, ambiguous cases or exceptions, we can name some principaloppositions rather regularly used in JS in accordance with classic Indiantradition, and bearing evidently a universal character: ascent — descent(falling), weeping-rejoicing, white-black (red), light-dark, North-South,raw-boiled, deities-ghosts, etc.

Aswe saw, certain signs can be interpreted differently even in an opposite way.The latter cases are sometimes connected with definite circumstances оfsleeper’s life. Thus, e.g. the man whose legs are pulled by lion, elephant,crocodile, or by another man must be freed soon, if by that time he isimprisoned or to be imprisoned if he is free (2.46). In 1.60 drinking offorbidden drink or freeing from bonds has also different results (though inboth cases positive) for a priest and non-priest. More often,however, different results of the same sign depend on other details(«transformers») of the same dream. The sight of a flower or a fruit e.g. canbe positive or negative in respect of appropriate or inappropriate time when itgrows (1.76–2.591. Among factors influencing the meaning of dreams we canmention high elevated place evidently favouring the positive situation and atthe same time neutralizing the negative one (2.41; cf. 1.33, 136 etc.)45. Objects in a broken state also «spoil»the situation (cf. embarking on a boat: 1.44–2.142). The function oftransformer is carried out also by certain effects accompanying the dream-suchis, for example, positive influence of fearlessness in intercourse withforbidden woman (1.113–2.24; cf. also 1.46, 52, 55), or absence of disgustconcerning excrement etc. (na jugupsate — 1.34, 37). The influence oftransformers (mentioned clearly or suggested) can possibly explain certainoutward contradictions of the text (like 1.113–2.24). We mean here a number ofobjects and situations that according to certain accessories generally permitopposite interpretations. Among such ambivalent signs we can name a wedding(1.47–2.27, 74, 148)46, losingcertain parts of the body (1.27 sq. — 2.6 sq.), death (1.46,131–2.154), binding (1.61–2.10), competition (1.40–42, 52, 61–2.141)47, playing the lute (vīṇā1.73, 127–2.61), rain (1.77–2.95)48,fire (1.74, 75, 77, 80, 111 etc. — 2.88, 134)49, snake (1.26, 81, 109, 115–2.10, 11, 16, 78), bee(1.64–2.23, 54), rice (vrīhl 1.30, 38, 96, 126–2.28, 31, 107, 125, 126),lotus (1.65, 67, 93–2.29), certain plants (lavalī 1.142–2.116; marica,black pepper 1.141–2.124), grain (1.125, 126–2.88, 97, 125, 126), wreath (1.90,133; 2.150–2.49, 62, 69), plant growing from one’s own body (1.108 — 2.34–36;cf. above, note 29), sickle (1.147–2.132)50.

Themost usual result of the positive dream — its «signified» — isforthcoming welfare in this or that form (vṛddhi, śubham, śivam,grace of goddess Lakṣmī etc. — 1.37, 39–41, 44, 50, 57, 89,138,139, etc. — altogether about half of the interpretations of the firstpart. Then follows receiving gold, money etc., the expression «wealth andgrain» — dhana-dyānya is also frequent (1.42, 47, 58, 82, 87etc.) — about one-fourth of all positive prophecies. Another frequentpromise— kingship, power (1.25, 27, 29, 31–33 etc — about one-fifth).Among relatively rare predictions — progeny (1.27, 32, 54, 61, 84), happymarriage (1.64, 73, 78, 104), recovering from illness (1.46, 83), duty ofcounsellor (1.91) mental achievements (buddhi-siddhi — 1.93) etc. In thesecond part the most common «signified» is likewise general mentioning of theunfavourable situation — misfortune, suffering (aśubham, kaṣṭam, duḥkhametc. — 2.8,15–19, 21, 23, 26, 39 etc.) — over one-third of allnegative predictions. With approximately the same frequency the death isforetold — its circumstances are sometimes described here; on the next day(2.40, 41), in the course of five days (2.12, 24), in the course of a year(2.73), from certain diseases — leprosy (kuṣṭha — 2.29),consumption (kṣaya — 2.31 cf. 89), dysentery(atīsāra — 2.32) etc. In comparison with the first part, theloss of wealth, particularly of dhana-dhānya (cf. 2.2, 3, 7, 22, 37 etc.)is rarely (about one-tenth) mentioned. Among other misfortunes we find herediseases (2.44, 64, 144 etc.), troubles from the king (2.3, 101, 151), death ofwife (2.5, 14) and children (2.6), fire (2.33), exile (2.44), imprisonment (2.46) etc.

Thecomparison of Jagaddeva’s work with other ancient Indian sources shows howcertain ideas concerning the nature of dreams were preserved in Indiantradition for thousands of years — from archaic Vedic hymns down tomediaeval treatises and it elucidates some specific traits of classical Indianculture. On the other hand, it presents a large material for further parallelspermitting to establish certain typological affinities and divergencies ofdifferent traditions. We come thus to perceive some more general principles ofdream interpretation, and therefore to understand better certain relevanttraits of natural and humanitarian phenomena. Rich material for suchinvestigation is supplied already by other ancient traditions51, beginning perhaps with the oldestinterpretations of Egyptian papyrus — Chester Beatty III (ca. 2000–1790B.C.), like JS dealing first with auspicious and then with non-auspcious dreams52. Apart from these testimonies(Babylonian, Assyrian, Hebrew, Greek, Roman, Muslim, Mediaeval European etc.),we can find perhaps still further examples in frames of oral folkloretradition, that can be traced back to most ancient times and doubtlessly servedas a source for the tradition of literary (and «scientific») interpretationdiscussed above53.

Thenumerous analogies drawn from these sources evidently go beyond the scope ofpresumable coincidence and are not accidental. One can suppose that definitepatterns of mentality and psychology are reflected here; as a result, a certainaffinity of notions and symbols can be traced along the history of humanculture54. Among suchparallels, first of all some more general principles of dream-theory must bespecified. Referring to designations proposed above, we can begin with«diagnostic» universalities: views on dependence of dream upon temperament,upon the mental and physical state of man can be mentioned55. Another kind of universalities is«pragmatic» — distinctions between dreams influenced by a certain event,i.e. non-prophetic, and those demanding interpretation with possible hierarchyset among them56, belief in thedecisive role of the last dream in the night (the later the dream is seen, thesooner it will bring results)57and so on. The next, perhaps the largest sphere of analogies is presented by anumber of «semantic» universalities. Among them we can likewise discern somemore general rules. Such is e.g. the principle of opposite interpretation ofopposed situations, qualities, etc.58.Another principle is the complementarity of the same sign’s meaning in dreamand in reality. Such tendency displays itself e.g. in positive interpretationsof crying, grief, burial and negative — of laughter, joy, marriage etc.testified in different and evidently independent sources — ancient Egyptian,Indian, Arabian, Byzantine, Russian, Estonian, Karaite and so on59. At last there are certainuniversalities in respect of concrete signs — actions, objects,situations. Such are, respectively, positive and negative meanings of black andwhite60, rise and fall61,favourable interpretation of blood62, of mirror63,associations between excrements and gold64, unfavourableinterpretations of clergy, of teeth falling out65, of snake66,monkey, tiger67, etc.

The analysis of thoseparallels is the subject of special investigations. Corresponding worksinevitably go beyond the scope of dream itself and involve important problemsof mythology, folklore, technique of artistic creations etc. These ties havealready been discussed in some works68,One of such connections concerns the role of dreams in myth creation, on onehand, and the reflection of myth in the material of dream on the other69, Likewise mutual for both spheres aresymbols of tree, snake, fire; such motifs as meeting the dead, nakedness etc.We have seen that JS and other texts often mention certain gods, spirits,mythological objects etc. — such as, for example, celestial treefulfilling desires and presenting its positive meaning in dream70,interpretations concerning certain animals — elephant, cow, gooseetc. — playing a prominent role in Indian mythology71,references to more general ideas and symbols72. Among motifswidespread in other traditions one can be reminded of a tree growing out ofone’s body (cf. above, n. 29), the symbolism of horse, deer, bear,insects, snakes etc73. The samerefers to the sphere of ritual — its connection with dreams also deservesspecial attention. We have already mentioned some details of Hindu ritual asreflected in JS — cf. also on sacrificial butter (1.134 — JN, 140),grass (darbha — 2.36), and other accessories of sacrifice (2.88 etc., cf.JN 352–353)74, on details ofburial ceremonies (2.40, 48 — JN 236), on certain ritual prohibitions andimpurity (1.60, 113; 2.24, 25, 159 etc. — cf. JN 118 sq.). There arelikewise numerous testimonies of dream sacralization in other traditions (cf.ancient Greek rituals in the sanctuary of Asclepios, rituals ofGermans, etc.).

Other problems areconnected rather with folklore and literary studies. The interaction of dream andoral folk tradition seems to be quite natural since the latter usually includessuch interpretations as its component (cf. publications mentioned above inn. 37, 59 etc.). We find here numerous thematic reflections (e.g. the roleof hero’s prophetic dream in fairy tales) and common traits of symbolics75. The same can be said of thecorresponding motifs of literary artistic traditions (cf. for example, popularlikening of life to dream — in Calderon’s «La Vida es sueño» a.o.)beginning with the most archaic texts — epos of Gilgamesh, Bible (cf.dreams of Joseph — Genesis 37, 5 sq.; 40, 5 sq.), Homeros etc.76.The dream often plays a decisive role not only in the plot but in thecomposition of the text — one can be reminded of M. Lermontov’s«Dream» — «a dream in cube» according to V. S. Soloviev’s aptexpression77; books of L. Carrol on Alice78 etc. Inthis respect the role of dream in creating an artistic text deserves specialattention (cf. creative activity of Goethe, Hoffmann, Heine, Hebbel, Maupassant,Flaubert, Baudelaire etc.)79. Similar problems arise in studyingfigurative art (works of Goya, of surrealists like Max Ernst, Delvaux etc.)80.These structural and semantic ties suggest further search for inherent traitsof a dream considered as a message in its own specific «language»; it isprobable that the study of this «language» can help for a better understandingof some linguistic phenomena81.

And one more aspect of thesubject’s value can be reminded — the pragmatic one. Independently fromits verisimilitude, every such interpretation (like other kinds of predictions)by itself lessens in our opinion the uncertainty of forthcoming events82, and thus plays an importantpsychotherapeutic and regulating (in certain respect functionally near to scientific)role. It is to remember that our inherent (one may say biological) tendency toreduce the degree of such uncertainty cannot be satisfied by rationalistic waysonly — the history of civilization obviously demonstrates it.

71 See, for example: J.P. Vogel,The goose in Indian literature and art, Leiden, 1962; J. Gonda,Mensch und Tier im alten Indien — «Studium generale» Jg. 20,H. 2, 1967, S. 109, 112, 113; H. Zimmer, Myths andsymbols in Indian art and civilization, Princeton, 1974, p. 102 sq.; B.G. Gokhale,Animal Symbolism in early Buddhist Literature and Art — «East and West»,N.S., v. 24, 1924, N 1–2, p. 111 sq. etc. We find here also someinterpretations contrary to traditional concepts, e.g. in respect to hare(JS 2.17) — see J. Maringer, Der Hase in Kunst und Mytheder vor- und frühgeschichtlichen Menschen — «Zeitschrift fürReligions- und Geistesgeschichte», Bd. XXX, 1978, H. 3,S. 219 sq. This digression (cf. JS 1.149) agrees, however, withcorresponding belief (cf. JS 2.158) according to which the penetrating of hareinto the house is not favourable (cf. Gonda, S. 107).

72 Cf. for example on ideas ofdeath, darkness etc. — W.O. Kaelber, The «dramatic» element inbrāhmaṇic initiation: symbols of death, danger and difficultpassage — «History of Religions», vol. 18, N l, 1978,p.55 sq.

73 See e.g. J. vonNegelein, Das Pferd in arischen Altertum, Königsberg, 1905; M. Lurker,Das Tier in der Bildwerk des Hieronymus Bosch — «Studium generale»,Jg. 20, H. 4, 1967, S. 217 sq. (negative images of insects,snakes, deer); Jacoby, S. 144 (negative image of bear); S.A. Pletneva,Životnyj mir v russkix volšebnyx skazkax — Drevnjaja Rus’ islavjane», Moskva, 1978, s. 390, 394 (negative image of snake,positive — of horse, goose etc.).

74 Such is e.g. noteworthy analogy(cf. 2.158) with the meaning of Southern direction (JS 2.37, 42, 66etc.) — Śb III 1.1.2; «Theterrain of the sacrifice should rise toward the south.... If the terrain shouldbe inclined toward the south the sacrificer would quickly go to the worldbeyond» («i.e. die incorrectly» — Kaelber, p. 64).

75 Cf. S. Freud, Theoccurrence in dreams of material from fairy tales — «Character andCulture», New York, 1963, p. 59–66; Winternitz, Review, p. 406; V. Adrianova-Peretz,Simvolika snovidenij Frejda v svete russkix zagadok — «Akademija Naukakademiku N. Ja. Marru», Moskva, Leningrad, 1935, s. 497–505; F. vonder Leyen, Das Märchen, Heidelberg, 1958, S. 63 sq.; S. Freud,D.E. Oppenheim, Dreams in folklore, New York, 1958.

76 Cf.M. Zambrano, Dreams and Literary Creation — «The dream andhuman societies», p. 189 sq.; J.E. Mack, Nightmares andhuman conflict, Boston, 1970, p. 85 sq. (Nightmares and creativity).Concerning the analysis of separate texts see, for example, J.J. A. vanDijk, IM. 52615, Un songe d’Enkidu — «Sumer», 1958,vol. XIV, N 1–2, p. 114–121; J. Hundt, DerTraumglaube bei Homer, Greifswald, 1935; E. Ehrich, Der Traum imAlten Testament, Berlin, 1933; A. Wickenhauser, Die Traumgesichtedes Neuen Testaments in religionsgeschichtlicher Sicht — «Pisciculi»,Münster, 1939, S. 320 sq.; A. Robitsek, Die Analysevon Egmonts Traum — «Jahbuch für psychoanalytische undpsychopathologische Forschungen», 1910, Bd. II, S. 451–464; O. Kaus,Die Träume in Dostojewskys «Raskolnikoff», München, 1926; G.K. Sčennikov,Funkcija snov v romanax Dostoevskogo, — «Russkaja literatura1870–1890 gg.», Sbornik 3, Sverdlovsk, 1970, s. 53–78, etc. Cf.also: Jezower; Les songes et leur interprétation, p.76 sq.;105 sq.; etc.

77 V.S. Solov’jev,Lermontov — «Sobranie Sočinenij», t. VIII, Sanktpeterburg, 1903,s. 387–404. Concerning «dream in dream» see also: W. Stekel,Beiträge zur Traumdeutung — «Jahrbuch für psychoanalytische undpsychopathologische Forschungen»,1909, Bd. I, S. 459 sq. (cf. its favourable interpretation inKaraite tradition — Zaiączkowski,р. 349).

78 See e.g. D. Rackin,Alice’s journey to the end of night — «Publications of the modern languageassociation of America», 1966, vol. 81, N 5, p. 313–326.

The study of dream language cannot be omitted if we wish toarrive at an understanding of language in its most general and universalaspects».

text: О древнеиндийской символике сновидений [к № 8]
html: О древнеиндийской символике сновидений [к № 8]

text: (резюме) Вслед за кратким образомдревнеиндийской традиции снотолкования (ведийская литература, эпические поэмы ит.д.) статья более подробно останавливается на трактате Svapnacintāmaṇi(«Волшебное сокровище сновидений» — JS), принадлежащем Джагаддеве (2пол. XII — нач. XIII в.). Текст состоит из двух частей, трактующихсоответственно благоприятные и неблагоприятные сны. Анализ трактата позволяетусловно выделить три типа текста: «диагностический» (объяснения в соответствиис физиологией и психологией сновидца) (ч. I. 4; 9–14);«прагматический» (оценка действенности сна и срока его исполнения в зависимостиот времени сновидения, деление снов на «вещие» и «не вещие», в связи с чемдаются отдельные практические рекомендации — I.5–8; 15–24; II.159) и«семантический», т.е. собственно толкования. В этой связи выделены «простые»сновидения (напр., подъем на гору, победа над врагом, освобождение от оков(I.25; 40; 60) и «сложные», напр., укус белой змеи в правую руку (I. 26).Отмечены некоторые болееобщие черты толкований — противоположные значения противопоставимыхситуаций, определенная взаимодополнительность значений (неблагоприятное наявублагоприятно в сновидении и наоборот — I.149) и т.д.Проведены отдельныесопоставления JS с другими индийскими памятниками (в этой связи, в частности,привлечены две рукописи: Ms. Ind. II.19 и Ms. Ind. II.20 из ПетербургскогоИнститута Восточных Рукописей). Наконец могут быть отмечены очевиднотипологические параллели с другими, неиндийскими традициями, отразившиеся,например, в западной и русской литературах (ср. Джаггаддева. Волшебноесокровище сновидений. Пер. с санскрита, статья и комментарий А.Я. Сыркина.М., 1996, с. 12 сл.).\n
