chapter: 14. ОБ ОТДЕЛЬНЫХ ЧЕРТАХ НАУЧНОГО И ХУДОЖЕСТВЕННОГО ТЕКСТОВ[16]*

text: Οὐδὲν ἔφη τὸν θάνατον διαφέρειν τοῦ ζῆν. «σὺ οὖν», ἔφη τις, διὰ τί οὐκ ἀποθνῄσκεις;» «ὅτι, ἔφη, οὐδὲν διαφέρει».Diog.Laert. Vita philos. I. 35.  Theapplication of binary oppositions for the description of different culturalphenomena is widespread in humanities during recent decades1. One can suppose it attracts thescientist by the integrality of the picture it offers and by the comparativeeconomy of the constructions as well. It must be said, however, that one has toatone for such qualities by a certain idealization of the subject and by thenecessity to omit some details (including rather important ones) — traits thatare common for the language of both traditions: scientific and mythopoetic2. At the same time this methodcorresponds to some trends of modern scientific description and to a certaindegree can be justified by the fact that the same dichotomies it introduceswere already used in the sources studied. In other words, a certain degree ofcorrespondence between the two levels of observation and construction ispreserved here. Certainly, this correspondence sometimes happens to be ratherconditional (for example, when only one part of contra-position is marked inthe source examined)3;therefore the cases when the pertinence of dichotomy is expressed hereexplicitly (rather than implicitly) seem to be of certain methodological value.It is fromthis point of view that the opposition of «alive — not alive» introduced by theinvestigator is perhaps one of the most justified. In different variants(«life-death», «immortality-death», «birth-death» etc.) it is not onlywidespread in the history of culture, but also (and this is very significant)typical of different kinds of creative activity: speculative, scientific on theone hand and mythopoetic, artistic on the other. The study of this dichotomy inits components4, variants andrelations to other universal opposites (cf. analogies between «life-death» andcorrespondingly: «spring-winter», «sun-moon», «day-night», «right-left»,«home-forest», «upper part-lower part», «earth-water», «dry-wet»5, «masculine-feminine» etc.) involves avast scope of problems dealing with ethnography, study of folklore, history ofreligion, history of science etc. right down to problems of modern sociology6. A number of investigations can bementioned in this connection7.We want to draw attention here to one of theaspects of this problem — cases where both parts of the dichotomy describesimultaneously one and the same object (a person, an act, a state) which leadsto their neutralization; the latter can be expressed in an ambivalent attitudetowards the object when the opposite qualities are combined and — in some cases— are even proclaimed to be identical qualities. We shall mention below someexamples of such combinations, important for a better understanding of specifictraits of creative ability — both «sacral» and «secular».Among the mostarchaic testimonies of this phenomenon one must refer to certain devices indescribing deity, characteristic of religious worship and depictedtraditionally by an apt expression: «coincidence of opposites» (coincidentiaoppositorum)8. Among theopposites neutralized in this manner («good-evil», «light-darkness»,«great-small» etc.) we also encounter «alive-not alive» (cf. «birth-death»,«young-old» etc.). For example, the Hindu pantheon presents combinations ofthese opposites already in Ṛgvedic testimonies9. Such is the god Rudra in whose imageconceptions of death and killing on the one hand (cf. Ṛgveda I.114.4; 8;II.33.14; 15; IV.3.6; VII.46.4 etc.) and of healing and fertility on the other(II.33.4 bhishaktamaṃ tvā bhishajāṃ ṣṛinomi;II.33.7 mṛiḷayākurhāsto yo asti bheshajo jalāshaḥ;cf. I.114.1 sq.; V.24. 11 etc.) merge10.The god Agni is old and young at the same time (Ṛgveda II.4. 5jujurvāṃ уomuhur ā yuvābhūt; VI.2. 7 jūryaḥ sūnur; cf.X.4.5 and also I.127.5 ajarā; I.128.2; I.144.4 yuvājaniajaro)11. The idea ofovercoming time (cf. below, note 37) can be traced in his simultaneousfunctioning as father and son (I.69.2 devānām pitā putraḥ san,cf. I.95.4; I.141.2; III.27.9 etc.)12.The sun(Sūrya, Savitar, āditya) is often associated in Vedic texts withlife, breathing, protection and death, annihilation (Ṛgveda VII.34. 19;X.14.1; 1702; Atharvaveda XIII.3.3; cf. also upaniṣadic evidences:Chāndogya up. 1.32; Bṛhadāraṇyaka up. I.5.23 —Chāndogya up. VIII.6.3; Bṛhadāraṇyaka up. V.15.2; VI.2.15etc.) — the combination typical for the cult of the Sun not only in Vedic andpost-Vedic Hinduism but in religions of Babylon, Egypt, Ancient Greece, etc.13. The connection between the Sun andman’s existence after death is well known (e.g. the custom of burying the deadbefore sunset so that the Sun should have time to lead them to the abode ofDeath); it must be said that ideas of birth and death are generally connectedwith celestial bodies and phenomena in different traditions14. One could note here also the image ofthe ancient Indian goddess of dawn, Uṣas, who also is old and young atthe same time (Ṛgveda III.61.1 purāṇī devi yuvatiḥ; cf. I.92.10; IV.51.4)15. Functions of life’s protector and ofkiller, destroyer are combined, in the image of Viṣṇu16 — the latter is more typical for thepost-Vedic (particularly — epic) tradition — cf. MahābhārataIII.189.4; list of his names — ibid, XIII.149.One can refer also to ambivalent attitudereflected in beliefs and rites connected with the cult of fertility — e.g. roleof grain as a symbol of death and resurrection17. A number of less important mythological and folklorepersonages can be mentioned in this connection (e.g. baba-jaga from Slavic folktales)18. The same can be said of certain objects playing aprominent part in religious symbolism. Such is, for example, the image of theworld’s egg as a source of life and death (MahābhārataV. 99, 17 sq.)19.The examples givenmay attest to the ambivalent attitude as a distinctive feature of the relationto the object of cult in different traditions. Such an attitude can beexplained specifically in the context of religion’s therapeutic function20;it contributes to the regulation of affects21 — a traitevidently characteristic not only for secular texts22 but for sacral as well. We can see here a need to reactto certain negative emotions and fixed ideas (torture, old age, death). Ithelps us to understand better the role of corresponding symbols in myths andrituals, including those that mark only the sphere of conceptions connectedwith death (see above). Such is the motif of the skeleton in Buddhist dogmaticsand iconography — e.g. Gautama’s sculpture from Gandhara, II–III cc. A.D.23, that is analogous to certain shamanicconceptions (e.g. procedure of contemplating one’s own skeleton)24, we can also mention the use of theskull as a utensil in the Shivaite sect of kāpālin’s etc.25. It must be said that the device of«mortifying» description of the human body as an aggregate of perishable parts(often with a tendency to denigrating definitions) is rather widespread.Buddhist tradition presents us with a number of such descriptions; see e.g. inPāli canonical literature: Dīgha Nikāya XXII, Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta, 5: «A brother reflects upon this very body from the soles of his feetbelow upward to the crown of his head, as something enclosed in skin and fullof diverse impurities: — «Here is in this body hair and down, nails, teeth,skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, kidney, heart, liver, membranes, spleen,lungs, stomach, bowels, intestines...»26.Another similar description from Hinduist tradition compares a body to abuilding (Maitrī Upaniṣad III.4: «This body arises from sexualintercourse... It is built up with bones, smeared over with flesh, covered withskin, filled with faeces, urine, bile, phlegm, marrow, fat, grease and withmany diseases...»27. Anotherpassage occurs in the context of Brahman’s pious duties in the «Laws of Manu»(Mānavadharmaśāstra VI.76 sq.). There are numerous examples fromanalogous precepts and admonitions in other ethico-religious traditions28 — see e.g. from recently publishedtexts — Russian «Pis’ma jurodivogo XVII. » (a kind of beggarly devotee)consequently describing the decay and annihilation of separate parts of thebody (face, eyes, hair, neck, eyebrows, tongue, hands, etc.)29. Western Christian tradition alsopresents examples of this kind — cf. image of corpse, used by St. Francis of Assisi— perhaps it was borrowed from him by Ignatius Loyola and expressed in theprinciples of Jesuits’ conduct («perinde ac cadaver») where we can note apersistent equation of alive and not alive. A subordinate is compared in theseperceptions with a corpse, a stick, a lump of wax, a small crucifix (also anambivalent image of death and resurrection) that can be moved in all directionsby his master30.A specialproblem is the analysis of ritualized forms of everyday behaviour connectede.g. with marriage and funerals (cf. the image of death as a wedding in Slavictradition31, «ritual laughter»etc.)32. The ambivalentattitude witnessed here: «life» (birth, marriage, laughter) — «death» (funeral,crying) can evidently be understood in its psychotherapeutic function providinga kind of supplement to more orthodox and strictly regulated forms of religiousbehaviour.Returning tosuch forms, it must be said that the combination of these conceptions plays (inaccordance with a procedure mentioned above, n. 24) an important role in thedogmatics of the cult being linked closely to recommendations of certainbehaviour. Neutralization of such dichotomies as «alive — not alive»,«life-death» etc. was evidently destined to lead an adept’s conscience toreconciling the opposites given due to certain procedures — leaving the world,rejecting mundane attachments, absorbing oneself in contemplation (a hermitgoing away to a forest — vānaprastha, a mendicant wanderer — saṃnyāsinin Hinduism33, a wandering monk— bhikkhu in Buddhism, ἐρημίτης in Christianity etc.). Correspondingdogmatic precepts (sometimes of mythological character) served an instrumentfor attaining such status in neutralizing certain opposites34.This dogmaticscorresponding to a final goal of religious behaviour — deliverance (mokṣa)from ties of mundane life — recalls a number of parallels that are found fromancient times in the tradition of speculative thought in its ethical and partlynatural scientific constructions. With respect to some of these speculations weshould perhaps speak rather of overcoming such a contraposition and not ofcombining the two parts of it, since the corresponding qualities are not onlycombined but presented here as identical, as surmounted in the object describedin the respective manner.Among the most ancient examples fromIndian culture we can cite speculations of principal Upaniṣads (Bṛhadāraṇyaka,Chāndogya, Kaṭha etc.) connected with the definition of the Highestprinciple, Absolute (Ātman, Brahman) and of a person attaining thecorresponding state (saṃnyāsin, brāhmaṇa). Some of thesedescriptions remind us of the principle of «coincidentia oppositorum» mentionedabove. Among «all the pairs of opposites» (cf. Kauṣītaki up. I.4sarvāṇi... dvandvāni)35surmounted on this level we see also «life (birth, progeny) — death (old age,destruction, killing) » — cf. Chāndogya up. VIII.1.5; 4.1 — about victoryover old age (jarā) and death (mṛtyu) in Ātman; Bṛhadāraṇyakaup. III.5.1 — similar definitions of Ātman and of brāhmaṇaovercoming the desire for offspring; ibid. III.9.25 — about Atman as remainingbeyond destruction (aśīryaḥ; cf. Kaṭha up. I.3.15)36; Śvetāśvatara up. IV.3 —about the identity of an old man (jīrṇo) and a newborn (jāto)37 etc.The neutralization of this dichotomycan be connected with the mode of distinguishing two spheres which is peculiarto Upaniṣads and some other Vedic texts: (1) objective principle,macrocosm (adhidaivatam — literally: «referring to deities»), i.e. worlds(heaven, aerial space, earth), phenomena of nature, gods that symbolize themand (2) subjective principle, microcosm (adhyātmam — literally: «referringto oneself), i.e. different organs and capacities of man (breathing, speech,smelling etc.). The system of identifications specific to these texts bringsthe elements of these two spheres into relation of one-to-one correspondencewith each other, while the ritual can fulfil here an intermediate function (cf.Chāndogya up. I.6–7; III.18. 1–2; Bṛhadāraṇyaka up.II.3.1 sq. Kauśītaki up. IV.2. etc). As a result, we can find heree.g. the identifications of speech and earth, breathing and fire etc. Such aprocedure is of great importance for Upaniṣad’s dogmatics since it leadsadherents to the final goal — to grasping the identity of subjective(ātman, aham) and objective (brahman, tad — «that») principles38connected correspondingly with the world of life and the world beyond life (cf.Chāndogya up. VI.8.7 sq.; Bṛhadāraṇyaka up. I.4.10; IV.4.5 etc.). It must be added that apart from the principle mentioned, the idea ofthe interrelation between worlds is closely connected, in certain archaicconceptions, with beliefs in posthumous ways of men, their turning intodeities, animals, plants etc. — such beliefs more or less developed arevariously reflected in different traditions, including ancient Indian (cf.theory of Karma providing a wide ethico-philosophical basis for them)39.Interesting analogies canbe traced in ancient Greek philosophic tradition. Aphorisms of Heraclitus areperhaps the most instructive. A large number of them contain exactly thesedichotomies (e g. Fragments 21, 26, 50, 62, 63, 76, 77, 78), proclaiming theidentity of life and death. Cf. Fragm. 50: γενετὸν ἀγένετον, θνητὸν ἀθάνατον; Fragm. 62: ἀθάνατοι θνητοί, θνητοὶ ἀθάνατοι and especiallyFragm.88: ταὐτό τ’ἔνι ζῶν καὶ τεθνηκὸς... καὶ νέον καὶγηραιόν (And as the same thing there existsin us living and dead, and young and old). Cf. also Fragm. 21 — identificationof death with birth (γένεσιν)40.Heraclitus depicts world and man, macrocosm and microcosm (cf. above:adhidaivatam — adhyātmam) with the aid of the same words not seeing anysubstantial difference between them41.According to Diogenes Laertius a similar aphorism belonged to Thales: «He heldthere was no difference between life and death. «Why then, » said one, «do younot die? » «Because, » said he, «there is no difference»42.This likening proved to be very stablein European thought — we can cite e.g. Leonardo da Vinci in whose aphorisms itshould be connected more probably with the history of natural science, withcomprehending human physiology. «Our life is made by the death of others. Indead matter insensible life remains» (H241b); «The body of any thingwhatever that takes nourishment constantly dies and is constantly renewed» (alcontinuo muore e al continuo rinasce) (W. An II 43b). There are interestingparallels to the following Leonardo’s thought: «Now you see that the hope andthe desire of returning home and to one’s former state (nel primo caso;according to E. Solmi’s explanation — «anteriore alia nascita», previous to birth)43 is like the moth to the light and thatthe man who with constant longing awaits with joy each new spring time, eachnew summer, each new month, and new year — deeming that the things he longs forare ever too late in coming — does not perceive that he is longing for his owndestruction. But this desire is the very quintessence... inseparable fromnature and... man is the image of the world (Br. M 156b)44. We find similar thoughts, writtenseveral centuries later in G. Hegel’s «Science of Logic»: «The nature of finitethings as such is to have the seed of passing away as their essential being,the hour of their birth is the hour of their death»45. It is interesting that modern psychoanalytical theorypresents a striking parallel to Leonardo’s aphorism — in S. Freud’s words from«Beyond the pleasure principle»: «The goal of all life is death»46.Another example important in thehistory of philosophical and scientific thought can be found in the works of H.Bergson whose views were to a certain degree based upon contraposition of thesenotions somewhat modified and presented in a dichotomy of creative, animated,organic principle (elan vital, evolution creatrice) andmechanical, artificial, inorganic. The combination of these principles when amachine’s inertness is given to an animated being, life itself is filled withautomatism and mechanical order and the person gives us an impression of athing («mecanisme superpose a la vie», «L’ideed’une mecanisation artificielle du corps humain» etc.) — is according tohim the main condition for creating the comic effect, the most general premisefor laughter47. Independentlyof the role of this cause (perhaps a bit exaggerated in the present case) oneof the typical devices for creating a comic effect is observed here; thisdevice, as we know, can at the same time serve also as a mechanism for creatinga tragic situation. Thus — this time from another point of view — a definitefunctional ambivalence displayed in the character of the aesthetic effect, isinherent in such combination.As we see, the fusion of these notions(alive-not alive) is of great importance for sacred texts where it ensures aduplicate tendency peculiar to the adept’s attitude towards the cult object andserves as one of the principal devices in corresponding ethical dogmatics,leading its adherents to mastering certain forms of behaviour. At the sametime, such neutralization in antiquity went beyond the scope of the orthodoxcult. It marks the early stage of natural science and philosophy beginning withtimes when mythopoetic and scientific thought were closely linked to each other(Yājnavalkya, Uddālaka, Heraclitus, Thales) and is preserved inscientific and philosophical constructions of our time. Absolutely differentaspects of culture are influenced by it: abstract philosophical speculations,more concrete views on physiology and psychology, ideas of the nature ofaesthetic reaction, of comic effect etc. — and in numerous cases the roots ofthese constructions can be traced to testimonies of archaic myths and rituals,to a long literary tradition, beginning with the oldest religious andmythopoetic texts.We shall point out in this connection severalexamples of artistic fiction. They display partly a functional affinity to somesources cited above and partly suggest new aspects of the research into thisdichotomy.The neutralization «alive-not alive»can be directly correlated to psychological and aesthetic constructionsmentioned above (ideas of L.S. Vygotskij close to the theory of catharsis)48. This device is traced here (first ofall on the level of plot) in the genres of tragedy, fable, etc.49. The inseparable combination of theideas of death, burial and birth, fertility, joy was noted in respect to«Gargantua et Pantagruel» of Rabelais (II.1; 3; III.48; IV.17 etc.) treated asa display of «carnival folk world-outlook»50.One can find possible analogies in other traditions. Such are e.g. Quatrains ofOmar Khayyām where ideas of the world’s transitoriness, of overcoming thefear of death, etc. are illustrated consequently by such comparisons as«flesh-clay», «curls-dust», «head (hands, feet) — vessel», etc.; combinationsof this kind form a peculiar leit-motif helping to overcome such dichotomies,and lead (in a certain functional correspondence to speculations cited above)to a specific psychic attitude marked here by the poet’s hedonistic tendency.Another cycle of examples is connectedwith a widespread image of the doll (buffoon, pulcinella, petruška, etc.)that displays, perhaps most obviously, the dual tragic-comic effect of thecorresponding device. It is rooted in archaic accessories of ritual51 and is variously reflected to our dayin literature and art (especially scenic) — cf. image of Pierrot —Petruška popular in European tradition (play of A. Blok, ballet ofStravinsky, etc.), motif of woman-doll («Sandman» of E.T.A. Hoffmann, andmusical embodiment of the theme in Offenbach’s «Tales of Hoffmann»; «Doll’sHouse» of Ibsen, etc.). This motif, as we know, was correlated with infantiletraits of the mind52. Thelatter sphere suggests another aspect of our problem — interesting material ispresented e.g. by English children’s literature. We mean the phenomenon ofchildren’s «mercilessness» reflected in corresponding genres: see for examplehumorous verses of H. Graham («Ruthless rhymes for heartless homes»)53, a merry obituary in «Ten little niggerboys» etc.54.Independently of the conceptual andpsychological factors mentioned above the annihilation of the differencebetween «alive» and «not alive», animate and inanimate can be considered as aspecific artistic device — either on more general levels of composition andplot, or in depicting a concrete image of a hero. The examples of such a devicecan be observed already in artistically expressed mythological motifs —connected e.g. with beliefs in reincarnation, transformation of man into ananimal, a plant etc. (see below, N 60 sq. cf; Puruṣasūkta from Ṛgveda(X.90) describing the creation of the world from the members of «primeval man»;a cosmological likening of horse’s limbs (Bṛhadāraṇyaka up.I.1.1), a likening of man’s members and parts of the tree (ibid. III.9.28) etc.55.A similar device can be observed in folk literature56.In this connection it is worth notingcorresponding feelings in the world-outlook of some artists. The most strikingexample is presented by Rilke, who said that it is the poet’s mission to bindlife and death together57. Some authors expressing correspondingideas in most general aphoristic form can be rather ascribed to the ancientmythopoetic tradition already mentioned — such are aphorisms of Novalis,reflecting his conception of the world as an indissoluble unity of polarities —e.g. «all ashes are pollen, calyx — heaven», «Death is the romanticising principleof our life» etc.58.Among characteristic examples of usingthis dichotomy as a decisive factor in the semantic structure of the work wecan mention «The Poem of the End» («Poema konca») of M. Cvetaeva. It wasshown recently that the opposition «life-death» is principal here; in anoteworthy typological affinity with certain archaic conceptions (particularly— Slavic; see above, N 7) it functions here in the context of othersymmetrically contrasted pairs. As a result, the text is based upon contrapositionof similar opposites, related by sense to the general one — respectively:«husband-wife», «dry-wet», «one’s own-alien», etc. The opposition «life-death»logically comes to neutralization in the words: «Life is a place where onecannot live»59.Turning to more special usage of thisdevice — in outlining separate images — we could mention already«Metamorphoses» of Ovid, where according to its main topic a number oftransformations are based upon coincidences of similarities both (verbal andqualitative) of corresponding signs. Such as, e.g. the description of stonesturning into men (I.400 sq.) — the veins of stones without changing theirdesignation (vena) begin to denote veins of a human body60. Another parallel — in the framework ofItalian dolce stil nuovo — is the image of the Stone Lady in Dante’s verses(with constant word-play on her name Pietra)61.To cite some examples from modernRussian literature one can refer to Ju. Tynjanov’s prose. Such is theobliteration of distinctions between a monster preserved in a jar and a livingman («The Wax Person»). A peculiar mechanization of heroes’ behaviour istypical for D. Kharms’ artistic manner — it leads (with a certain resemblanceto the English nonsense tradition) to the humorous presentation of violence,accident, death (cf. above, N 53, 54). One can refer to his miniature storieslike «Dream» where the hero is doubled up and thrown away with rubbish,“Falling-out old woman», «Cases», «Accident in the Street», etc. withdeliberately unmotivated, nonsensical endings62.Describing men as inanimate objects often recurs in the prose of Ju.Oleša. His heroes (like Volodja Makarov, Andrej Babičev from «Envy»)now and then petrify, turn into dolls, into robots; they are — «men-things»reminding of an inanimate world, their external activity only makes theirinternal lifelessness more evident63.There remains another sphere ofcreativity presenting the same combination: figurative art — both sacral (cf.above, N 23) and secular. First of all, one can find here numerousillustrations to corresponding literary themes. Among them — a widespread motifof the «Dance of Death» (Totentanz, Danse macabre) reflected in Europeanmediaeval literature, in folk-theatre (Fastnachtspiel) and in drawings — cf.e.g. a painting of B. Notke (1463); a cycle of engravings by H. Holbein theYounger; from later specimen — picture of F. Rops, etc.64.Independently of possible literaryparallels and analogies a common device can be traced here: the combining ofthe animate and the inanimate, the organic and the inorganic, the living andthe dead in human traits. Remarkably interesting examples are presented byHieronymus Bosch — cf. his «Alchemic man» (separate drawing and a fragment ofthe right part of the triptych «Garden of delights» (Hell)65. In particular a noteworthy combinationof a man’s head, an egg, and a tree can be mentioned here — an interestingparallel to well-known mythological concepts66.Another example — representation of a man’s head as a part of a landscape by J.de Momper in XVIII century67(cf. above, on macrocosm–microcosm equations). This device in general is verytypical in contemporary works of surrealists. The problem deserves a specialresearch — here we should note only that an analysis of the school’s artisticcredo could be of interest (the role of unconscious associations, of «psychicautomatism» not controlled by common sense68).Such an attitude helps to understand better striking (and perhaps not random)coincidences with some archaic mythological conceptions; furthermore, itreminds us of the therapeutic function of such themes.To cite several examples, let us nameR. Magritte’s «Perpetual Motion», «Madame Recamier’s perspective» (withthe well-known figure from J.-L. David’s picture replaced by a coffin),«Philosophy in boudoir», «Therapeutist», the cover of the magazine «Minotaurus»(X, 1936)69, M. Ernst’s«Celebes», «Woman in the Wall», «Paramythe», «Sainte Сecilie»70; S. Dali’s «Giraffe in flames», coverof «Minotaurus» (VIII, 1936), «Mae West», where a woman’s face at the same timerepresents an interior71; G.Bellmer’s «Doll» — a construction of wood, metal and papier-mache — aninteresting analogy to the infantile-sadistic motif mentioned above72; Man Ray’s «Priority of matter overthought»73 etc.74. Surrealist drawings rather oftenpresent a combination of a human body and a tree — cf. analogies in variouscosmological concepts and iconography in India (e.g. Buddhism), in ancientGreece (worship of Dionysos), in Bosch’s drawings mentioned above, etc.75. One can refer here to P. Delvaux’«Dawn» with figures of women-trees (cf. motif of dryads of Daphne, etc.), A.Kubin’s «Nietzsche-pillar» etc.76.A psychiatric aspect of such images can also be of interest here (cf. e.g.drawings of S.K.)77.Further, certain devices in thetechnique of such combination (similarly to corresponding literary examples)can be traced. Such are, among the pictures mentioned above, a clear spatialdemarcation of «alive» and «not alive» in R. Magritte’s «Therapeutist», agradual transition from one to another in H. Bellmer’s «Doll», M. Ernst’s«Women in the Wall» of Man Ray’s «Priority of matter over thought»; fusion ofboth opposites with complete spatial superposition of one upon another — theliving body is rendered here with the aid of «inorganic» material and thepicture can be «read» in two corresponding ways — cf. «Mae West» of S. Dali.The last variant is very effective e.g. in the cycle: «Stones cry» by thePolish artist B. Linke, where human bodies are consequently represented asbeing built of bricks — the device results in a striking animation of Warsaw’sruins and a great expressiveness of drawing (cf. water-colours: «El Molerahmim», «House-warriors», «Image of Job», «Mystery», etc.)78. Separate devices can also be combined— see the application of the first two in Bosch’s «Temptation of St. Antony».The study of such devices within the limits of figurative art or in the broadersphere of artistic fiction, mythology, and history of culture, bears further witnessto the universality and cultural significance of the phenomenon, some aspectsof which have been touched upon here.

Οὐδὲν ἔφη τὸν θάνατον διαφέρειν τοῦ ζῆν.

«σὺ οὖν», ἔφη τις, διὰ τί οὐκ ἀποθνῄσκεις;»

«ὅτι, ἔφη, οὐδὲν διαφέρει».

Diog.Laert. Vita philos. I. 35.

 

 

Theapplication of binary oppositions for the description of different culturalphenomena is widespread in humanities during recent decades1. One can suppose it attracts thescientist by the integrality of the picture it offers and by the comparativeeconomy of the constructions as well. It must be said, however, that one has toatone for such qualities by a certain idealization of the subject and by thenecessity to omit some details (including rather important ones) — traits thatare common for the language of both traditions: scientific and mythopoetic2. At the same time this methodcorresponds to some trends of modern scientific description and to a certaindegree can be justified by the fact that the same dichotomies it introduceswere already used in the sources studied. In other words, a certain degree ofcorrespondence between the two levels of observation and construction ispreserved here. Certainly, this correspondence sometimes happens to be ratherconditional (for example, when only one part of contra-position is marked inthe source examined)3;therefore the cases when the pertinence of dichotomy is expressed hereexplicitly (rather than implicitly) seem to be of certain methodological value.

It is fromthis point of view that the opposition of «alive — not alive» introduced by theinvestigator is perhaps one of the most justified. In different variants(«life-death», «immortality-death», «birth-death» etc.) it is not onlywidespread in the history of culture, but also (and this is very significant)typical of different kinds of creative activity: speculative, scientific on theone hand and mythopoetic, artistic on the other. The study of this dichotomy inits components4, variants andrelations to other universal opposites (cf. analogies between «life-death» andcorrespondingly: «spring-winter», «sun-moon», «day-night», «right-left»,«home-forest», «upper part-lower part», «earth-water», «dry-wet»5, «masculine-feminine» etc.) involves avast scope of problems dealing with ethnography, study of folklore, history ofreligion, history of science etc. right down to problems of modern sociology6. A number of investigations can bementioned in this connection7.

We want to draw attention here to one of theaspects of this problem — cases where both parts of the dichotomy describesimultaneously one and the same object (a person, an act, a state) which leadsto their neutralization; the latter can be expressed in an ambivalent attitudetowards the object when the opposite qualities are combined and — in some cases— are even proclaimed to be identical qualities. We shall mention below someexamples of such combinations, important for a better understanding of specifictraits of creative ability — both «sacral» and «secular».

Among the mostarchaic testimonies of this phenomenon one must refer to certain devices indescribing deity, characteristic of religious worship and depictedtraditionally by an apt expression: «coincidence of opposites» (coincidentiaoppositorum)8. Among theopposites neutralized in this manner («good-evil», «light-darkness»,«great-small» etc.) we also encounter «alive-not alive» (cf. «birth-death»,«young-old» etc.). For example, the Hindu pantheon presents combinations ofthese opposites already in Ṛgvedic testimonies9. Such is the god Rudra in whose imageconceptions of death and killing on the one hand (cf. Ṛgveda I.114.4; 8;II.33.14; 15; IV.3.6; VII.46.4 etc.) and of healing and fertility on the other(II.33.4 bhisháktamaṃ tvā bhishájāṃ ṣṛinomi;II.33.7 mṛiḷayā́kurhāsto yó ásti bheshajó jálāshaḥ;cf. I.114.1 sq.; V.24. 11 etc.) merge10.The god Agni is old and young at the same time (Ṛgveda II.4. 5jujurvā́ṃ уómúhur ā́ yúvābhū́t; VI.2. 7 jū́ryaḥ sūnúr; cf.X.4.5 and also I.127.5 ajárā; I.128.2; I.144.4 yúvājaniajáro)11. The idea ofovercoming time (cf. below, note 37) can be traced in his simultaneousfunctioning as father and son (I.69.2 devānām pitā́ putráḥ sán,cf. I.95.4; I.141.2; III.27.9 etc.)12.

The sun(Sūrya, Savitar, āditya) is often associated in Vedic texts withlife, breathing, protection and death, annihilation (Ṛgveda VII.34. 19;X.14.1; 1702; Atharvaveda XIII.3.3; cf. also upaniṣadic evidences:Chāndogya up. 1.32; Bṛhadāraṇyaka up. I.5.23 —Chāndogya up. VIII.6.3; Bṛhadāraṇyaka up. V.15.2; VI.2.15etc.) — the combination typical for the cult of the Sun not only in Vedic andpost-Vedic Hinduism but in religions of Babylon, Egypt, Ancient Greece, etc.13. The connection between the Sun andman’s existence after death is well known (e.g. the custom of burying the deadbefore sunset so that the Sun should have time to lead them to the abode ofDeath); it must be said that ideas of birth and death are generally connectedwith celestial bodies and phenomena in different traditions14. One could note here also the image ofthe ancient Indian goddess of dawn, Uṣas, who also is old and young atthe same time (Ṛgveda III.61.1 purāṇī́ devi yuvatíḥ; cf. I.92.10; IV.51.4)15. Functions of life’s protector and ofkiller, destroyer are combined, in the image of Viṣṇu16 — the latter is more typical for thepost-Vedic (particularly — epic) tradition — cf. MahābhārataIII.189.4; list of his names — ibid, XIII.149.

One can refer also to ambivalent attitudereflected in beliefs and rites connected with the cult of fertility — e.g. roleof grain as a symbol of death and resurrection17. A number of less important mythological and folklorepersonages can be mentioned in this connection (e.g. baba-jaga from Slavic folktales)18. The same can be said of certain objects playing aprominent part in religious symbolism. Such is, for example, the image of theworld’s egg as a source of life and death (MahābhārataV. 99, 17 sq.)19.

The examples givenmay attest to the ambivalent attitude as a distinctive feature of the relationto the object of cult in different traditions. Such an attitude can beexplained specifically in the context of religion’s therapeutic function20;it contributes to the regulation of affects21 — a traitevidently characteristic not only for secular texts22 but for sacral as well. We can see here a need to reactto certain negative emotions and fixed ideas (torture, old age, death). Ithelps us to understand better the role of corresponding symbols in myths andrituals, including those that mark only the sphere of conceptions connectedwith death (see above). Such is the motif of the skeleton in Buddhist dogmaticsand iconography — e.g. Gautama’s sculpture from Gandhara, II–III cc. A.D.23, that is analogous to certain shamanicconceptions (e.g. procedure of contemplating one’s own skeleton)24, we can also mention the use of theskull as a utensil in the Shivaite sect of kāpālin’s etc.25. It must be said that the device of«mortifying» description of the human body as an aggregate of perishable parts(often with a tendency to denigrating definitions) is rather widespread.Buddhist tradition presents us with a number of such descriptions; see e.g. inPāli canonical literature: Dīgha Nikāya XXII, Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta, 5: «A brother reflects upon this very body from the soles of his feetbelow upward to the crown of his head, as something enclosed in skin and fullof diverse impurities: — «Here is in this body hair and down, nails, teeth,skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, kidney, heart, liver, membranes, spleen,lungs, stomach, bowels, intestines...»26.Another similar description from Hinduist tradition compares a body to abuilding (Maitrī Upaniṣad III.4: «This body arises from sexualintercourse... It is built up with bones, smeared over with flesh, covered withskin, filled with faeces, urine, bile, phlegm, marrow, fat, grease and withmany diseases...»27. Anotherpassage occurs in the context of Brahman’s pious duties in the «Laws of Manu»(Mānavadharmaśāstra VI.76 sq.). There are numerous examples fromanalogous precepts and admonitions in other ethico-religious traditions28 — see e.g. from recently publishedtexts — Russian «Pis’ma jurodivogo XVII. » (a kind of beggarly devotee)consequently describing the decay and annihilation of separate parts of thebody (face, eyes, hair, neck, eyebrows, tongue, hands, etc.)29. Western Christian tradition alsopresents examples of this kind — cf. image of corpse, used by St. Francis of Assisi— perhaps it was borrowed from him by Ignatius Loyola and expressed in theprinciples of Jesuits’ conduct («perinde ac cadaver») where we can note apersistent equation of alive and not alive. A subordinate is compared in theseperceptions with a corpse, a stick, a lump of wax, a small crucifix (also anambivalent image of death and resurrection) that can be moved in all directionsby his master30.

A specialproblem is the analysis of ritualized forms of everyday behaviour connectede.g. with marriage and funerals (cf. the image of death as a wedding in Slavictradition31, «ritual laughter»etc.)32. The ambivalentattitude witnessed here: «life» (birth, marriage, laughter) — «death» (funeral,crying) can evidently be understood in its psychotherapeutic function providinga kind of supplement to more orthodox and strictly regulated forms of religiousbehaviour.

Returning tosuch forms, it must be said that the combination of these conceptions plays (inaccordance with a procedure mentioned above, n. 24) an important role in thedogmatics of the cult being linked closely to recommendations of certainbehaviour. Neutralization of such dichotomies as «alive — not alive»,«life-death» etc. was evidently destined to lead an adept’s conscience toreconciling the opposites given due to certain procedures — leaving the world,rejecting mundane attachments, absorbing oneself in contemplation (a hermitgoing away to a forest — vānaprastha, a mendicant wanderer — saṃnyāsinin Hinduism33, a wandering monk— bhikkhu in Buddhism, ἐρημίτης in Christianity etc.). Correspondingdogmatic precepts (sometimes of mythological character) served an instrumentfor attaining such status in neutralizing certain opposites34.

This dogmaticscorresponding to a final goal of religious behaviour — deliverance (mokṣa)from ties of mundane life — recalls a number of parallels that are found fromancient times in the tradition of speculative thought in its ethical and partlynatural scientific constructions. With respect to some of these speculations weshould perhaps speak rather of overcoming such a contraposition and not ofcombining the two parts of it, since the corresponding qualities are not onlycombined but presented here as identical, as surmounted in the object describedin the respective manner.

Among the most ancient examples fromIndian culture we can cite speculations of principal Upaniṣads (Bṛhadāraṇyaka,Chāndogya, Kaṭha etc.) connected with the definition of the Highestprinciple, Absolute (Ātman, Brahman) and of a person attaining thecorresponding state (saṃnyāsin, brāhmaṇa). Some of thesedescriptions remind us of the principle of «coincidentia oppositorum» mentionedabove. Among «all the pairs of opposites» (cf. Kauṣītaki up. I.4sarvāṇi... dvandvāni)35surmounted on this level we see also «life (birth, progeny) — death (old age,destruction, killing) » — cf. Chāndogya up. VIII.1.5; 4.1 — about victoryover old age (jarā) and death (mṛtyu) in Ātman; Bṛhadāraṇyakaup. III.5.1 — similar definitions of Ātman and of brāhmaṇaovercoming the desire for offspring; ibid. III.9.25 — about Atman as remainingbeyond destruction (aśīryaḥ; cf. Kaṭha up. I.3.15)36; Śvetāśvatara up. IV.3 —about the identity of an old man (jīrṇo) and a newborn (jāto)37 etc.

The neutralization of this dichotomycan be connected with the mode of distinguishing two spheres which is peculiarto Upaniṣads and some other Vedic texts: (1) objective principle,macrocosm (adhidaivatam — literally: «referring to deities»), i.e. worlds(heaven, aerial space, earth), phenomena of nature, gods that symbolize themand (2) subjective principle, microcosm (adhyātmam — literally: «referringto oneself), i.e. different organs and capacities of man (breathing, speech,smelling etc.). The system of identifications specific to these texts bringsthe elements of these two spheres into relation of one-to-one correspondencewith each other, while the ritual can fulfil here an intermediate function (cf.Chāndogya up. I.6–7; III.18. 1–2; Bṛhadāraṇyaka up.II.3.1 sq. Kauśītaki up. IV.2. etc). As a result, we can find heree.g. the identifications of speech and earth, breathing and fire etc. Such aprocedure is of great importance for Upaniṣad’s dogmatics since it leadsadherents to the final goal — to grasping the identity of subjective(ātman, aham) and objective (brahman, tad — «that») principles38connected correspondingly with the world of life and the world beyond life (cf.Chāndogya up. VI.8.7 sq.; Bṛhadāraṇyaka up. I.4.10; IV.4.5 etc.). It must be added that apart from the principle mentioned, the idea ofthe interrelation between worlds is closely connected, in certain archaicconceptions, with beliefs in posthumous ways of men, their turning intodeities, animals, plants etc. — such beliefs more or less developed arevariously reflected in different traditions, including ancient Indian (cf.theory of Karma providing a wide ethico-philosophical basis for them)39.

Interesting analogies canbe traced in ancient Greek philosophic tradition. Aphorisms of Heraclitus areperhaps the most instructive. A large number of them contain exactly thesedichotomies (e g. Fragments 21, 26, 50, 62, 63, 76, 77, 78), proclaiming theidentity of life and death. Cf. Fragm. 50: γενετὸν ἀγένετον, θνητὸν ἀθάνατον; Fragm. 62: ἀθάνατοι θνητοί, θνητοὶ ἀθάνατοι and especially

Fragm.88: ταὐτό τ’ἔνι ζῶν καὶ τεθνηκὸς... καὶ νέον καὶ

γηραιόν (And as the same thing there existsin us living and dead, and young and old). Cf. also Fragm. 21 — identificationof death with birth (γένεσιν)40.Heraclitus depicts world and man, macrocosm and microcosm (cf. above:adhidaivatam — adhyātmam) with the aid of the same words not seeing anysubstantial difference between them41.According to Diogenes Laertius a similar aphorism belonged to Thales: «He heldthere was no difference between life and death. «Why then, » said one, «do younot die? » «Because, » said he, «there is no difference»42.

This likening proved to be very stablein European thought — we can cite e.g. Leonardo da Vinci in whose aphorisms itshould be connected more probably with the history of natural science, withcomprehending human physiology. «Our life is made by the death of others. Indead matter insensible life remains» (H241b); «The body of any thingwhatever that takes nourishment constantly dies and is constantly renewed» (alcontinuo muore e al continuo rinasce) (W. An II 43b). There are interestingparallels to the following Leonardo’s thought: «Now you see that the hope andthe desire of returning home and to one’s former state (nel primo caso;according to E. Solmi’s explanation — «anteriore alia nascita», previous to birth)43 is like the moth to the light and thatthe man who with constant longing awaits with joy each new spring time, eachnew summer, each new month, and new year — deeming that the things he longs forare ever too late in coming — does not perceive that he is longing for his owndestruction. But this desire is the very quintessence... inseparable fromnature and... man is the image of the world (Br. M 156b)44. We find similar thoughts, writtenseveral centuries later in G. Hegel’s «Science of Logic»: «The nature of finitethings as such is to have the seed of passing away as their essential being,the hour of their birth is the hour of their death»45. It is interesting that modern psychoanalytical theorypresents a striking parallel to Leonardo’s aphorism — in S. Freud’s words from«Beyond the pleasure principle»: «The goal of all life is death»46.

Another example important in thehistory of philosophical and scientific thought can be found in the works of H.Bergson whose views were to a certain degree based upon contraposition of thesenotions somewhat modified and presented in a dichotomy of creative, animated,organic principle (élan vital, évolution créatrice) andmechanical, artificial, inorganic. The combination of these principles when amachine’s inertness is given to an animated being, life itself is filled withautomatism and mechanical order and the person gives us an impression of athing («mécanisme superposé à la vie», «L’idéed’une mécanisation artificielle du corps humain» etc.) — is according tohim the main condition for creating the comic effect, the most general premisefor laughter47. Independentlyof the role of this cause (perhaps a bit exaggerated in the present case) oneof the typical devices for creating a comic effect is observed here; thisdevice, as we know, can at the same time serve also as a mechanism for creatinga tragic situation. Thus — this time from another point of view — a definitefunctional ambivalence displayed in the character of the aesthetic effect, isinherent in such combination.

As we see, the fusion of these notions(alive-not alive) is of great importance for sacred texts where it ensures aduplicate tendency peculiar to the adept’s attitude towards the cult object andserves as one of the principal devices in corresponding ethical dogmatics,leading its adherents to mastering certain forms of behaviour. At the sametime, such neutralization in antiquity went beyond the scope of the orthodoxcult. It marks the early stage of natural science and philosophy beginning withtimes when mythopoetic and scientific thought were closely linked to each other(Yājnavalkya, Uddālaka, Heraclitus, Thales) and is preserved inscientific and philosophical constructions of our time. Absolutely differentaspects of culture are influenced by it: abstract philosophical speculations,more concrete views on physiology and psychology, ideas of the nature ofaesthetic reaction, of comic effect etc. — and in numerous cases the roots ofthese constructions can be traced to testimonies of archaic myths and rituals,to a long literary tradition, beginning with the oldest religious andmythopoetic texts.

We shall point out in this connection severalexamples of artistic fiction. They display partly a functional affinity to somesources cited above and partly suggest new aspects of the research into thisdichotomy.

The neutralization «alive-not alive»can be directly correlated to psychological and aesthetic constructionsmentioned above (ideas of L.S. Vygotskij close to the theory of catharsis)48. This device is traced here (first ofall on the level of plot) in the genres of tragedy, fable, etc.49. The inseparable combination of theideas of death, burial and birth, fertility, joy was noted in respect to«Gargantua et Pantagruel» of Rabelais (II.1; 3; III.48; IV.17 etc.) treated asa display of «carnival folk world-outlook»50.One can find possible analogies in other traditions. Such are e.g. Quatrains ofOmar Khayyām where ideas of the world’s transitoriness, of overcoming thefear of death, etc. are illustrated consequently by such comparisons as«flesh-clay», «curls-dust», «head (hands, feet) — vessel», etc.; combinationsof this kind form a peculiar leit-motif helping to overcome such dichotomies,and lead (in a certain functional correspondence to speculations cited above)to a specific psychic attitude marked here by the poet’s hedonistic tendency.

Another cycle of examples is connectedwith a widespread image of the doll (buffoon, pulcinella, petruška, etc.)that displays, perhaps most obviously, the dual tragic-comic effect of thecorresponding device. It is rooted in archaic accessories of ritual51 and is variously reflected to our dayin literature and art (especially scenic) — cf. image of Pierrot —Petruška popular in European tradition (play of A. Blok, ballet ofStravinsky, etc.), motif of woman-doll («Sandman» of E.T.A. Hoffmann, andmusical embodiment of the theme in Offenbach’s «Tales of Hoffmann»; «Doll’sHouse» of Ibsen, etc.). This motif, as we know, was correlated with infantiletraits of the mind52. Thelatter sphere suggests another aspect of our problem — interesting material ispresented e.g. by English children’s literature. We mean the phenomenon ofchildren’s «mercilessness» reflected in corresponding genres: see for examplehumorous verses of H. Graham («Ruthless rhymes for heartless homes»)53, a merry obituary in «Ten little niggerboys» etc.54.

Independently of the conceptual andpsychological factors mentioned above the annihilation of the differencebetween «alive» and «not alive», animate and inanimate can be considered as aspecific artistic device — either on more general levels of composition andplot, or in depicting a concrete image of a hero. The examples of such a devicecan be observed already in artistically expressed mythological motifs —connected e.g. with beliefs in reincarnation, transformation of man into ananimal, a plant etc. (see below, N 60 sq. cf; Puruṣasūkta from Ṛgveda(X.90) describing the creation of the world from the members of «primeval man»;a cosmological likening of horse’s limbs (Bṛhadāraṇyaka up.I.1.1), a likening of man’s members and parts of the tree (ibid. III.9.28) etc.55.A similar device can be observed in folk literature56.

In this connection it is worth notingcorresponding feelings in the world-outlook of some artists. The most strikingexample is presented by Rilke, who said that it is the poet’s mission to bindlife and death together57. Some authors expressing correspondingideas in most general aphoristic form can be rather ascribed to the ancientmythopoetic tradition already mentioned — such are aphorisms of Novalis,reflecting his conception of the world as an indissoluble unity of polarities —e.g. «all ashes are pollen, calyx — heaven», «Death is the romanticising principleof our life» etc.58.

Among characteristic examples of usingthis dichotomy as a decisive factor in the semantic structure of the work wecan mention «The Poem of the End» («Poèma konca») of M. Cvetaeva. It wasshown recently that the opposition «life-death» is principal here; in anoteworthy typological affinity with certain archaic conceptions (particularly— Slavic; see above, N 7) it functions here in the context of othersymmetrically contrasted pairs. As a result, the text is based upon contrapositionof similar opposites, related by sense to the general one — respectively:«husband-wife», «dry-wet», «one’s own-alien», etc. The opposition «life-death»logically comes to neutralization in the words: «Life is a place where onecannot live»59.

Turning to more special usage of thisdevice — in outlining separate images — we could mention already«Metamorphoses» of Ovid, where according to its main topic a number oftransformations are based upon coincidences of similarities both (verbal andqualitative) of corresponding signs. Such as, e.g. the description of stonesturning into men (I.400 sq.) — the veins of stones without changing theirdesignation (vena) begin to denote veins of a human body60. Another parallel — in the framework ofItalian dolce stil nuovo — is the image of the Stone Lady in Dante’s verses(with constant word-play on her name Pietra)61.

To cite some examples from modernRussian literature one can refer to Ju. Tynjanov’s prose. Such is theobliteration of distinctions between a monster preserved in a jar and a livingman («The Wax Person»). A peculiar mechanization of heroes’ behaviour istypical for D. Kharms’ artistic manner — it leads (with a certain resemblanceto the English nonsense tradition) to the humorous presentation of violence,accident, death (cf. above, N 53, 54). One can refer to his miniature storieslike «Dream» where the hero is doubled up and thrown away with rubbish,“Falling-out old woman», «Cases», «Accident in the Street», etc. withdeliberately unmotivated, nonsensical endings62.Describing men as inanimate objects often recurs in the prose of Ju.Oleša. His heroes (like Volodja Makarov, Andrej Babičev from «Envy»)now and then petrify, turn into dolls, into robots; they are — «men-things»reminding of an inanimate world, their external activity only makes theirinternal lifelessness more evident63.

There remains another sphere ofcreativity presenting the same combination: figurative art — both sacral (cf.above, N 23) and secular. First of all, one can find here numerousillustrations to corresponding literary themes. Among them — a widespread motifof the «Dance of Death» (Totentanz, Danse macabre) reflected in Europeanmediaeval literature, in folk-theatre (Fastnachtspiel) and in drawings — cf.e.g. a painting of B. Notke (1463); a cycle of engravings by H. Holbein theYounger; from later specimen — picture of F. Rops, etc.64.

Independently of possible literaryparallels and analogies a common device can be traced here: the combining ofthe animate and the inanimate, the organic and the inorganic, the living andthe dead in human traits. Remarkably interesting examples are presented byHieronymus Bosch — cf. his «Alchemic man» (separate drawing and a fragment ofthe right part of the triptych «Garden of delights» (Hell)65. In particular a noteworthy combinationof a man’s head, an egg, and a tree can be mentioned here — an interestingparallel to well-known mythological concepts66.Another example — representation of a man’s head as a part of a landscape by J.de Momper in XVIII century67(cf. above, on macrocosm–microcosm equations). This device in general is verytypical in contemporary works of surrealists. The problem deserves a specialresearch — here we should note only that an analysis of the school’s artisticcredo could be of interest (the role of unconscious associations, of «psychicautomatism» not controlled by common sense68).Such an attitude helps to understand better striking (and perhaps not random)coincidences with some archaic mythological conceptions; furthermore, itreminds us of the therapeutic function of such themes.

To cite several examples, let us nameR. Magritte’s «Perpetual Motion», «Madame Récamier’s perspective» (withthe well-known figure from J.-L. David’s picture replaced by a coffin),«Philosophy in boudoir», «Therapeutist», the cover of the magazine «Minotaurus»(X, 1936)69, M. Ernst’s«Celebes», «Woman in the Wall», «Paramythe», «Sainte Сécilie»70; S. Dali’s «Giraffe in flames», coverof «Minotaurus» (VIII, 1936), «Mae West», where a woman’s face at the same timerepresents an interior71; G.Bellmer’s «Doll» — a construction of wood, metal and papier-maché — aninteresting analogy to the infantile-sadistic motif mentioned above72; Man Ray’s «Priority of matter overthought»73 etc.74. Surrealist drawings rather oftenpresent a combination of a human body and a tree — cf. analogies in variouscosmological concepts and iconography in India (e.g. Buddhism), in ancientGreece (worship of Dionysos), in Bosch’s drawings mentioned above, etc.75. One can refer here to P. Delvaux’«Dawn» with figures of women-trees (cf. motif of dryads of Daphne, etc.), A.Kubin’s «Nietzsche-pillar» etc.76.A psychiatric aspect of such images can also be of interest here (cf. e.g.drawings of S.K.)77.

Further, certain devices in thetechnique of such combination (similarly to corresponding literary examples)can be traced. Such are, among the pictures mentioned above, a clear spatialdemarcation of «alive» and «not alive» in R. Magritte’s «Therapeutist», agradual transition from one to another in H. Bellmer’s «Doll», M. Ernst’s«Women in the Wall» of Man Ray’s «Priority of matter over thought»; fusion ofboth opposites with complete spatial superposition of one upon another — theliving body is rendered here with the aid of «inorganic» material and thepicture can be «read» in two corresponding ways — cf. «Mae West» of S. Dali.The last variant is very effective e.g. in the cycle: «Stones cry» by thePolish artist B. Linke, where human bodies are consequently represented asbeing built of bricks — the device results in a striking animation of Warsaw’sruins and a great expressiveness of drawing (cf. water-colours: «El Molerahmim», «House-warriors», «Image of Job», «Mystery», etc.)78. Separate devices can also be combined— see the application of the first two in Bosch’s «Temptation of St. Antony».The study of such devices within the limits of figurative art or in the broadersphere of artistic fiction, mythology, and history of culture, bears further witnessto the universality and cultural significance of the phenomenon, some aspectsof which have been touched upon here.

Thimme, Vom Sinnder Bilder und Ornamente auf Griechischen Vasen) «Antaios», XI.1970, S. 489 f.32 Cf. combination of skull and animate face in old-Mexicansculpture — F. Anton, Alt Mexico und seine Kunst, Leipzig, 1965, pl.154, 152; modern Mexican holiday («Day of death») etc. See Ivanov, Toporov,Slavjanskie, s. 123 sq.; Baxtin, Tvorčestvo, s. 58 sq. a.o. About theproblem of ritual laughter, particularly laughter connected with the perceptionof death (cf. so-called «sardonic laughter», ancient testimony of Strabo XVI,4.17 about an Egyptian tribe accompanying his funerals with laughter, similarcustoms in Ukraine etc.) see Propp, Ritual’nyi smex v fol’klore — «Fol’klor idejstvitel’nost’», M., 1976, s. 188 sq. In connection with this custom one canremind of a similar attitude displaying itself in the modern genre of «humorousepitaphy» — its most typical examples are found in Anglo-Saxon tradition (cf. Asmall book of grave humour, London, 1979). See also: Abram Terc, V teniGogolja. London, 1975, p. 149, 170 sq.33 Cf. a noteworthy precept to samnyāsin in «Laws of Manu»(Mānavadharmaśāstra VI. 45): nābhinandeta maraṇaṃnābhinandeta jīvitam — «Let him not crave for death, let him notcrave for life».34 Cf. conception of myth as a device for neutralization ofopposites (A.M. Pjatigorskij, Nekotorye obščie zamečanijaо mifologii s točki zrenija psixologa — «Uč. zap. Tartuskogo gos.un-ta», vyp. 185, Tartu 1965, s, 44–45.35 Cf. Principal Upaniṣads, p. 757.36 Cf. also Bṛhadaraṇyaka up. IV.3.22 — about identityof killer and non-killer. See J. Jorens, Death in the Upaniṣads —«Journal of the Oriental Institute», Baroda, vol. 14, 1965, N 3–4, p. 297 sq.; Idem.The development of the idea of immortality in the Upaniṣads — ibid., vol.16, 1966, N 1, p. 1 sq.; P. Horsch, Vorstuben des IndischenSeelenvanderungslehre. — «Asiatische Studien», 24, 1971, S. 132 sq.37 One can refer here to another idea peculiar to Hinduistdogmatics: losing perception of continuity, annihilation of time in the higheststate — cf. images of the lowest, «incarnated» (mūrta), and the highest,«not incarnated» (amūrta) Brahmans identified respectively as «time» and«timeless» (kālaś cākālaś ca — Maitrī up. VI.15;cf. ibid., VI.3; Brhadāranyaka up. I.3. 1 — see Principal Upaniṣads,p. 828 a.o.); an image of immobile sun symbolizing in Chāndogya up.III.11.1 sq. rescue of beings etc. Cf. J. Scheftelowit, Die Zeit alsSchicksals-Gottheit in der indischen und iranischen Religion (Kalā undZruvan), Stuttgart, 1929, S. 10 sq.; H. Zimmer, Some aspects of time inIndian art — «Journal of the Indian Society of Oriental Arts», June 1933, p. 30sq.; M. Eliade, Time and Eternity in Indian thought — «Man and Time.Papers from the Eranos yearbooks», vol. III, N. Y., 1957, p. 186 sq. See alsoabout ties between notions of time and death: H. Plessner, On therelation of Time to Death. «Man and Time. Papers from Eranos Yearbooks», vol.III, p. 233–263; N. Brown, Life against death. The psychoanalyticalmeaning of history. L., 1970, p. 102.38 See M. Eliade, The Sacred and the profane. The nature ofreligion, N. Y., 1961, p. 167 sq. (Sanctification of Life). Regardingsystematization of similar correlations in different cultures see a very usefultable in: V.N. Toporov, О structure nekotoryx arxaičeskix tekstov,sootnosimyx s koncepciej «mirovogo dereva» — «Uč. zap. Tartuskogo un-ta»,vyp. 284, Tartu, 1971, s. 46–47 sq. Cf. A.Ja. Syrkin, Nekotorye problemyizučenija upanišad M., 1971, s. 249 sq.39 See e.g. H. Zimmer, Tod und Wiedergeburt in IndischenLicht — «Eranos Jahrbuch, 1939», Zürich 1940, S. 251–289 (particularly p.181 — about ties connecting such beliefs with macrocosm equations). Fornumerous parallels from Slavic tradition (including specific funeral rites) offollowing the dead to the yonder world — cf. Veleckaja,Jazyčeskaja, p. 15 sq., 33 sq., 202 sq. Some of these rites present anoteworthy tendency contrary to the «mortification» of living image mentionedabove (in Buddhist and other traditions) — to preserve in a certain manner thedead’s relics by «vitalizing» them — «from the earliest cavemen, who kept theirdead alive by dyeing the bones red... down to the Hollywood funeral cult»(Brown, Life, p. 95). These two devices we may call correspondingly«homoeopathic» and «allopathic» therapies of death.40 Heraclitus, The cosmic fragments, ed. by G.S. Kirk,Cambridge, 1962, p. 65 sq., 135 sq. a.o.41 Among the works analysing Heraclitus’ dichotomies see A.Rivier, L’homme et l’experience humaine dans les fragmentsd’Heraclite — «Museum Helveticum», v. 13, 1956, p. 155–164; G.S.Kirk, Man and Opposites in Heraclitus — ibid., v. 14, 1957, p. 155–163; A.Jeanniere, La pensee d’Heraclite d’Ephese,Paris, 1959, p. 77 sq., Toporov, K istorii, p. 2038–2039, 2045, etc.42 Vita Philosophorum. Thales I.35 (Diogenes Laertius, Livesof eminent philosophers, ed. by R.D. Hick, v. I. London, Cambridge, 1950, p.36–38).43 Leonardo da Vinci, Frammenti letterari e filosofici,trascelti dal E. Solmi, Firenze, 1900, p. 167 sq.44 See: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci, ed. by J. P. Richter,vol. II, N. Y., 1970, p. 129; 291. In the last aphorism one can notice somerepetitions characteristic for the organisation of the text on the phoneticlevel (desiderio... desiderî... desiderate... desidera... desiderio...desidera... medesimo desiderio... l’uomo e modello dello mondo). M.Bachtin (Tvorčestvo, s. 58) supposes that this aphorism is based upon «carnivalworld-outlook». Compare it with almost word-for-word repetition in Sanskritpoetry (Rāmāyana II.105, 22–23: nandantyudita ādityenandantyastamite ’pi ca ātmano nāvabudhyante manuṣyājīvitakṣayam // hṛṣyantyṛtumukhaṃ dṛṣṭvānavaṃ navamivāgatam ṛtūṇām parivartenaprāṇināṃ prāṇasaṃkṣaya — also withartistic sound-repetitions; cf. Indische Sprüche, Hrsg. v. O.Böhtlingk, St. Petersburg, 1863, I Th., S. 216; III Th. S. 355.).45 G.W. Hegel, Science of Logic, tr. by W.H. Johnson andL.G. Struthers, L. 1929, I, 142.46 S. Freud, Jenseits des Lustprinzips, Leipzig, Wien, 1923,S. 49’ sq., a.o.: Das Ziel alles Lebens ist der Tod... das gesamte Trieblebender Herbeiführung des Todes dient (S. 52–53); see ibid., on p. 53–54noteworthy parallels to ideas of «one’s own death» (cf. R.M. Rilke, A. Malrauxa.o. — above, N 4) connected with instinct of self-preservation: «es sindparzialtriebe, dazu bestimmt, den eigenen Todesweg des Organismus zu sichern...Es erübrigt dass der Organismus nur auf seine Weise sterben will.» Cf.Brown, Life, p. 91, 94 sq. about Greek pre-Socratic philosophers (includingHeraclitus) as a model for Freud’s speculations.47 H. Bergson, Le rire. Essai sur la signification ducomique. Paris, 1950, p. 8, 17 sq., 35 sq. etc.; cf. R. Johnson, Tworealms of a joke: bisociation theories of joking — «Semiotica», v. 16, N 3,1976, p. 197 sq. Anticipating some further remarks we can recall well-knownsimilar devices in artistic fiction making heroes comic — likening them toinanimate objects (cf. below), duplicating them with a certain reiteration andautomatism of behaviour following from it. The last device is e.g. often usedby N. Gogol’, displaying itself already on onomastical level — such are hispersonages’ pairs: Bočinskij-Dobčinskij, Mitjaj-Minjaj, etc. (cf. V.Ja.Prop, Problema smexa i komizma — Uč. zap. LGU, N 355, Serija filolog.nauk, vyp. 76, 1971, s. 162 sq.; idem. Problemy komizma i smexa, M.,1976, s. 54 sq. At the same time, one may refer to cases where the device ofduplication playing a mechanizing and «mortifying» role leads to an effectwhich is tragic rather than comic (the case typical for Ju. Tynjanov’s novel«Smert’ vazirmuxtara» — see apt remarks in: V. Belinkov, Jurij Tynjanov, M.,1965, s. 244 sq.). Cf. also: Abram Terc, V teni Gogolja, p. 301 sq.; 518 sq.48 Aristotelis De Arte poetica liber. Rec. R. Cassel, Oxonii, 1968,1449b; cf. Vygotskij, Psixologija, s. 100 sq., 255 sq., 278 sq., 305 sq., 311sq., and others.49 Cf. e.g. combinations like «perishing-joy», «killing-notkilling», etc., observed in Shakespeare’s «Hamlet»; in fables of I.A. Krylovetc. See Vygotskij, Psixologija, s. 165, 185 sq., 243 a.o.; cf. also Ivanov,Toporov, Slavjanskie, s. 124, N 171 about laughing at death (sf. above, N 32)in denouements of Shakespeare’s tragedies, noted by B. Pasternak (B.Pasternak, Zametki к perevodam šekspirovskiix tragedij —«Literaturnaja Moskva», M., 1956, s. 807.50 See: Baxtin, Tvorčestvo, s. 354 sq., 442 sq. a.o. Cf.ibid., s. 58: «Death is a part of life’s wholeness here, is a necessary elementof it, a condition for constant renovation and rejuvenation of life. Deathalways corresponds here to birth, the grave to earth’s womb giving birth». Theauthor reminds us here of Leonardo da Vinci’s thoughts (see above, N 44) and ofmemorable lines from Goethe’s «Faust»: «Geburt und Grab, Ein ewiges Meer, Einwechselnd Weben, Ein glühend Leben» (cf. a characteristic sound-play:g-b-r — g-r-b of notions correlated).51 Cf. about the role of masque: Baxtin, Tvorčestvo, s. 47. Onthe other hand, we meet it already in ancient Greek didactics — cf. about manas god’s doll (θαῦμα) in Plato’s Laws (644D; cf. ibid. 803C). Anotion of a puppet or plaything ruled by the Highest Being often recurs in theworld literature (cf. e.g. Mahābhārata, V. 39. 1; Plautus, Captivi23; D.I. Fonvizin, Epistle to my servants, a.o.) up to the modern genreof science fiction. Cf. in this connection: W. Blum, KleistsMarionettentheater und das Drahtpuppengleichnis bei Platon — «Zeitschriftfür Religions- und Geistesgeschichte», Bd. 23. 1971. S. 40–49; I.Linder, Za strokoj Omara Xajjama — «Voprosy literatury», 1978, N 9, s.254–259 etc.52 Compare with Th. Reik’s analysis of the three women’s images inthe opera of Offenbach mentioned above (Th. Reik, The Search within. Theinner experiences of a psychoanalyst, N. Y., 1956, p. 442 sq.).53 Cf. for example: «Making toast at the fireside, Nurse fell inthe grate and died; And what makes it ten times worse, All the toast was burntwith nurse» («Misfortunes never come singly» — An anthology of Children’sliterature, M.–L., 1965, p. 157).54 Cf. S. Èjzenštein, Charlie the Kid —«Izbrannye proizvedenija», t. 5, M., 1968, s. 512 sq. (see ibid., remarks aboutCexov’s novel, «Sleepytime», about analogous observations of Leo Tolstoj etc.).Typical phrases of children were compiled by K. Čukovskij (see: «Ot dvuxdo pjati» (From two to five), M., 1957, s. 138 sq., e.g. boastful reaction atthe sight of solemn funerals: «My daddy will be carried like that soon!» or anxiousquestion of little daughter to her mother, saying she will die and be burnt —«And what will become of your shoes?» About humorous epitaph, see above, note32. Many examples of a similar «obituary» are presented in the genre oflimerick — cf. «There was a young lady of Niger...», «There was a young fellowfrom Tyne...», «A cute debutant from St. Paul...», etc. (The Pan book oflimericks, ed. by L. Untermeyer, L., 1963, p. 29, 46, 153 a.o.).55 Principal Upanisads, p. 149 sq., 243 sq. Cf. e.g. Toporov, ОStrukture, s. 24 sq.56 See e.g. a likening of parts of the tree and members of a personkilled in a Transcarpathian ballad (Veleckaja, Jazyčeskaja, s. 33–34).57 Cf. another saying of his: «Whoever rightly understands andcelebrates death at the same time magnifies life» — See W. Rehm,Orpheus. Der Dichter und die Toten, Dusseldorf, 1950, p. 583. cf. Brown, Life,p. 101.58 Cf. A. Carlsson, Die Fragmente des Novalis. Basel, 1939;N. Besset, Novalis et la pensee mystique, Paris, 1947.59 See O.G. Revzina, Iz nabljudenij nad semantičeskojstrukturoj «Poemy konca» M. Cvetaevoj — «Uč. zap. Tartuskogo gos.Un-ta», vyp. 422, Tartu, 1977, s. 62 sq., especially 81.60 Cf. Ju. Ščeglov, Nekotorye čerty struktury«Metamorfoz» Ovidija — «Strukturno-tipolopgičeskije issledovanija». M.,1962, s. 161 sq.61 Cf. I.N. Goleniščev-Kutuzov, Stixi о KamennojDame — «Dante i vsemirnaja literatura», M., 1967, s. 72 sq.62 See: Daniil Kharms, Izbrannoe (Selected works). Würzburg,1974, s. 48 sq.63 M.O. Čudakova Poetika Jurija Oleši —«Voprosy literatury», 1968, N 4, str. 131; eadem: Masterstvo Jurija Oleši,M., 1972, s. 64.64 Cf. H. Rosenfeld, Der mittelalterliche Totentanz:Entstehung, Entwicklung, Bedeutung, Münster, 1954; S. Cosachi,Makabertanz: der Totentanz in Kunst, Poesie und Brauchtum des Mittelalters,Meisenheim am Glan, 1965; Povesti о spore, s. 3 sq., a.o. See: DerTotentanz, Vierzig Holzschnitte von Hans Holbein dem Jüngeren miteiner Einl. v. J. Springer, Berlin, 1907; cf. V. Friče, Poezijakošmarov i užasa, M., 1912, s. 188–189, 199, 227, 251, 288–289 (cf. ibid.,s. 255, 308–309 pictures of F. Rops and A. Beardsley illustrating the puppetmotif). The theme is reflected in music also — cf. vocal cycle of M. Musorgskij«Songs and dances of Death» with characteristic titles of separate songs(«Lullaby», «Serenade», «Trepak» — cf. L. Žukova-Minenko,Tragičeskoe i komišeskoe v tvoršestve M.P. Musorgskogo —«Voprosy teorii i estetiki muzyki», vyp. 14, L., 1975, s. 46. Theproblem of the «alive — not alive» dichotomy in musical art cannot be examinedhere — we should like to name only one, perhaps the greatest, reflection of oneof its variants «Love-Death» in Wagner’s «Tristan and Isolde», where theseopposites are dissolved and fused in the leit-motif of langour (Sehnsucht)permeating the entire musical drama. (Cf. e.g. E. Kurth. RomantischeHarmonik und ihre Krise in Wagner’s «Tristan». Berlin, 1923).65 J. Combe, Jerome Bosch. Paris 1957, pl. 90, 94–95;cf. R.L. Delevoy, Bosch. Geneve, 1960, p. 82–83 — details of thecentral part of the triptych «Temptation of St. Anthony».66 Cf. F.D.K. Bosch, The golden germ. An introduction toIndian symbolism, ’s Gravenhage, 1960, p. 51 sq.; Toporov, Кrekonstrukcii mifa, s. 85 sq.67 M. Jean, Histoire de la peinture surrealiste,Paris, 1959, p. 235.68 Cf. words of A. Breton, analogies with Novalis’ idea of«wonderful unity of the most alien objects», etc. — Knaurs Lexicon ModernerKunst, München, Zürich, 1955, S. 291–292; A. Schrneller,Surrealismus, Wien, 1956, S. 9. See: Surrealists on Art, ed. by L.R. Liprard,N. Y. 1970. p. 10 sq.; Surrealism, ed. by H. Read, N. Y.–Washington, 1971, p.29 sq.; A. Breton, Mainifestoes of Surrealism, Ann Arbor, 1974, 3 sq.;«Psychoanalytical notes on modern art» — in: R. Hülsenbeck. Memoirs of aDada-drummer, N. Y., 1974, p. 149 sq., a.o.69 See respectively: Jean, Histoire, p. 176 (cf. ibid., 184–185),353 (an analogous substitute is found in his «perspective» of E. Manet’s«Balcony» — cf. P. Waldberg, Rene Magritte, Bruxelles, 1965, p.89; ibid., p. 47: «Par une belle fin d’apres midi»); 193;Schmeller, Surrealismus, Taf. 15; Jean, Histoire, p. 241 a.o. See also hispictures «La condition humaine» (Waldberg, Rene Magritte, p. 70; idem,Surrealism, Lausanne, 1962, p. 82) with neutralization of the oppositionbetween «living» and «drawn» nature.70 Jean, Histoire, p. 95: Schmeller, Surrealismus, Taf. 5; E.Trier, Max Ernst. III. 9.26;Chāndogya up. VI.11.1–3 a.o.); see R. Much, Holz und Mensch,Wörter und Sachen. Bd. I, 1909, S. 39 f.; A.K. Seifert, Gut andBüse als Antinomie und Polarität — «Der Archetyp, The Archetype,Verh. des 2 Intern. Kongr. für analytische Psychologie, Zürich 1962»,Basel–New York, 1964, p. 68 sq.; A.M. 3 Ivanov, Toporov, Slavjanskie, s. 116, 133, 180 sq.; A.Ja. Syrkin, К xarakteristike induistskogo panteona — «Uč. zap.Tartuskogo gos. un-ta», vyp. 309, Oriental Studies, II, Tartu, 1973, s. 173, N3.

4 Cf. e.g., its (totalization in the contraposition «to die one’sown death — to die an alien death» (V.V. Ivanov, V.N. Toporov, Krekonstrukcii praslavjanskogo teksta — «Slavjanskoje jazykoznanie. Dokladysovetskoi delegacii. V Meždunarodnyj s’ezd slavistov», M, 1963; idem.Slavjanskie, s. 159.

5 Cf. Śamkara’s explanation of “lindu” (picchala) inChāndogya upaniṣad, VIII.14.1 as a name for the maternal womb — asource of birth and death (Čxandog’ja upanišada, M., 1965, s. 234).

6 See, for example, on the role of such dichotomy in theconscience of modern youth: D. Gutman, The premature gerontocracy:themes of aging and death in the youth culture — «Social Research», Albany,1972, vol. 39, N 3, p. 416–448.

(a rich material on Slavictradition); idem. Issledovanija v oblasti slavjanskix drevnostej, M., 1974, s.73 a.o., especially — table on p. 259 sq.; V.V. Ivanov, Dvoičnajasimvoličeskaja klassifikacija v afrikanskix i aziatskix tradicijax —«Narody Azii i Afriki», 1969, N 5, s. 106, 108, 112; M. Baxtin,Tvorcestvo Fransua Rable i narodnaja kul’tura srednevekov’ja i renessansa, M.,1965, s. 58, 354 sq. a.o.

9 Cf. Le Renou, L’ambiguité du vocabulaire du Ṛgveda— «Journal Asiatique», t. 231, 1939, p. 161–235; M. Fowler, Polarity inthe RigVeda — «The Review of religion», v. VII, N 2, 1943. p. 115 sq.; J.Gonda, Stylistic repetitions in the Veda, Amsterdam, 1959, p. 87 sq.; A.Syrkin, K xarakteristike, s. 148–188.

Toporov, О nekotoryxosobennostjax xettskix ritualov s učastiem salŠU.GI [J1] v svjazi s paralleljami iz drugixtradicij — «Uč. zap. Tartuskogo gos. un-ta», vyp. 201, Oriental Studies I,Tartu, 1968, s. 291sq.

11 Cf. in this connection: J. Hillman, Senex and puer. Anaspect of the historical and psychological present. — «Eranos Jahrbuch 1967»,Zürich, 1968, p. 301–360.

12 Der Rig-Veda aus dem Sanskrit ins Deutsche übers. und miteinem laufenden Kommentar versehen v. K.F. Geldner, I Teil, Cambridge,Mass., 1951. S. 197, Anm. 2; 360–361. Anm. 96.

13 Cf. A Bergaigne, La religion védiqued’après des hymnes de Rig-Veda, Paris, 1963, t. I, p. 7 sq., t. II. p.461 sq. a.o.; Macdonell, Vedic, p. 30 sq.; Renou, L’ambiguitè, p. 224; E.W.Hopkins, Epic Mythology, Strassburg, 1915, p. 84 sq.; Eliade,Trattato, p. 145 sq.; A. Ja. Syrkin, Černoje solnce — «Kr.Soobšč. In-ta narodov Azii», 80, 1965, s. 20 sq.

14 Cf. A.A. Potebnja, О mifičeskom značeniinekotoryx obrjadov i poverij, M., 1865, s. 34; N.N. Veleckaja,Jazyčeskaja simvolika slavjanskix arxaičeskix ritualov, M., 1978, s.23 sq.

15 J. Gonda, Epithets in the Ṛgveda, s’Gravenhage,1959, p. 191.

16 Hopkins, Epic, p. 202 sq.

17 Cf. E. Baumgartel, Tomb and feritility — «Jahrbuchfür Kleinasiatisches Forschung,» Bd. I, 1950, S. 56 sq.; V.Ja.Propp, Russkie agrarnye prazdniki, L., 1963, s. 16 sq. etc. The idea iswell known from its Evangelic reflection (John 12.24: In truth, in very truth Itell you, a grain of wheat remains a solitary grain unless it falls into theground and dies, but if it dies it bears a rich harvest). This motif oftenrecurs — with transference of grain’s qualities to human behaviour and fate —in religious and secular tradition. 28 We shall briefly refer here to one aspect of this problemimportant in the history of culture. The notion of analytical dissection of theliving body as mortifying during the analysis has a noteworthy echo inscientific methodology. A corresponding analytical procedure applied in thehumanitarian sphere (particularly to an artistic work) inevitably «disturbs»its object, characterised by certain integral qualities (cf. to some degreeanalogous «disturbance» caused by an instrument to the object of physicalstudy) and thus often meets with objections. The case is well known in thehistory of development of corresponding humanitarian branches (e.g. «formal»method in literary studies, semiotics etc.) where similarly to natural sciencesa principle of complementarity of different descriptions should be introduced(cf. N. Bohr, Atomic physics and human knowledge, L., 1957; idem.Physical Science and the Study of religions — «Studia Orientalia Ioanni Pedersen».Hauniae, 1953, p. 385–390). It is interesting that the nature of suchinterference was clearly felt and reflected in classical literature. See e.g.lines from Puškin’s «Mozart and Salieri»: «Having mortified sounds Idissected music like a corpse, I examined harmony by algebra» (the last wordshave entered Russian phraseology).

(резюме)

 

Онсказал, что между жизнью и смертью нет разницы.

-«Почему же ты не умрешь?» - спросили его.

-«Именно поэтому», - сказал Фалес.

ДиогенЛаэрций. О жизни философов.

I.35.(пер. М.Л. Гаспарова)

 

Заметки затрагивают некоторые аспектыуниверсального в мировой культуре противопоставления, с древности и до нашихдней сохраняющего первостепенное значение в системе поведения человека — егорелигии, творчестве, повседневной жизни. Отмечены некоторые семантическиродственные пары: «жизнь — смерть», «бессмертие — смерть», «рождение — смерть»и т.д.

В центре внимания примеры нейтрализацииуказанного противопоставления в ее связи с достижением совершенства,освобождения (принцип coincidentia oppositorum — «совпаденияпротивоположностей» — в религии, философии). Приводятся свидетельстваиндуистских (Ригведа, упанишады), буддийских, православных, католическихтекстов, характерные афоризмы Гераклита (фрагменты 21, 50, 62 и др.), запискиЛеонардо да Винчи.

Интересны в этом плане основополагающие идеиАнри Бергсона — противопоставление творческого, органического начала(élan vital, évolution creatrice) механическому искусственному,неорганическому. Совмещением их он объяснял феномен смешного. Другой примерсвязан с эстетикой Л.С. Выготского.

И наконец — ряд характерных образов в разныхжанрах творчества в Европе и России: «Метаморфозы» Овидия, «танец смерти»(Гольбейн Младший), женщина –кукла (Гофман, Оффенбах), Пьеро - Петрушка (Блок,Стравинский), художники –сюрреалисты (Тынянов, Хармс).
